Study in Australia from Your Country — Document Prep Guides | YouSafe 
Skip to main content Country of citizenship
Study in Australia from your country — document prep
Hub only. We are not shipping two hundred thin /from/[slug]/ pages. The notes below cover frequent sending countries: funds-proof patterns, police certificates, and Genuine Student issues. Procedure checklists stay on the legal panel.
India
Funds often mix education-loan sanction letters, sponsor ITR, and bank statements. Genuine Student answers should explain why this CRICOS course, not a US F-1 SOP. Police certificates and name-variation on passports are common upload issues.
Nepal
Sponsor capacity and relationship evidence get read closely. Keep CoE, OSHC, and the GS answers consistent with the same sponsor. We do not promise processing times; Home Affairs publishes those.
China
Notarial translations and hukou / relationship documents for dependants are frequent extras. English-test timing must match the CoE. GS is not a personal-statement essay.
Philippines
NBI clearance timing and employment certificates for GS work-history answers. Packaged English plus a VET or degree CoE should sit in one folder.
Vietnam
Sponsor bank books and relationship evidence. Translate consistently. Genuine Student should address why Australia and why this provider, not a recycled Canada study-permit SOP.
Nigeria
Funds source, name consistency across WAEC / degree certificates, and police character documents. GS answers must match the occupation story if the course is vocational.
Continue to Subclass 500 prep , GS workshop , or the study sequence .
Book country-specific prep

Genuine Student (GS) evidence preparation
Genuine Student replaced Genuine Temporary Entrant on 23 March 2024. This page is a document workshop: what to gather so the four short GS answers match CoE, funds, and work history. It is not a US statement of purpose and not a recycled GTE essay. Home Affairs reads consistency. We do not write answers that invent a biography.
What the workshop does
Map each GS prompt to evidence you already have: offer, CoE, transcripts, employment letters, sponsor documents.
Flag mismatches (course vs work history, funds vs claimed sponsor, packaged English dates vs principal CoE).
Keep answers inside Home Affairs' word limits. We do not pad them into a Canadian SOP.
Send the file to a licensed Australian lawyer on the YouSafe legal panel when the story needs legal review — refusal risk, prior visas, or dependants.

1. Introduction
YouSafe Consultancy, operated by Youssef Hammoud and based in Online, Australia, is committed to protecting your privacy. This Privacy Policy explains how we collect, use, disclose, and safeguard your personal information when you use our study document preparation, education planning, and settlement support services. We comply with the Privacy Act 1988 and the Australian Privacy Principles (APPs) and applicable Australian privacy laws.
2. Information We Collect
We collect information that you provide directly to us, including:
Personal identification information (name, date of birth, nationality, passport details)
Contact information (email address, phone number, mailing address)
Educational background and employment history
Immigration history and travel documents
Financial information for proof of funds documentation
Payment information for processing fees
Communications between you and our team

We use the information we collect to:
Provide study document preparation, education planning, and settlement support services
Communicate with you about your case and our services
Process payments and maintain financial records
Help organize materials for Department of Home Affairs and educational institutions when requested by you
Comply with legal obligations and regulatory requirements
Improve our services and client experience
4. Information Sharing and Disclosure
We do not sell, trade, or rent your personal information to third parties. We may share your information only in the following circumstances: with government agencies (such as Department of Home Affairs) when you authorize us to help with document submission or support; with educational institutions as part of your admission applications; with service providers who assist us in operating our business (subject to confidentiality agreements); and when required by law, court order, or government regulation.
5. Data Security
We implement appropriate technical and organizational measures to protect your personal information against unauthorized access, alteration, disclosure, or destruction. This includes encrypted storage of sensitive documents, secure communication channels, and restricted access to client files. However, no method of transmission over the Internet is 100% secure, and we cannot guarantee absolute security.
6. Data Retention
We retain your personal information for as long as necessary to fulfill the purposes for which it was collected, typically for seven (7) years after the conclusion of your case. This retention period allows us to comply with legal requirements, resolve disputes, and enforce our agreements. After this period, your information will be securely deleted or anonymized.

Initial consultation fees are non-refundable once the consultation has taken place. If you cancel a scheduled consultation at least 48 hours in advance, you may reschedule at no additional cost or receive a full refund. Refunds for service packages are calculated based on the work completed at the time of cancellation:
Before work begins: 90% refund (10% administrative fee) 
Document review stage: 70% refund 
Application preparation stage: 50% refund 
After application submission: No refund 
4. Government Fees
Government fees paid to Australian Department of Home Affairs (immigration authority) or other government agencies are non-refundable through YouSafe Consultancy. These fees are paid directly to the government and are subject to their own refund policies. We are not responsible for refunding any government fees.

If your visa, student visa, or immigration application is refused by Department of Home Affairs or any other government authority, you are not entitled to a refund of our consulting fees. However, we offer discounted rates for re-applications if you choose to apply again with our assistance.

Skip to main content Canada Study Permit Guide
Canada Study Permit Guide for Algeria
This page gives Algerian students the precise Canada study permit steps, from letter of acceptance to IRCC decision, with checks that reduce delays.
Algeria is a major francophone-African source country for Canadian study permits, with consistently high application volumes, according to IRCC.
A Canada study permit from Algeria runs through the standard study permit stream. Algeria sends large numbers of French-speaking applicants, and it is a focus of Canada's francophone-recruitment effort. Algeria was eligible for the Student Direct Stream before it closed in November 2024, so the expedited route some Algerian applicants used is gone, and everyone now files through the standard process. There is no interview; an IRCC officer decides the case on the documents you submit.
The steps are clear. A Canada study permit from Bangladesh runs through the standard study permit stream. Bangladesh was never part of the Student Direct Stream, so the closure of that fast-track route in November 2024 changed nothing procedural for Bangladeshi applicants. They have always used the standard process. There is no interview; an IRCC officer decides the case on the documents you submit.
The steps are clear. You receive a letter of acceptance from a designated learning institution, obtain the Provincial Attestation Letter your province issues, prepare proof of funds, complete the online application, and give biometrics. For Bangladeshi applicants, the funding evidence and a coherent study plan are the two things an officer weighs most heavily, so prepare both with care.
Where you apply
Bangladeshi applicants generally submit online via IRCC and attend biometrics at VACs serving Bangladesh. Verify locations and booking steps on official VFS/IRCC pages only.
Financial evidence
Officers look for credible liquid funds and sponsor income aligned to the LOA. Education loans help when personal balances are limited but must match the study period.

VAC appointment demand near popular intakes.
Unexplained deposits before filing.
Weak study-plan narratives for program changes.

LOA → PAL/CAQ if required → funds → IRCC apply → biometrics → medical if asked → decision letter / POE letter handling.

Upload clear, complete PDFs—blurry bank scans cause delays.
GIC use should be documented with certificates that match applicant identity.

Canada Study Permit Guide for Brazil
This page gives Brazilian students the exact Canada study permit workflow, from letter of acceptance to IRCC decision, with checks that prevent delays.
Brazil had 7,015 study permit holders in Canada at the end of 2024, down from 10,370 in 2023, a consistent top source country from Latin America, according to IRCC.
A Canada study permit from Brazil now runs through the standard study permit stream. Brazil was eligible for the Student Direct Stream, the fast-track route that closed in November 2024, so Brazilian applicants have lost the expedited channel and now file through the standard process. There is no interview; an IRCC officer decides the case on the documents you submit.
The steps are clear. You receive a letter of acceptance from a designated learning institution, obtain the Provincial Attestation Letter your province issues, prepare proof of funds, complete the online application, and give biometrics. Brazilian demand includes a large share of language and shorter-term programs alongside college and university study, and an officer wants the study plan to make sense whatever the program length.
Where you apply
Brazilian applicants typically apply online through IRCC and complete biometrics at VACs serving Brazil. Confirm city coverage on official channels before interstate travel.
Financial evidence
Present liquid funds and sponsor proof matched to the LOA. Currency movement between real and CAD should still leave a clear available-funds story.
Common challenges for Brazil applicants
FX changes after bank letters are issued.
Document translation needs for Portuguese civil papers when requested.
Medical exam timing if IRCC issues a request.
Process and interview notes
Assemble LOA/PAL, funds, and identity documents; submit IRCC application; complete biometrics; monitor the portal.
Local facts for Brazil applicants
Refresh bank evidence if balances drop materially before a decision.
Use the same name order as the passport on every upload.

Skip to main content Canada Study Permit Guide
Canada Study Permit Guide for France
This page gives French students the precise Canada study permit steps, from letter of acceptance to IRCC decision, with checks that reduce delays.
France is one of Canada's largest Western European source countries for international students, with consistently strong study permit volumes, according to IRCC.
A Canada study permit from France sits at the centre of Canada's francophone-recruitment strategy. Canada actively courts French-speaking students, and that shapes the experience for French applicants in a way it does not for many other countries. France was never part of the Student Direct Stream, so its closure in November 2024 had little practical effect; French applicants have always used the standard study permit stream. There is no interview; an IRCC officer decides the case on your documents.
The steps are clear. You receive a letter of acceptance from a designated learning institution, obtain the Provincial Attestation Letter your province issues, prepare proof of funds, complete the online application, and give biometrics. If you plan to study in Quebec, you also need a Quebec Acceptance Certificate, the CAQ, before the federal study permit.
Where you apply
Applicants in France usually file online and complete biometrics at VACs serving France. Confirm the city list on official IRCC/VFS pages before booking trains or flights.
Financial evidence
EUR bank evidence, parent support, and any French student-loan or savings proof should map to LOA tuition plus Canadian living-cost guidance for the study period.
Common challenges for France applicants
Assuming Schengen mobility experience replaces Canadian study-permit evidence.
Currency conversion that understates living costs IRCC expects.
Quebec CAQ steps missed when the DLI is in Quebec.
Process and interview notes
LOA (+ CAQ for Quebec) → IRCC filing → biometrics in France → medical if requested → decision. Keep bilingual document labels clear when mixing French and English PDFs.
Local facts for France applicants
Quebec programs need CAQ sequencing before or alongside the federal permit—confirm current MIFI rules.
Prior European study helps the story only when funds and program fit are also strong.

This page gives Hong Kong students the full Canada study permit path, from letter of acceptance to IRCC decision, with checks that reduce delays.
Hong Kong is a consistent source of Canadian study permit holders, supported by deep migration ties and dedicated immigration measures, according to IRCC.
A Canada study permit from Hong Kong runs through the standard study permit stream, but it sits within a wider set of options. Canada has dedicated immigration measures for Hong Kong residents, including permanent-residence pathways and an open work permit for recent graduates, which makes a study permit a recognised first step toward working and settling in Canada. Hong Kong was never part of the Student Direct Stream, so its closure in November 2024 changed nothing procedural. There is no interview; an IRCC officer decides on your documents.
The steps are clear. You receive a letter of acceptance from a designated learning institution, obtain the Provincial Attestation Letter your province issues, prepare proof of funds, complete the online application, and give biometrics. Because the Hong Kong measures have their own rules and timelines, confirm the current details on the IRCC site before you build a longer-term plan around them.

Financial evidence
HKD bank evidence and sponsor proof should map to LOA tuition and Canadian living costs. Label multi-currency accounts clearly.

Assuming prior overseas study alone proves purpose of study in Canada.
Split funding across parents and self without a single coherent narrative.
Quebec CAQ missed for Quebec DLIs.

This page gives Indian students the full Canada study permit path, from letter of acceptance to IRCC decision, with checks that reduce refusal risk.
India had 188,630 study permit holders in Canada at the end of 2024, down from 278,065 in 2023, remaining the single largest source country, according to IRCC.
A Canada study permit from India looks different now than it did two years ago. India was the heaviest user of the Student Direct Stream, the fast-track route that closed in November 2024. Every Indian applicant now files through the standard study permit stream, where timelines are more variable and the documentary review is the whole game. There is no interview; an IRCC officer decides the case on the file you submit.
The steps are clear. You receive a letter of acceptance from a designated learning institution, obtain the Provincial Attestation Letter your province issues, gather proof of funds, complete the online application, and give biometrics. The work that decides the outcome is the quality of three things: your funding evidence, a study plan that makes sense, and clear ties to India.
Where you apply
Most study-permit applications from India are submitted online through an IRCC secure account. After you apply you may need biometrics at a VAC in cities such as New Delhi, Mumbai, Chandigarh, Hyderabad, Kolkata, or Bengaluru—confirm current VAC locations on the official VFS/IRCC channels for India before you travel between states.
Financial evidence
Indian study-permit files are reviewed closely for proof of funds. Common strong exhibits include multi-month bank history, education loans from recognised banks, GIC purchases where used, and sponsor income proof that matches the LOA tuition. Sudden large deposits without a trail raise refusal risk.
Common challenges for India applicants
PAL seat timing for popular provinces while Indian VACs are busy.
Funds packages that do not match LOA tuition and IRCC living-cost figures.
Study plans that do not explain program choice versus options in India.
Incomplete biometrics after application submission within the required window.
Process and interview notes
Secure a DLI letter of acceptance, complete PAL/CAQ steps where required, assemble funds, submit the IRCC application, give biometrics, and track the portal for medical exam requests. Do not book non-refundable Canadian housing until you understand permit timing risk.
Local facts for India applicants
India is a top source country—processing times and VAC appointment demand fluctuate by season.
GIC pathways simplify funds proof when used correctly with matching LOA details.
A PAL (or CAQ in Quebec) is separate from IRCC approval—sequence both correctly.

Canada Study Permit Guide for Mexico
This page gives Mexican students the precise Canada study permit steps, from letter of acceptance to IRCC decision, with checks that reduce delays.
Mexico had 8,375 study permit holders in Canada at the end of 2024, compared with 11,360 in 2023, a leading Latin American source country, according to IRCC.
A Canada study permit from Mexico runs through the standard study permit stream. Mexico was never part of the Student Direct Stream, so the closure of that fast-track route in November 2024 changed nothing procedural for Mexican applicants. They have always used the standard process, and they continue to do so. There is no interview; an IRCC officer decides the case on the documents you submit.
The steps are clear. You receive a letter of acceptance from a designated learning institution, obtain the Provincial Attestation Letter your province issues, prepare proof of funds, complete the online application, and give biometrics. Mexican demand spans language schools, colleges, and universities, and an officer wants to see a study plan that fits whichever path you choose.
Where you apply
Mexican applicants generally file online and book biometrics through VACs serving Mexico. Confirm locations on official IRCC/VFS guidance.
Financial evidence
Show LOA tuition and living costs with bank evidence. Cross-border sponsor help should be documented without looking like an immigrant settlement package.
Common challenges for Mexico applicants
Confusing US tourist travel history with Canadian study-permit rules.
Incomplete prior Canadian or US status disclosures when asked.
Last-minute DLI changes that invalidate PAL assumptions.
Process and interview notes
Confirm DLI and province first, complete PAL if required, apply to IRCC, give biometrics, and wait for medical/additional document requests.
Local facts for Mexico applicants
A US B1/B2 history does not replace Canadian study-permit funds proof.
Keep LOA program dates aligned with your intended entry plan.

A Canada study permit from Morocco runs through the standard study permit stream. Morocco is a priority market in Canada's francophone-recruitment push: Canada actively recruits French-speaking Moroccan students, and that focus shapes the pathways open to you. Morocco was eligible for the Student Direct Stream before it closed in November 2024, so the expedited route Moroccan applicants used is gone, and everyone now files through the standard process. There is no interview; an IRCC officer decides the case on your documents.

You receive a letter of acceptance from a designated learning institution, obtain the Provincial Attestation Letter your province issues, prepare proof of funds, complete the online application, and give biometrics. PAL timing for constrained provinces.

Translate critical financial pages where needed, submit IRCC forms, complete biometrics quickly, and watch for medical requests.

Skip to main content Canada Study Permit Guide
Canada Study Permit Guide for Nigeria
This page gives Nigerian students the full Canada study permit path, from letter of acceptance to IRCC decision, with checks that reduce refusal risk.
Nigeria had 26,540 study permit holders in Canada at the end of 2024, down from 37,505 in 2023, one of Canada's largest African source countries, according to IRCC.
A Canada study permit from Nigeria now runs through the standard study permit stream. Nigeria had its own expedited route, the Nigeria Student Express, which closed alongside the Student Direct Stream in November 2024. Nigerian applicants have lost that dedicated fast lane and now file through the standard process, where the documentary review is the whole game. There is no interview; an IRCC officer decides the case on your file.
The steps are clear. You receive a letter of acceptance from a designated learning institution, obtain the Provincial Attestation Letter your province issues, prepare proof of funds, complete the online application, and give biometrics. For Nigerian applicants, financial documentation receives the closest attention, so the strength of that evidence often decides the outcome.
Where you apply
Nigerian applicants typically file the study permit online via IRCC and complete biometrics at VACs serving Nigeria (confirm current cities on VFS/IRCC). There is usually no routine in-person visa interview like a US F-1 consular interview—your documents carry the case.
Financial evidence
Show liquid funds covering first-year tuition and IRCC living costs with bank statements, loan letters, or GIC evidence. Officers scrutinise sustainability of funds from Nigeria; unexplained cash deposits are a common weakness.
Common challenges for Nigeria applicants
Proving genuine temporary study intent with a coherent study plan.
Funds volatility across monthly statements without explanation.
Medical exam timing after IRCC requests.
Aligning LOA start dates with biometrics and permit processing.
Process and interview notes
LOA → funds package → IRCC apply → biometrics → medical if requested → decision. Keep passport validity longer than the intended stay. Use only official IRCC/VFS channels for biometrics bookings.
Local facts for Nigeria applicants
Online filing does not mean light funds review—document quality still decides outcomes.
Keep digital and paper copies of LOA, PAL, and bank PDFs for border and school check-in.

Canada Study Permit Guide for Philippines
This page gives Filipino students the precise Canada study permit steps, from letter of acceptance to IRCC decision, with checks that reduce delays.
The Philippines had around 48,870 study permit holders in Canada at the end of 2023, ranking as the third-largest source country, according to IRCC.
A Canada study permit from the Philippines now runs through the standard study permit stream. The Philippines was a high-volume Student Direct Stream country, and the closure of that fast-track route in November 2024 removed a quick, predictable channel many Filipino students relied on. Applicants now face standard-stream timelines and heavier documentary scrutiny. There is no interview; an IRCC officer decides the case on the file you submit.
The steps are clear. You receive a letter of acceptance from a designated learning institution, obtain the Provincial Attestation Letter your province issues, prepare proof of funds, complete the online application, and give biometrics. A credible study plan and clear ties to the Philippines carry real weight, because strong family networks in Canada can raise questions about whether you intend to leave at the end of your studies.
Where you apply
Philippine applicants usually file online with IRCC and book biometrics through the VAC network serving the Philippines. Confirm city locations and appointment rules on official channels before inter-island travel.
Financial evidence
Show LOA tuition plus living costs with bank history and sponsor proof. Education loans and remittance histories should be explained if balances fluctuate.
Common challenges for Philippines applicants
Biometrics appointments that lag peak intakes.
Funds stories that rely on last-minute remittances.
Program explanations that sound purely work-driven rather than study-driven.
Process and interview notes
LOA and PAL first, then IRCC submission, biometrics, and medicals if asked. Track the IRCC account daily after biometrics.
Local facts for Philippines applicants
Keep passport bio page clear scans ready for IRCC uploads.
A study plan letter helps when switching fields from prior Philippine credentials.

This page gives Korean students the full Canada study permit path, from letter of acceptance to IRCC decision, with checks that reduce refusal risk.
South Korea had 8,485 study permit holders in Canada at the end of 2024, compared with 10,470 in 2023, a long-standing top-ten source country, according to IRCC.
A Canada study permit from South Korea has been a stable, well-understood process for years. South Korea was never part of the Student Direct Stream, so the closure of that fast-track route in November 2024 changed nothing procedural for Korean applicants. They have always used the standard study permit stream, and they continue to do so. There is no interview; an IRCC officer decides the case on your documents.
The path is the same one Korean families have followed for a long time. You receive a letter of acceptance from a designated learning institution, obtain the Provincial Attestation Letter your province issues, prepare proof of funds, complete the online application, and give biometrics. Korean demand includes a notable share of younger students in secondary and language programs alongside college and university applicants.

Show first-year tuition and living costs with multi-month bank history and parent or self-funding proof. Scholarship letters must state coverage clearly against the LOA fee schedule.
Common challenges for South Korea applicants
Romanisation mismatches between passport, LOA, and IRCC forms.
Assuming strong academics replace a complete funds package.
PAL timing for the destination province when seats are constrained.
Process and interview notes
LOA + provincial attestation (where required) → IRCC submission → biometrics → medical if requested → decision. Align name spellings before you pay fees.
Local facts for South Korea applicants
Use only official biometrics booking channels.

Canada Study Permit Guide for South Sudan
Applying for a Canada study permit from South Sudan? Here is the LOA, PAL, funds, and biometrics sequence.
Students from South Sudan choose Canada for its high-quality education and welcoming policies, making it a top source country for Canadian study permits.
To study in Canada from South Sudan, you need a study permit issued by IRCC. Accept an offer from a DLI, gather documents including acceptance letter and proof of funds, and submit online.
IRCC assesses each application based on financial ability, ties to South Sudan, and intent to leave Canada after your stay.
Where you apply
Applicants in South Sudan normally submit a Canada study permit online through IRCC and complete biometrics at a VAC serving their country. Confirm current VAC cities on official IRCC/VFS pages before you travel.
Financial evidence
Show first-year tuition and IRCC living costs with liquid bank evidence, sponsor income proof, and loan or GIC documents where used. Officers reviewing files from South Sudan look for sustainability, not a single-day balance.
Common challenges for South Sudan applicants
Documenting funds from South Sudan in a format IRCC can verify.
Completing biometrics within the deadline after submission.
Aligning PAL/CAQ steps with IRCC processing before term start.
Process and interview notes
LOA → provincial attestation if required → funds package → IRCC apply → biometrics → medical if requested → decision.
Local facts for South Sudan applicants

A strong LOA does not replace proof-of-funds rules.

Canada Study Permit from Sri Lanka: 2026 Guide 
Skip to main content Canada Study Permit Guide
Canada Study Permit Guide for Sri Lanka
This page gives Sri Lankan students the precise Canada study permit steps, from letter of acceptance to IRCC decision, with checks that reduce delays.
Sri Lanka is a smaller but steady source country for international students in Canada, according to IRCC.
A Canada study permit from Sri Lanka runs through the standard study permit stream. Sri Lanka was never part of the Student Direct Stream, so its closure in November 2024 changed nothing procedural for Sri Lankan applicants. They have always used the standard process. There is no interview; an IRCC officer decides the case on the documents you submit.
The steps are clear. You receive a letter of acceptance from a designated learning institution, obtain the Provincial Attestation Letter your province issues, prepare proof of funds, complete the online application, and give biometrics. For Sri Lankan applicants, the pressure point is documentary: clear, well-sourced proof of funds and a study plan that makes sense for your background.
Where you apply
Sri Lankan applicants file online and complete biometrics at VACs serving Sri Lanka. Verify current locations on official IRCC/VFS sources before travel.
Financial evidence
Show multi-month bank history, sponsor income, and education-loan sanction letters that match LOA totals. Sudden deposits without source letters weaken credibility.
Common challenges for Sri Lanka applicants
Loan letters that do not cover living costs as well as tuition.
Prior visa refusals not disclosed consistently.
Program start dates that ignore biometrics wait times.
Process and interview notes
Secure LOA/PAL, submit IRCC forms, complete biometrics promptly, and respond quickly to medical or document requests in the portal.
Local facts for Sri Lanka applicants
Education loans help when the sanction letter period matches the program.
Keep LOA fee figures reconcilable with every bank PDF.

Canada Study Permit Guide for United Kingdom
This page gives British students the precise Canada study permit steps, from letter of acceptance to IRCC decision, with checks that reduce delays.
The United Kingdom is a steady source country for Canadian study permit holders, with many applicants being international students already based in the UK, according to IRCC.
A Canada study permit from the UK covers two distinct applicant groups. The first is British citizens, who generally face a low-friction process and strong approval outcomes. The second is the population of international students already living in the UK on British visas, who apply to Canada as third-country nationals. The standard study permit stream covers both. There is no interview; an IRCC officer decides the case on the documents you submit.
The steps are clear. You receive a letter of acceptance from a designated learning institution, obtain the Provincial Attestation Letter your province issues, prepare proof of funds, complete the online application, and give biometrics. If you are not a British citizen, the officer also looks at your lawful status in the UK, so document that clearly alongside your home-country ties.
Where you apply
UK-based applicants file online and complete biometrics at VACs serving the United Kingdom. Confirm locations on official IRCC/VFS sources; do not use unofficial appointment sellers.
Financial evidence
GBP bank history, Student Finance (if any), and parent sponsorship should meet LOA tuition plus IRCC living-cost expectations. Convert figures transparently.
Common challenges for United Kingdom applicants
Assuming prior UK Student Route experience auto-satisfies Canadian purpose-of-study review.
Funds that cover UK costs but fall short of Canadian LOA totals.
Quebec CAQ missed for Montreal/Quebec DLIs.
Process and interview notes
LOA (+ CAQ if Quebec) → IRCC submission → UK biometrics → medical if requested → decision.
Local facts for United Kingdom applicants
Keep LOA, bank PDFs, and biometrics receipt together for port of entry.
Program changes after filing may require IRCC updates through the portal.

This page gives Vietnamese students the precise Canada study permit steps, from letter of acceptance to IRCC decision, with checks that reduce delays.
Vietnam had 10,550 study permit holders in Canada at the end of 2024, close to the 10,745 recorded in 2023, ranking among Canada's top source countries, according to IRCC.
A Canada study permit from Vietnam now runs through the standard study permit stream. Vietnam was eligible for the Student Direct Stream, the fast-track route that closed in November 2024, and Vietnamese students used it heavily. Its closure removed a predictable channel, so applicants now face standard-stream timelines and a fuller documentary review. There is no interview; an IRCC officer decides the case on the file you submit.
The steps are clear. You receive a letter of acceptance from a designated learning institution, obtain the Provincial Attestation Letter your province issues, prepare proof of funds, complete the online application, and give biometrics. For Vietnamese applicants, the two areas that decide most cases are the funding evidence and a study plan that explains why this program and Canada fit your goals.

Privacy Policy
Last updated: January 1, 2026
1. Introduction
YouSafe Consultancy, operated by Youssef Hammoud and based in Toronto, Canada, is committed to protecting your privacy. This Privacy Policy explains how we collect, use, disclose, and safeguard your personal information when you use our study document preparation, education planning, and settlement support services. We comply with the Personal Information Protection and Electronic Documents Act (PIPEDA) and applicable Canadian privacy laws.
2. Information We Collect
We collect information that you provide directly to us, including:
Personal identification information (name, date of birth, nationality, passport details)
Contact information (email address, phone number, mailing address)
Educational background and employment history
Immigration history and travel documents
Financial information for proof of funds documentation
Payment information for processing fees
Communications between you and our team
3. How We Use Your Information
We use the information we collect to:
Provide study document preparation, education planning, and settlement support services
Communicate with you about your case and our services
Process payments and maintain financial records
Help organize materials for IRCC and educational institutions when requested by you
Comply with legal obligations and regulatory requirements
Improve our services and client experience
4. Information Sharing and Disclosure
We do not sell, trade, or rent your personal information to third parties. We may share your information only in the following circumstances: with government agencies (such as IRCC) when you authorize us to help with document submission or support; with educational institutions as part of your admission applications; with service providers who assist us in operating our business (subject to confidentiality agreements); and when required by law, court order, or government regulation.
5. Data Security
We implement appropriate technical and organizational measures to protect your personal information against unauthorized access, alteration, disclosure, or destruction. This includes encrypted storage of sensitive documents, secure communication channels, and restricted access to client files. However, no method of transmission over the Internet is 100% secure, and we cannot guarantee absolute security.
6. Data Retention
We retain your personal information for as long as necessary to fulfill the purposes for which it was collected, typically for seven (7) years after the conclusion of your case. This retention period allows us to comply with legal requirements, resolve disputes, and enforce our agreements. After this period, your information will be securely deleted or anonymized.
7. Your Rights
Under Canadian privacy law, you have the right to:
Access the personal information we hold about you
Request correction of inaccurate or incomplete information
Withdraw consent for certain uses of your information
Request deletion of your information (subject to legal retention requirements)
File a complaint with the Office of the Privacy Commissioner of Canada

Study Permit Guide for Trent University
Admitted to Trent University? Here is how the Canada study permit, PAL, and funds proof fit around your LOA.
Trent University in Peterborough draws international applicants across undergraduate and graduate pathways; recent counts are near 1,500 students from abroad.
Trent University welcomes international students under Canada's study permit framework. After admission, the institution issues a letter of acceptance that you attach to your IRCC application. Quebec-bound students may also need a CAQ from MIFI before the federal permit.
Your application should show genuine temporary intent, sufficient funds, and a clear study plan. Incomplete financial evidence is a common refusal reason.
Institution
Trent University
Location
Peterborough , Ontario
International Students
1,500 +
Type
University · Public
LOA and the international student office
The international student office at Trent University supports LOA issuance, arrival orientation, and study-permit-related campus compliance. Contact them early about program start dates, full-time enrolment expectations, and co-op authorisation that must match your permit conditions. They cannot overturn an IRCC refusal, but they can confirm DLI status and whether a PAL or CAQ is required for your intake.
Financial documentation for your study permit
Ontario study-permit files still need first-year tuition plus IRCC living-cost proof. Officers commonly expect clear, liquid funds—recent bank statements, education loans, or a GIC where used—matched to the LOA fee line. Trent University applicants often mix sponsor support with personal savings—include a sponsor letter, relationship proof, and the sponsor’s bank evidence so the story matches the LOA fee schedule.
Arriving in Peterborough
Arriving in Peterborough for Trent University: Trent University residences and downtown shared houses fill before September; book early for peak intake. Local transit; GO and regional buses connect toward the GTA for some placements. Eastern Ontario winters with ice and snow. Symons campus vs downtown trade-offs—measure commute before you sign. Complete Trent University's international check-in with your passport, study permit, and LOA, and store PDFs of your PAL/CAQ documents where applicable.

Securing a Provincial Attestation Letter (PAL) for your Ontario intake while provincial allocations remain open.
Proving liquid funds that match LOA tuition plus the current IRCC living-cost figure without last-minute transfers that look staged.

What MyCaseworks does
MyCaseworks is a document-preparation and attorney-matching platform built for international students and immigrants navigating the United States, Canada, and the United Kingdom. We prepare the paperwork — visa forms, tenancy reviews, sponsorship packets — and a licensed attorney reviews it before you file.
We charge flat fees that are a fraction of traditional hourly legal billing. The legal advice in any MyCaseworks service comes from a licensed attorney through their own practice; MyCaseworks connects you with that attorney and handles the workflow, secure document portal, and payment.
MyCaseworks is a sister site of YouSafe Consultancy , which has placed 500+ international students across 30+ countries.

Every matter begins with a structured intake. You answer questions about your situation — country, visa type, deadlines, and concerns. Gathering papers before you open ImmiAccount reduces incomplete lodgements. The Department of Home Affairs assesses Temporary Graduate applications against the Migration Regulations and the instrument in force on your lodgement date. What the 485 visa document checklist covers
Subclass 485 lets certain international graduates stay in Australia temporarily after study. Two main streams sit under the current framework: Post-Higher Education Work and Post-Vocational Education Work. Stream names and criteria have changed over recent years, so always read the live page for Temporary Graduate visa (subclass 485) on the Home Affairs site before you finalise your pack: https://immi.homeaffairs.gov.au/visas/getting-a-visa/visa-listing/temporary-graduate-485 .

Identity and travel documents

body:

From Student to PR: Australia Skilled Migration Pathways 
Skip to main content MyCaseworks 
Home 
Library 
Profile 
Your stats 
Following 
Discover 
Get weekly immigration updates
Join 
In 60 seconds
01 Sequence: Subclass 500 → Subclass 485 → Skilled migration (189/190/491) → PR. Each step has its own eligibility requirements and time frames. 
02 The 485 visa gives you 2-4 years (depending on qualification and location) to gain Australian skilled work experience — which adds points under the points test. 
03 A two-year Australian degree gives 5 points for the Australian study requirement. Regional study adds 5 more points. PhD adds 30 total points. 
04 Graduates with health, education, or engineering qualifications are prioritised under Ministerial Direction 111, which may result in faster invitations at lower points scores. 
05 The regional 491 pathway offers 15 bonus points — making it accessible to graduates with base scores as low as 50 before nomination. 
The standard graduate-to-PR sequence
The most common pathway from student to PR follows a predictable sequence. You arrive on a subclass 500 student visa, complete your course (minimum two academic years to satisfy the Australian study requirement), then apply for a Temporary Graduate subclass 485 visa. The 485 gives you permission to work full-time in Australia for two to four years depending on your qualification level. During this period, you gain Australian skilled work experience, improve your English test scores, and potentially obtain a skills assessment if your occupation requires one. With one to two years of Australian work experience and a competitive English score, you can lodge an Expression of Interest for skilled migration through SkillSelect.
For a detailed breakdown of how points are calculated for each visa subclass, see the skilled migration points test guide . For the regional pathway, see the subclass 491 regional visa guide . Both guides explain the specific occupation lists, evidence requirements, and invitation dynamics that apply to each subclass. Understanding which visa subclass matches your profile at each stage is essential for a smooth transition from study to permanent residence.
Which PR pathway fits your profile
Your choice of PR pathway depends on three factors: your occupation, your points score, and your willingness to live in a regional area. If your occupation is on the Medium and Long-term Strategic Skills List (MLTSSL) and you have 85+ points, subclass 189 gives you the most flexibility (no residence restrictions). If your occupation is on the MLTSSL or STSOL and you have 75-85 points, subclass 190 with state nomination (5 bonus points) is your strongest option. If your score is below 75 or your occupation is in demand regionally, subclass 491 with 15 bonus points provides the fastest invitation path.
Employer-sponsored PR through subclass 186 is an alternative path if you secure a job with an approved sponsor. This route does not use the points test — it is based on the employer's nomination and your skills. 03 Main risk: Transferring to a lower-level course (lower AQF) or changing providers without a release letter within the 6-month restricted period can breach visa conditions and require a new visa application. 
The rule in plain English
Condition 8516 on the subclass 500 visa requires you to continue to satisfy the criteria for the grant of the visa. This means that if your visa was granted because you were enrolled in a specific course at a specific level, changing to a different course or provider must not cause you to stop meeting the visa criteria. The most common scenario where condition 8516 becomes an issue is when a student changes from a higher AQF level course (e.g., a Master's degree, AQF level 9) to a lower level (e.g., a Diploma, AQF level 5). In that case, the student may no longer meet the genuine temporary entrant criteria that were assessed when the visa was granted, and a new visa application may be required.
The provider transfer process is governed by the ESOS National Code 2018. Standard 7 of the National Code sets out the rules for releasing international students to transfer to another provider. If you have been enrolled in your principal course for less than six months (the "restricted period"), you need a letter of release from your current provider before the new provider can issue a CoE. If the current provider refuses release, you cannot transfer unless you meet one of the exceptions (compassionate or compelling circumstances, the provider cannot deliver the course, or the provider agrees the transfer is in your best interest).
After six months in your principal course, you do not need a release letter. You can enrol with a new provider directly, and the new provider can issue a CoE. However, condition 8516 still applies — if the new course is at a lower AQF level, you may still need a new visa. The six-month period runs from the start date of the principal course (not any preparatory or foundation course that preceded it).
Who this guide is for
Subclass 500 visa holders who are considering changing their course or education provider and want to understand the visa implications before making the change. Students who have already changed providers and want to confirm they have not breached visa conditions. Education agents and student advisers who help students navigate provider transfers within the ESOS framework.

What the GS requirement asks you to prove
The Genuine Student (GS) requirement replaced the Genuine Temporary Entrant (GTE) requirement for student visa applications lodged on or after 23 March 2024. Home Affairs states that the GS requirement focuses on whether study is the primary purpose for entering and staying in Australia, while recognising that a genuine student may later develop skills Australia needs and may choose to apply for permanent residence. The shift from GTE to GS was part of the Migration Strategy reforms announced in December 2023.
The GS requirement is assessed through a structured set of questions in the visa application form. You are asked to explain: your current circumstances, including ties to your home country, your reasons for choosing the specific course and education provider, how the course fits your academic background and career plan, and the value of the course to your future. The case officer assesses whether your answers are consistent with the supporting documents in your file, including financial evidence, academic records, and prior visa history.
The GS requirement does not ask you to prove you will leave Australia. Unlike the GTE, it explicitly acknowledges that a genuine student may later explore work or migration options. However, if your file makes it look like study is incidental to a primary work or migration goal, the GS requirement will not be met. 01 Current public rule: Home Affairs processes student visa applications according to Ministerial Direction No. 111, which assigns priority tiers based on the education provider and the applicant’s enrolment. 
02 Controlling source: Department of Home Affairs Ministerial Direction No. 111 (in force from December 2024, replacing MD107). 
03 Main risk: Choosing a high-risk or over-allocation provider can slow processing, but the visa criteria themselves are not affected by MD111. 
What Ministerial Direction 111 does
Ministerial Direction No. 111 is a direction issued by the Minister for Immigration under section 67 of the Migration Act 1958. It tells Home Affairs how to prioritise the processing of student visa applications. It does not change the legal criteria for the visa — the Genuine Student test, financial capacity, English language, health, and character requirements remain the same. What MD111 changes is the order in which applications are processed when the department faces resource constraints or high application volumes.
MD111 replaced the previous Ministerial Direction No. 107 in December 2024. The key change was a shift to a more granular, tiered priority system based on the education provider’s risk profile and the percentage of Confirmation of Enrolment (CoE) allocations the provider has used. Applications from lower-risk providers with available CoE capacity are processed first. The Direction reflects the government’s policy of directing student visa processing toward providers with strong compliance records and genuine student outcomes.
MD111 does not give you a right to faster processing. If your application is complete and meets all criteria, it will eventually be processed regardless of the priority tier. But processing times for applications in lower priority tiers can be significantly longer — in some cases, months longer than the published median processing time. If you are planning your study start date, factor in potential processing delays based on your provider profile.
Who this guide is for
Prospective international students who have applied or are about to apply for a subclass 500 student visa and want to understand how processing priority works. Current student visa holders who are applying for a subsequent visa (e.g., extending their stay for a second course) and want to anticipate processing time. Education agents and advisers who help students choose providers and plan visa timelines.
If you are applying to a well-established Australian university with a strong compliance record, MD111 likely works in your favour — your application will be processed at a higher priority. If you are applying to a private college or a newer provider, you may face slower processing. Ask the provider about their recent visa processing times for students from your country before committing to enrolment.
Documents and evidence to prepare
MD111 does not add any new document requirements beyond what the subclass 500 visa already requires

01 Combined application: You lodge a single application for both the 820 (temporary) and 801 (permanent) visas. The 820 is assessed first; the 801 is assessed two years after lodgement. 
02 The four relationship pillars: Financial aspects, nature of the household, social aspects, and nature of the commitment. Evidence must cover all four pillars and span the entire relationship — from the start of the relationship to the date of application. 
03 Onshore requirement: The applicant must be in Australia at the time of lodgement and at the time of grant for both stages (with some COVID-era exceptions now phased out). 
04 Sponsor obligations: The Australian sponsor must provide police checks, evidence of citizenship or permanent residence, and a signed sponsorship undertaking. Sponsorship is limited to two people in a lifetime, with a five-year gap between sponsorships. 
05 Processing time: Home Affairs publishes current processing times — the 820 stage typically takes 12-24 months. A Bridging visa A is granted automatically on lodgement for applicants who hold a substantive visa, allowing them to remain lawfully in Australia until a decision. Applicants who are unlawful at lodgement receive a Bridging Visa C or E instead, which may not include work rights. 
The two-stage structure: 820 then 801
The onshore partner visa is a combined application. You submit one application and pay one fee. Home Affairs assesses the subclass 820 (temporary) stage first. If satisfied the relationship is genuine and continuing, and all other criteria are met, the 820 is granted. Two years after the date of the original application (not the date of 820 grant), Home Affairs assesses the 801 (permanent) stage. At that point, you provide updated evidence that the relationship is still genuine and ongoing.
The two-stage structure means the evidence you submit at lodgement must be strong enough for the 820, and you must maintain records throughout the two-year waiting period for the 801 assessment. Many applicants submit strong 820 evidence but fail to continue documenting the relationship after lodgement — and then struggle to produce updated evidence for the 801 stage. Keep collecting joint bills, updated photographs, joint travel records, and statements from friends throughout the waiting period.
Who this guide is for
People already in Australia who are in a genuine relationship with an Australian citizen, permanent resident, or eligible New Zealand citizen and want to apply for permanent residence through the partner visa pathway. Couples who are engaged or newly married and want to understand the evidence standard before applying. Applicants whose circumstances are more complex — recent relationship, age difference, the applicant has overstayed or holds no substantive visa — and who need to assess whether their evidence is sufficient or whether a Schedule 3 waiver is required.

Confirm who you are renting from
Before paying money, identify whether you are dealing with the landlord, agent, provider, head-tenant, or a roommate. The evidence you need changes depending on that relationship.
Treat the condition report as a bond document
Take dated photos and videos before moving furniture in. Match them to the condition report and keep a copy of everything sent to the agent or landlord.
Put repairs and promises in writing
For repairs, furniture, cleaning, keys, utilities, or rent reductions, keep written messages. A verbal promise is hard to use later if the bond or repair dispute becomes formal.
The NSW renting framework for students
Renting in New South Wales is governed by the Residential Tenancies Act 2010 (NSW) and the Residential Tenancies Regulation 2019. These laws apply to most residential tenancies, including students renting apartments, houses, or rooms. The key protections include: bond lodgement with NSW Fair Trading, minimum notice periods for rent increases and lease terminations, the landlord’s obligation to maintain the property in a reasonable state of repair, and the tenant’s right to a fair condition report at the start and end of the tenancy.
For international students, the most common set-up is a fixed-term lease of 6 or 12 months, followed by a periodic (month-to-month) agreement if you stay beyond the fixed term. Students living in purpose-built student accommodation (PBSA) may have different rights under a licence agreement rather than a residential tenancy agreement. Check which type of agreement you have signed — the protections differ.
If you are sharing a rental property with other students, you have two possible arrangements: you may be joint tenants on the same lease (each tenant is jointly and severally liable for the full rent), or you may be a subtenant renting from a head-tenant who holds the lease. Your rights are different in each arrangement, so confirm which applies before signing anything.

International students who are renting or about to rent accommodation in New South Wales. Students living in shared housing who need to understand their rights as a tenant or subtenant. Students who are in a rental dispute and need to know what evidence to gather and where to get help.

The points test is a self-assessment system. You claim points across seven categories when you lodge your EOI through SkillSelect. If your claimed points are not supported by the evidence you submit with the visa application, the visa will be refused. Your points score at the time of invitation is locked in. The PR pathway map in plain English
The standard student-to-PR pathway in Australia has four steps: complete an Australian qualification (minimum 2 academic years for most pathways), apply for the Temporary Graduate visa (subclass 485) to gain work experience and prepare for skilled migration, meet the points test threshold or secure employer sponsorship, and lodge a skilled migration visa application (subclass 189, 190, 491) or an employer-sponsored visa (subclass 482 transitioning to ENS 186). Each step depends on having your occupation on the relevant skilled occupation list at that time.
The subclass 485 Temporary Graduate visa is the bridge between study and skilled migration. It gives you 2-4 years (depending on your qualification level and passport) to work in Australia, gain skilled experience, complete a skills assessment, and improve your points score. During the 485 period, you should: complete a skills assessment with the relevant assessing authority for your occupation, achieve competent or proficient English (higher than the 485 minimum), gain skilled employment experience that counts toward points, and research state nomination opportunities (for 190/491) if your occupation is on the state's list.
The skilled migration pathways form a hierarchy. The subclass 189 (Skilled Independent) is the most flexible — no employer or state ties — but requires the highest points score. The subclass 190 (Skilled Nominated) adds 5 points and has lower invitation thresholds but requires you to live and work in the nominating state. The subclass 491 (Skilled Work Regional) has the lowest invitation thresholds but requires 3 years in a regional area before you can transition to permanent residence. The new Skills in Demand visa (subclass 482) replaces the TSS and offers a direct employer sponsorship route if you find an approved sponsor.

01 Condition 8105 (work): Up to 48 hours per fortnight when your course is in session. Unlimited hours during scheduled course breaks. Work that is a formal registered part of your course (e.g. work placement, internship required for completion) does not count toward the limit. 
02 Condition 8202 (study): Remain enrolled in a registered course (8202(1)), maintain satisfactory academic progress (8202(2)), and do not change to a course at a lower AQF level than the course for which the visa was granted unless an exception applies. 
03 Condition 8501 (health): Maintain adequate health insurance (OSHC) for the entire period of your stay, with no gaps in cover. Your dependants must also be covered. 
04 Condition 8533 (notification): Notify your education provider of your residential address within 7 days of arriving in Australia, and notify them of any change of address within 7 days of moving. Also keep your contact details current in ImmiAccount. 
05 Breach consequences: Condition breaches can result in visa cancellation, a three-year exclusion period, and adverse impact on future Australian visa applications. Minor or inadvertent breaches may result in a warning; systematic breaches lead to cancellation. 
Why visa conditions matter
Your subclass 500 visa grant letter lists the conditions that apply to your visa. These are legal obligations under the Migration Act 1958 — they are not suggestions or guidelines. Breaching a visa condition can lead to visa cancellation, detention, and removal from Australia. Even if you are not immediately detected, a condition breach discovered during a subsequent visa application (e.g. a 485 or skilled migration visa) can result in refusal on character or compliance grounds.
The four conditions that most commonly affect international students are: 8105 (work limitations), 8202 (enrolment and academic progress), 8501 (health insurance), and 8533 (address notification). Each condition is monitored differently — some through data-matching with the ATO and your education provider, others through Home Affairs compliance operations and tip-offs. Understanding the specific requirements of each condition and how compliance is monitored helps you avoid inadvertent breaches.
Condition 8105: work limits and what counts as work
Condition 8105 limits you to 48 hours of work per fortnight when your course is in session. A fortnight is a 14-day period starting on a Monday. The 48-hour limit applies to all paid work, including casual employment, part-time employment, gig economy work (Uber, Deliveroo, Airtasker), and self-employment where you receive payment for services. Unpaid work, such as volunteering for a charity or participating in an unpaid internship that is not part of your course, may still count as "work" if it displaces an Australian worker or creates an employment relationship.
During scheduled course breaks, there is no limit on work hours. A scheduled break means a period published in your education provider'

Expenses management and budget planning
A proper budget planning approach goes beyond meeting the minimum Home Affairs financial capacity threshold. Create a spreadsheet that accounts for all your living expenses in your chosen Australian city: rent, utilities, groceries, transport, phone plan, OSHC, textbooks, and a contingency fund. The cost of living varies significantly between Australian cities — a budget that works in Adelaide may not cover expenses in Sydney or Melbourne.
Good expenses management in your first semester sets the foundation for the rest of your studies. Track your spending weekly against your budget to identify areas where you are overspending. Build a contingency fund of at least one month of living expenses before you arrive — unexpected costs in the first week (bond payment, transport pass, phone plan, initial groceries) can quickly consume a budget that looked adequate on paper. Many Australian universities offer financial literacy workshops and budget planning tools through their international student support services — take advantage of these resources early. Keeping track of expenses using a money management app helps you stay within your fortnightly budget while also ensuring you do not accidentally breach the 48-hour work limit by working more than permitted.

Group evidence by student funds, sponsor funds, income, course costs, living costs, scholarships or loans, and translations. Do not make the reviewer reconstruct the story from scattered statements.

02 Controlling source: Department of Home Affairs (health requirement, OSHC, condition 8501), privatehealth.gov.au for OSHC provider information. 
03 Main risk: OSHC start or end dates not matching the visa period, dependants not covered, or health examination results expiring before the visa decision. 
The health requirement for the subclass 500 visa
Home Affairs requires all subclass 500 student visa applicants to meet the health requirement. This has two components. First, you must have adequate health insurance (Overseas Student Health Cover, or OSHC) for the entire period of your intended stay in Australia, as required by condition 8501. Second, you must undergo a health examination if you plan to stay in Australia for more than 6 months, if you are applying for a visa that specifically requires health assessment, or if you have a medical condition that may require significant treatment or care during your stay.
The health examination is arranged through Home Affairs' panel physician system. You first receive a HAP ID (Health Assessment Pointer) reference number from Home Affairs, which you use to book an appointment with an approved panel physician in your country. The physician conducts a medical examination (including a physical check, chest x-ray, and blood tests) and submits the results electronically to Home Affairs. The results are typically valid for 12 months from the date of the examination.
If you do not meet the health requirement — for example, if you have a condition that would impose significant cost on the Australian healthcare system — Home Affairs may refuse the visa. However, some health conditions can be managed with a health waiver if you have strong compelling circumstances and the cost is below the threshold set by Home Affairs. The waiver is not automatic and requires a specific application.
Who this guide is for
Prospective subclass 500 visa applicants who need to understand the health examination and OSHC requirements before applying. Current student visa holders who need to renew their OSHC or update their health examination before applying for a subsequent visa. Dependants of student visa holders who need their own health examinations and OSHC cover.
This guide covers the health requirement specifically. It does not restate the full document checklist for the subclass 500 — for the complete checklist including CoE, GS statement, financial capacity, and English evidence, use the subclass 500 document checklist .

02 Controlling source: Department of Home Affairs (subclass 500 refusal and review rights), Administrative Review Tribunal (which replaced the AAT in October 2024). 
03 Main risk: Reapplying without fixing the refusal reason. The most common mistake after a refusal is lodging a near-identical application and expecting a different result. Home Affairs case officers can see your application history. If the new application does not address the specific reason for the first refusal, it will likely be refused again. Take the time to understand and fix the weakness before reapplying. 
Subclass 500 refusal: what the decision record tells you
When Home Affairs refuses a subclass 500 student visa application, the decision record states the legal reasons. The most common refusal grounds are: the applicant did not meet the Genuine Student (GS) criterion, the financial capacity evidence was insufficient, the enrolment (CoE) was not valid or was cancelled, the English language requirement was not met, or the health or character requirements were not satisfied. The decision record also states whether you have review rights and the time limit for applying to the ART.
Read the decision record carefully before deciding what to do next. The refusal reason determines whether a fresh application or ART review is the better path. If the case officer found that your GS answers did not demonstrate a genuine intention to stay temporarily in Australia, a fresh application with a stronger GS statement is usually the right response. If the case officer misapplied the criteria or failed to consider evidence you submitted, ART review may be appropriate.
Home Affairs states that a fresh application is assessed independently, but applying without addressing the refusal reason is unlikely to produce a different outcome. If you reapply and the same GS officer reviews your file, they will see the previous refusal. Address the weaknesses head-on in the new application.

Onshore student visa holders whose subclass 500 application was refused and who need to decide between reapplying and seeking ART review within the time limits. Offshore applicants whose student visa was refused and who need to understand whether they have review rights and how to prepare a stronger fresh application.
If you are on a bridging visa after your student visa expired and a subsequent visa application was refused, the timing is urgent — your bridging visa may cease 28 days after the refusal decision, and you may become unlawful. This guide helps you understand the two paths available so you can act before the deadlines pass.

01 Current public rule: Study Australia states 48 hours per fortnight during study terms and semesters. 
02 Break periods: Study Australia states students can work unlimited hours during study breaks. 
03 Main risk: Casual shifts, overlapping payroll periods, or unclear semester dates make hour-counting harder than students expect. 
Count by fortnight, not by pay period
Rosters, payroll cycles, and visa fortnights may not line up neatly. Keep a separate hour log for study periods and another for official breaks.
Know the employment type
Full-time, part-time, and casual work have different practical records. Casual work can change week by week, so payslips and roster screenshots matter.
Separate visa compliance from workplace rights
A student can have workplace protections and still need to comply with visa work conditions. Keep evidence for both: pay, hours, contract terms, and course calendar dates.
The 48-hour fortnight rule in practice
Home Affairs states that international students on a subclass 500 student visa can work up to 48 hours per fortnight while their course is in session. A fortnight is calculated as a 14-day period starting on a Monday. The 48-hour limit applies to all paid work combined — if you work for two different employers, the hours from both count toward the same 48-hour limit.
During scheduled study breaks (semester breaks, trimester breaks, or official holidays), the 48-hour limit does not apply. Study Australia states that students can work unlimited hours during these periods. However, the definition of a study break depends on your provider’s academic calendar. Check with your education provider for the exact dates of each study period and break period.
If you are enrolled in a course that is not in session (such as during the period after completing all course requirements but before graduation), you may be considered to be on a study break and can work unlimited hours. However, if you are enrolled in a course that has continuous assessment with no scheduled breaks, the 48-hour limit applies year-round.
Who this guide is for
Current subclass 500 student visa holders who work while studying and need to stay within the 48-hour fortnight limit. Students who are considering taking on casual or part-time work and want to understand the rules before starting. Students who have received warnings from their employer or DSO about potential work-hour breaches and need to correct their record.
If you are working more than 48 hours per fortnight, you may be breaching your visa condition 8105 (or 8104 for some visa subclasses). A breach of work conditions can lead to visa cancellation under section 116 of the Migration Act. If you are concerned about your work hours, reduce them immediately and keep records of the reduction.

Rosters and work schedules. Keep copies of your work rosters showing the days and hours you are scheduled to work. If your employer uses an online rostering system, take screen

03 Third most common: Enrolment issues — expired, cancelled, or invalid Confirmation of Enrolment (CoE) at the time of assessment.

Why subclass 500 applications get refused: the common grounds
Home Affairs refuses subclass 500 applications on specific legal grounds set out in the Migration Regulations 1994. The most common are: the Genuine Student (GS) criterion under clause 500.212, financial capacity under clause 500.214, enrolment requirements under clause 500.211, English language under clause 500.213, and health or character under clauses 500.216 and 500.217. Each refusal ground requires a different type of evidence to fix — the first step is identifying which ground applies to your case.
When you receive a refusal letter, it will state the specific regulation or clause the case officer relied on. Do not skim this section. The legal reference tells you exactly what evidence was missing or insufficient. A refusal under clause 500.212 (GS) requires a completely different approach than a refusal under clause 500.214 (financial capacity). Treating all refusals the same way is the most common mistake applicants make when reapplying.
Who this guide is for
International students whose subclass 500 application was refused and who want to understand the specific reason before reapplying. Education agents and advisers helping students prepare a stronger fresh application. Students who have not yet applied and want to understand the most common refusal grounds so they can avoid them in their initial application.

01 PHEW stream: For bachelor's, bachelor honours, master's (coursework, research, extended), and doctoral degrees. Duration: 2 years (bachelor), 3 years (master's), 4 years (doctoral). 
02 PVEW stream: For diploma, advanced diploma, associate degree, and trade qualifications at Certificate III level or above. Duration: typically 18 months. 
03 Shared requirements: Both streams require the Australian study requirement (92+ weeks CRICOS-registered study, 16+ calendar months in Australia), English at IELTS 6.0 or equivalent, AFP check, and adequate health insurance. 
04 Critical check: Confirm your qualification's AQF level on your completion letter and cross-reference with the current Home Affairs stream eligibility table before lodging. Lodging under the wrong stream results in refusal with no fee refund. 
The two streams: what each one requires
The Temporary Graduate visa subclass 485 has two streams, and the choice depends entirely on your qualification level. The Post-Higher Education Work (PHEW) stream — formerly called the Post-Study Work stream before the July 2024 rebrand — covers degree-level qualifications: bachelor's degrees (including honours), master's degrees (coursework, research, and extended), and doctoral degrees (PhD). The Post-Vocational Education Work (PVEW) stream — formerly called the Graduate Work stream — covers sub-degree qualifications: diplomas, advanced diplomas, associate degrees, and trade qualifications at Certificate III level or above.
The distinction matters because the visa duration, cost, and career-plan implications differ between streams. A PHEW visa typically grants 2-4 years depending on your qualification level, giving you a substantial window to gain skilled work experience and explore permanent residence pathways. A PVEW visa is generally shorter, so your post-study planning timeline is more compressed.
Home Affairs has changed the qualification-level eligibility several times since 2023, particularly around graduate diplomas and packaged programs. Always check the current rules on the Home Affairs website at the time of application — rules that applied to a friend's successful application last year may no longer apply to yours.
Who this guide is for
International students who have completed or are about to complete an Australian qualification and are deciding which 485 stream to apply under. Students with packaged programs or combined qualifications who are unsure which stream their qualification falls under. Education agents helping graduates choose the correct stream before lodgement.
If you have not yet completed your course, this guide helps you plan which stream to target so you can gather the right evidence well before your completion date. 01 Current public rule: Home Affairs states condition 8202 requires the holder of a subclass 500 visa to remain enrolled in a registered course and meet the education provider’s attendance and course progress requirements. 
02 Controlling source: Department of Home Affairs (condition 8202), ESOS Act / National Code 2018 provider obligations. 
03 Main risk: Provider reports non-compliance to Home Affairs via PRISMS, issuing a s.20 notice that can lead to visa cancellation and a three-year re-entry bar. 
What condition 8202 requires
Condition 8202 is a mandatory condition on every subclass 500 student visa. Home Affairs states that condition 8202 requires you to: remain enrolled in a registered course of study that is a CRICOS-registered course (a course listed on the Commonwealth Register of Institutions and Courses for Overseas Students), meet the attendance requirements of your education provider, and meet the course-progress requirements of your education provider. If you hold more than one CoE (for a package enrolment), condition 8202 applies to each component of the package.
The condition does not set a specific minimum attendance percentage or course-progress benchmark in the Migration Regulations themselves. Instead, it requires you to meet those requirements as set by your education provider under the ESOS National Code 2018. The National Code requires providers to have documented policies for monitoring attendance and course progress, and to intervene when a student falls below the expected standard. These interventions are called "at-risk" processes and give you a chance to improve or explain before the provider reports the breach to Home Affairs.
If you transfer to a different provider or course, you must maintain enrolment in a CRICOS-registered course at all times. A gap in enrolment, even a short one, means you are not meeting condition 8202. If you change to a course that is not CRICOS-registered (such as a purely online course from a non-registered provider), you breach the condition regardless of whether you are still studying.
Who this guide is for
Subclass 500 student visa holders who want to understand their ongoing obligations while in Australia. Students who have received attendance warnings or "at risk" notices from their provider and need to know what happens next. Students who have received a section 20 notice (cancellation warning) and need to respond within 28 days.
If you have not received any warnings, this guide helps you stay compliant and avoid the escalation path from informal intervention to formal reporting. If you have already received a section 20 notice, the timing is urgent — you have 28 days to respond before the CoE is cancelled and visa cancellation begins.
