Proving funds for a Canadian study permit
A short orientation on what IRCC means by proof of funds, and the deposits that look borrowed. Routes you to the full evidence guide.
One-sentence answer: IRCC is not only asking whether the bank balance is high enough today. The officer needs to see that the money is available, legal, traceable, and enough for tuition, living costs, travel, and any accompanying family members. Start here if
You have an admission offer or you are close to getting one, but the financial side is not yet organized. You may be using your own savings, a parent or guardian, a bank loan, a scholarship, a GIC, or a mix of sources.
This is a short overview. The full evidence logic belongs in the study permit proof-of-funds guide .
The practical answer
A proof-of-funds section is strong when the reviewer can answer four questions without guessing:
How much is required for this applicant's case?
Where is the money held?
Where did the money come from?
Who controls it, and is it truly available for the student's education?
A single bank statement often cannot answer all four. That is why sponsored applications usually need a sponsor letter, relationship proof, income evidence, account history, and an explanation for any large movement of funds.
Budget planning and expenses management
Beyond the minimum financial proof required for your study permit, create a detailed budget planning spreadsheet that accounts for all your living expenses in your chosen Canadian city. Include rent, utilities, groceries, transport, phone plan, and a contingency fund. The cost of living varies significantly between Canadian cities — a budget that works in Winnipeg may not cover expenses in Toronto or Vancouver.
Good expenses management in your first semester sets the foundation for the rest of your studies. Track your spending weekly against your budget to identify areas where you are overspending. Build a contingency fund of at least one month of living expenses before you arrive. Many Canadian banks offer newcomer banking packages with budget planning tools and free money management features in their mobile apps.
What documents usually matter
Depending on the funding route, the packet may include:
Bank statements showing history, not just a closing balance.
Tuition receipt or fee invoice.
Scholarship or bursary letter.
GIC confirmation where used.
Education-loan sanction letter.
Sponsor letter, sponsor ID, relationship proof, and sponsor income evidence.
Source-of-funds explanation for lump-sum deposits.
Business documents or tax records where the sponsor is self-employed.
The goal is not to create a huge pile of documents. The goal is to remove doubt from the money story.
What goes wrong most often
Financial refusals often start with one of these issues:
A large deposit appears shortly before filing with no explanation.
The sponsor's income does not match the amount being promised.
The student uploads only a balance cert

One-sentence answer: start with the school and the document trail, not the visa form. A Canadian study-permit file usually rises or falls on the Letter of Acceptance, the PAL/TAL or Quebec CAQ where required, proof of funds, and whether the study plan makes sense for your history. Start here if
You are researching Canada as a study destination and you have not yet built the full application packet. You may have an offer, you may still be comparing schools, or you may be trying to understand why people get refused even when they have the right grades.

The practical answer
A study permit is not only about being accepted by a Canadian school. IRCC looks at the whole file: the institution, the program, the money, the applicant's history, the sponsor evidence, and whether the plan is believable. A strong file lets an officer answer five questions quickly:
Is the school a Designated Learning Institution?
Is the offer real and tied to the correct program dates?
Is the PAL/TAL or Quebec CAQ requirement handled, where it applies?
Can the applicant actually pay tuition, living costs, and travel without unexplained money?
Does the program make sense after the applicant's previous education or work?
If the answer to any one of those is unclear, the file may look incomplete even if every document has been uploaded.

Letter of Acceptance from the DLI.
PAL/TAL where required, or Quebec CAQ for Quebec-bound students.
Passport and identity documents.
Proof of financial support.
Tuition receipt, scholarship letter, GIC, loan letter, or sponsor evidence where available.
Study plan explaining why this program, why Canada, and what happens after study.
Biometrics and medical evidence where required by IRCC instructions.
Country-specific forms or local visa office documents where the checklist asks for them.
The mistake is treating this as a random upload folder. The better approach is to order the evidence like a reviewer would read it: admission first, attestation next, funds next, then the explanation that ties the facts together.

A school is a DLI, but the student assumes that also means a future PGWP will be available.

One-sentence answer: F-1 visa interview questions fall into seven categories — school choice, program fit, funding, prior refusal, post-study plans, home-country ties, and document consistency. Every answer should be supported by a document in your file; the strongest preparation is file consistency, not rehearsed answers.
Start here if
You have an upcoming F-1 consular appointment and want to understand what kinds of questions the officer is likely to ask, how to prepare your answers, and why document consistency matters more than a rehearsed response.
The seven question categories
1. Why this school?
The officer wants to understand why you chose this specific U.S. school rather than an institution in your home country or another country. Your answer should be supported by the documents: the school's program description, your academic record, and any evidence that the school fits your stated goals. A generic answer ("it is a good school") without documentary support is a weak response.
If you chose a school because it admits students with your academic profile, because it offers a specific program your home country lacks, or because it has strong placement in your field, those reasons should be visible in the documents you bring.
2. Why this program?
The officer evaluates whether your chosen field of study connects logically to your prior education and stated career goals. A student with a degree in biology who applies for a master's in public health can explain the connection; one who applies for an unrelated certificate program faces a higher burden.
Your study plan should show the logical progression: prior education → U.S. program → intended career. The officer does not expect a detailed five-year plan, but they should be able to see the connection from the sequence of documents presented.
3. Who pays, and how?
Funding questions probe whether the financial evidence matches the named sponsor and the stated amount. Common questions include "Who is paying for your studies?", "How does your sponsor earn this money?", and "What happens if the funds run out?"
The officer will compare the sponsor letter, bank statements, and the I-20 cost estimate. If the sponsor is a family member, the bank statements should show consistent balances and predictable deposits that match the sponsor's declared income. A sudden large deposit or funds from an unrelated third party without a clear explanation is a red flag.
4. What changed after a prior refusal?
If you have a previous U.S. visa refusal — especially a prior 214(b) refusal — the officer will ask what has changed. The answer must be supported by new or stronger evidence: a different school, stronger financial evidence, improved language scores, or changed home-country circumstances.
The most common mistake is reapplying with the same evidence and a different verbal answer. The officer reviews the previous refusal file; if nothing in the documents has material

One-sentence answer: An F-1 visa requires admission to a SEVP-certified school, a matching Form I-20, financial evidence covering the full course of study, a coherent study plan, and credible nonimmigrant intent. Each requirement must be provable by documents that the consular officer can verify at the interview window.
Start here if
You are researching F-1 visa requirements for the first time and need to understand the basic eligibility shape before reading the full procedural guide or speaking with a Designated School Official.
The five core requirements
1. Admission to a SEVP-certified school
Only schools certified by the Student and Exchange Visitor Program can issue a Form I-20 for an F-1 visa. The school must be actively SEVP-certified at the time they issue your I-20 and at the time you begin your program. You can verify a school's SEVP status through the DHS Study in the States school search tool before applying. Community colleges, language programs, and universities all appear on the certified list if they meet SEVP standards.
If the school loses SEVP certification while you are enrolled, your F-1 status may be affected. Check the school's certification status each semester, not just at admission.
2. A Form I-20 that matches the DS-160
The consular officer compares your Form I-20 (issued by the school) against your DS-160 online application. The school name, program level, start and end dates, and estimated costs must match across both documents. If your I-20 says your program costs USD 40,000 per year but your DS-160 states a different figure, the officer will flag the inconsistency.
The SEVIS number on the I-20 must also match the one USCIS generates when the school creates your record in the SEVIS database. If your I-20 was issued more than 12 months before your visa interview, request a new, updated I-20 from your DSO.
3. Credible financial evidence
You must prove you can cover tuition, living expenses, and any dependant costs for at least the first year of study, with a credible plan for the remaining years. USCIS does not prescribe a minimum bank balance; instead, the officer evaluates whether the funds shown are realistic given the sponsor's documented income, the country's banking norms, and the cost of the program.
Common financial evidence includes bank statements covering the most recent 6–12 months, a sponsor letter, scholarship award letters, education loan sanction letters, and employer sponsorship documentation. A sudden large deposit with no supporting explanation is a frequent reason for requests for additional evidence.
4. A study plan that fits your academic history
The officer will evaluate whether your chosen program makes academic sense given your prior education and stated career goals. A student with a bachelor's degree in engineering who applies for a certificate in culinary arts faces a higher burden of explanation than one pursuing a master&

One-sentence answer: OPT is a temporary work authorization that ends — it is not a pathway to a green card. The actual pathways (employer sponsorship, self-petition, family, or investor) require planning that begins during OPT, not after it expires. The most common mistake is waiting until OPT ends before exploring options.
Start here if
You are an F-1 student currently on OPT or STEM OPT and want to understand which long-term immigration pathways exist after your work authorization ends. This summary helps you identify the family of pathways that fits your situation; it does not replace a strategic consultation with a licensed immigration attorney.
The four green card pathways
1. Employer-sponsored green card (EB-1, EB-2, EB-3)
The most common pathway for OPT students who find a U.S. employer willing to sponsor permanent residence. The employer must typically obtain a PERM labor certification proving no qualified U.S. worker is available for the role, then file an I-140 petition. Processing times range from 18 months to several years depending on the category and the applicant's country of birth.
Key considerations: Not all employers sponsor green cards. Even employers that do may have policies about timing (e.g., waiting until after the H-1B lottery). The PERM process is expensive and time-consuming for the employer, so the relationship must be strong. Country-of-birth backlogs for India and China can add years of waiting.
2. Self-petition pathways (EB-1A, EB-2 NIW)
The EB-1A (Extraordinary Ability) and EB-2 National Interest Waiver allow you to petition for a green card without a specific employer sponsor. These pathways require meeting a high evidentiary standard: published research, awards, media recognition, or — for the NIW — demonstrating that your work has substantial merit and national importance.
Who qualifies: STEM PhD candidates, researchers with publications, startup founders whose work has clear national-interest implications, and professionals with exceptional credentials. The standard is fact-specific; not every talented professional qualifies. An experienced immigration attorney can evaluate your profile against the legal standard before you invest in the application.
3. Family-based green card
If you have a qualifying family member who is a U.S. citizen or lawful permanent resident, they may sponsor you for a family-based green card. Immediate relatives of U.S. citizens (spouse, unmarried minor child, parent) have no annual visa cap. Other categories have limited annual visas and priority-date backlogs that vary by category and country of birth.
Note on timing: Family-based petitions filed while you are on OPT may raise questions about nonimmigrant intent at the visa stage, but having an approved I-130 petition does not automatically violate F-1 status if you maintain all F-1 requirements. Consult an attorney about maintaining OPT while a family petition is pending.

US OPT vs Canada PGWP
The three structural differences that matter most when choosing between the US and Canada for post-study work. Routes you to the full comparison.
One-sentence answer: OPT and PGWP are both post-study work pathways, but they are built differently. OPT is tied to F-1 status and employment authorization in the US; PGWP is a Canadian open work permit route that can feed more directly into Canadian work-experience immigration planning. Start here if
You are choosing between studying in the United States and Canada and you want the work-after-graduation difference explained without legal jargon. This short page is for early decision-making. The full comparison is US OPT vs Canada PGWP .
The practical answer
The difference is not only how long each permit lasts. The bigger differences are:
Employer flexibility. PGWP is generally framed as an open work permit. OPT is tied to F-1 practical-training rules and must connect to the student's field of study.
Eligibility check. PGWP depends heavily on the Canadian school/program and current IRCC rules. OPT depends on F-1 status, school authorization, timing, and USCIS employment authorization.
Long-term planning. Canadian work experience after a PGWP may fit defined permanent-residence pathways. US post-study work often requires a separate employer-sponsored or family/self-petition strategy.
Neither route is automatically better. The better route is the one that matches the student's program, risk tolerance, employer prospects, and long-term plan.
What documents usually matter
For the Canada side, students should check:
DLI and program PGWP eligibility.
Completion letter and transcript requirements.
Field-of-study or language-test rules where they apply.
Passport validity and post-completion application timing.
For the US side, students should check:
F-1 status and DSO recommendation.
I-20 dates and requested OPT dates.
Form I-765 employment authorization process.
Whether STEM OPT is possible later.
What goes wrong most often
The common mistake is comparing slogans instead of rules:
“Canada always gives a work permit after graduation.” Not true.
“A US degree always leads to a work visa.” Not true.
“A DLI admission equals PGWP eligibility.” Not always.
“OPT is just a job permit.” It is still tied to F-1 practical training rules.

PGWP in Canada: a plain-English overview
A short orientation on what a PGWP is, who qualifies, and where to read the field-of-study rules that decide most cases.
One-sentence answer: a PGWP is a post-graduation work permit for eligible graduates of eligible Canadian programs, but it is not automatic just because a school accepted you or because the school appears on the DLI list. Start here if
You are considering a Canadian program, already studying in Canada, or close to graduation and trying to understand whether you can work after finishing school.
This page is only the plain-English overview. The full decision page is PGWP eligibility in Canada , and the evidence page is the PGWP document checklist .
The practical answer
A PGWP decision starts before you graduate. The school, program, program length, study mode, field of study, and completion evidence all matter. The safest question to ask before paying tuition is not “Is this school a DLI?” The safer question is: “Does this exact program at this exact school support PGWP eligibility under current IRCC rules?”
For many students, the PGWP is the bridge between study and Canadian work experience. That work experience may later support a permanent-residence plan. That is why the eligibility check should happen before enrolment, not after graduation.
What documents usually matter
The PGWP packet usually depends on:
Passport validity.
Current or recent study permit status.
Completion letter from the school.
Final transcript or official marks.
DLI/program eligibility evidence.
Field-of-study/CIP-code evidence where IRCC requires it.
Language-test evidence where IRCC requires it.
Explanation for any leave, part-time term, transfer, or status gap.
Completion timing matters. The date on the completion letter or final transcript may start the application window, so do not wait casually after graduation.
What goes wrong most often
PGWP mistakes usually come from assumptions:
Assuming every DLI program is PGWP-eligible.
Assuming every private college program qualifies.
Ignoring field-of-study rules until the end of the program.
Letting the study permit expire without a plan.
Filing after the post-completion window.
Submitting completion evidence that does not clearly show the program is finished.
Using a passport that expires before the full permit length the applicant could otherwise receive.

One-sentence answer: The STEM OPT 24-month extension requires three conditions that must all be met before filing: a qualifying STEM degree with the correct CIP code, an active post-completion OPT Employment Authorization Document (EAD), and an E-Verify-enrolled employer willing to sign Form I-983 as the training supervisor. Missing any one of these conditions means the extension cannot be approved.
Start here if
You are an F-1 student currently on post-completion OPT and want to understand whether you qualify for the 24-month STEM OPT extension. This overview covers the eligibility shape; the canonical STEM OPT extension checklist covers the detailed filing requirements, timeline, and evidence specifications.
The three conditions for STEM OPT eligibility
1. A qualifying STEM degree with a matching CIP code
Your degree must be in a field the Department of Homeland Security has designated as STEM. The degree's CIP code must match one on the DHS STEM Designated Degree Program List. This list includes traditional STEM fields (engineering, computer science) as well as data analytics, financial mathematics, and certain social science research methods.
The CIP code on your I-20 must match the STEM-designated code. If it does not, your DSO may need to correct it before filing. This is a common error: students enrolled in STEM programs that have a non-STEM CIP code on their I-20.
2. An active post-completion OPT EAD
You must be in a valid period of post-completion OPT when you file the STEM OPT extension. The I-765 for the STEM extension must be filed before the post-completion OPT EAD expires. USCIS recommends filing at least 90 days before the EAD expiration date but no earlier than 120 days before expiration.
If your post-completion OPT EAD is about to expire and you have not yet filed the STEM OPT extension, you risk a status gap. There is no grace period for late filing: if the EAD expires before USCIS receives the I-765, the extension application must be denied. Plan to file well before the expiration date, not on it.
3. An E-Verify employer willing to sign Form I-983
Your employer must be enrolled in E-Verify under the same EIN that employs you. Not all employers participate; check your employer's E-Verify status before planning a STEM OPT extension. Some employers are enrolled under one EIN but use another for STEM OPT workers.
The employer must also sign Form I-983 (Training Plan for STEM OPT Students) as the training supervisor. The form requires the employer to describe learning objectives, evaluation methods, and how the training relates to the student's degree.
Unemployment days and the STEM OPT extension
The standard OPT 90-day unemployment cap and the STEM OPT 150-day unemployment cap are separate and cumulative. Total unemployment across all of OPT (post-completion + STEM OPT) must not exceed 150 days. Unemployment accrued during post-completion OPT counts toward the 150-day total. If you accr

What are category-based draws?
Category-based draws are Express Entry invitation rounds that target candidates with specific skills, work experience, or language abilities that align with Canada's economic needs. First introduced in 2023, they operate alongside general draws (which invite the highest-ranked candidates regardless of occupation). In a category draw, only candidates who meet the category criteria are considered, and the CRS cutoff is typically significantly lower than in general rounds.
As of mid-2026, IRCC runs category draws in six streams: healthcare occupations, STEM occupations (science, technology, engineering, mathematics), trade occupations, transport occupations, agriculture and agri-food occupations, and French-language proficiency (CLB 7 or higher in all four competencies). IRCC announces its category priorities annually, and the list can change based on labour market needs and immigration targets.
Which categories exist in 2026?
The 2026 category list continues the six streams from 2025, with minor adjustments to eligible occupation lists. Here is how each category works:
Healthcare: Covers physicians, nurses, pharmacists, dentists, medical laboratory technologists, and allied health professionals. At least 6 months of experience in the past 3 years in an eligible NOC. Read the full guide at CA Express Entry healthcare category 2026 .
STEM: Software engineers, data scientists, electrical engineers, civil engineers, and other STEM professionals. This category is highly competitive due to the large applicant pool. Explore CA Express Entry STEM category 2026 .
Trades: Carpenters, electricians, welders, plumbers, and other skilled trades. Cutoffs are typically moderate due to smaller applicant pools.
Transport: Truck drivers, airline pilots, aircraft mechanics, and transport managers. A newer category with growing importance.
Agriculture: Farm supervisors, butchers, agricultural managers, and related occupations. Smaller pool with targeted draws.
French-language: CLB 7 or higher in French (NCLC 7) in all four competencies, regardless of occupation. This consistently has the lowest cutoffs and can be combined with any other category for dual eligibility.

Category draw cutoffs vary significantly by stream and draw date. In recent 2026 rounds, French-language draws have had CRS cutoffs in the low-to-mid 400s, while healthcare and STEM draws have typically landed in the high 400s to low 500s. General draws (no category restriction) have tren

PGP 2026: what has changed?
The Parents and Grandparents Program has remained largely consistent for 2026. IRCC continues to use the random lottery approach introduced in 2020, selecting candidates from the interest-to-sponsor pool. The key change for 2026 is a modest increase in the minimum necessary income threshold, reflecting inflation and cost-of-living adjustments. The number of invitations issued (target: 15,000–20,000 complete applications) has remained stable compared to 2025.
One important note for international graduates who recently became PRs: you must have filed Canadian tax returns for three consecutive years before you can sponsor. If you became a PR in 2023 or later, you will not meet the three-year filing requirement until 2026 or 2027. Plan accordingly and use the Super Visa as a bridge option in the meantime. Read the full program guide at CA PGP program guide .
Income requirements and family size
The minimum necessary income (MNI) is the most common reason PGP applications are refused. IRCC requires the sponsor to meet or exceed the MNI for three consecutive tax years. The MNI is calculated based on the total family size, which includes: the sponsor, the sponsor's spouse or common-law partner, the sponsor's dependent children, and the sponsored parents or grandparents (plus their spouses and dependent children).
For example, a couple with one child sponsoring both parents would have a family size of 5 (sponsor + spouse + child + 2 parents). The MNI for a family of 5 in 2025 was approximately CAD 68,000. Quebec's income requirement is assessed differently — the province sets its own threshold based on family size and the number of people being sponsored. Check Quebec immigration PEQ/PRTQ guide for Quebec-specific rules.
Super Visa — the practical alternative
If you are not selected in the PGP lottery, the Super Visa is the most practical way to bring parents or grandparents to Canada for extended stays. Unlike the PGP (which grants permanent residence), the Super Visa is a temporary resident visa that allows stays of up to 5 years per visit, with validity up to 10 years. It does not require a lottery entry and does not count toward the family sponsorship cap.

Last updated 2026-05-29 · Editorial review by MyCaseworks Editorial 
Canada's Express Entry system uses the Comprehensive Ranking System (CRS) to rank candidates in the pool for permanent residence. Your CRS score — out of a maximum of 1,200 points — determines whether you receive an Invitation to Apply (ITA) during a draw. This walkthrough explains how the CRS calculator works, how points are distributed across the four main factors, what counts as a competitive score in 2026, and which documents you need ready before and after receiving an ITA.
If you are also preparing the full document package for your Express Entry application, our Express Entry post-ITA document checklist provides a detailed breakdown of what to gather after you receive an invitation. For professional support with your immigration pathway, our Canadian immigration document preparation services may be relevant.
What the CRS measures
The CRS is a points-based system designed to identify candidates most likely to succeed economically in Canada. It awards points for human capital attributes — age, education, language ability and work experience — plus skill transferability combinations and additional factors such as provincial nominations, Canadian study experience and French language skills.
Before you can enter the Express Entry pool and receive a CRS score, you must first qualify under one of three federal immigration programs:
Federal Skilled Worker Program (FSWP) — for skilled workers with foreign work experience
Canadian Experience Class (CEC) — for candidates with at least 12 months of skilled Canadian work experience
Federal Skilled Trades Program (FSTP) — for qualified tradespeople
You can check your program eligibility using the IRCC eligibility tool on canada.ca. Only after confirming eligibility should you proceed to calculate your CRS score.
The four CRS factor groups
The CRS allocates points across four categories. The distribution differs depending on whether you have an accompanying spouse or common-law partner.

Canadian family sponsorship lets citizens and permanent residents bring their spouse, common-law partner, dependent children, parents, and grandparents to Canada as permanent residents. The two main routes are spousal or partner sponsorship — which can be processed inland or outland — and the Parents and Grandparents Program, which is invitation-only. The 5 most important things to know
You do not need to be married to sponsor a partner. Canadian immigration law recognises legally married spouses, common-law partners (12 months continuous cohabitation), and conjugal partners (exceptional circumstances preventing marriage or cohabitation). See IRCC sponsorship guidance.
Inland sponsorship is for applicants already inside Canada with valid temporary status and usually includes an open work permit during processing. Outland sponsorship is processed by the visa office for the applicant's country of residence or citizenship and generally permits travel during processing.
The financial undertaking for spousal sponsorship lasts 3 years from the date the partner lands as a permanent resident. There is no minimum income requirement for spousal or partner sponsorship, unlike the Parents and Grandparents Program, which does require proof of income.
The Parents and Grandparents Program is invitation-only. Eligible sponsors submit an Interest to Sponsor form during the annual intake window. If selected, IRCC sends an invitation to apply. Do not prepare a full application unless invited. Invitations are not transferable and deadlines have no exceptions.
Proving a genuine relationship requires evidence of a shared life over time — joint bank statements, utility bills, lease or mortgage documents, insurance policies naming each other as beneficiaries, and dated photographs with locations. Wedding photos and love letters alone are not sufficient.

01 The LMIA is issued by ESDC/Service Canada, not IRCC. A positive LMIA is submitted to IRCC as part of the worker's work permit application. 
02 Two main streams: high-wage (at or above provincial median hourly wage) and low-wage (below median). Each has different requirements for recruitment, caps, transition plans, and duration. 
03 Minimum recruitment: employers must advertise the position on the Job Bank and at least two additional methods for at least 4 consecutive weeks within the 3 months before applying. 
04 Compliance inspections can occur at any time within 6 years of LMIA issuance. Non-compliance can result in fines up to $100,000 per violation, a ban from the TFWP, and publication on the non-compliant employer list. 
05 An LMIA for PR support (arranged employment) adds 50 or 200 CRS points in Express Entry. The position must be permanent and the employer must indicate PR support on the application. 
Who this is for — and who it isn't
This guide is for Canadian employers who need to hire a foreign worker and must obtain an LMIA through the Temporary Foreign Worker Program. It covers the high-wage and low-wage streams, recruitment requirements, the transition plan obligation, compliance inspections and penalties, and how to use an LMIA to support a permanent residence application. It is also relevant for foreign workers who want to understand what their employer must do before they can apply for a work permit.
This guide is not for employers hiring through the International Mobility Program (LMIA-exempt), the Global Talent Stream (which uses a simplified LMIA process under the Global Skills Strategy), or the Seasonal Agricultural Worker Program (SAWP, which has a separate LMIA process). If the position is in Quebec, the employer must also obtain a Certificat d'acceptation du Québec (CAQ) from the MIFI — an additional step not covered here. Employers with a history of TFWP non-compliance or who have been subject to a ban should consult an immigration lawyer before applying.
High-wage vs low-wage: which stream applies
The dividing line between the two LMIA streams is the provincial or territorial median hourly wage for the occupation. ESDC publishes the median wage table by province and occupation on its website and updates it periodically. The wage used for the determination is the wage the employer is offering, not the prevailing wage for the occupation. If the offered wage is at or above the provincial median, the application is processed under the high-wage stream. If below, the low-wage stream applies.
The high-wage stream imposes two additional requirements that the low-wage stream does not: a transition plan and (in most cases) no cap on the number or proportion of TFWs. Before assembling documents, confirm that the completion letter and transcript agree on the completion date; if they differ by more than a few days, request a clarifying letter from the DLI registrar. Align the three dates first, then assemble everything else around them.

One-sentence answer: IRCC is not asking how much money is in the account today . IRCC is asking whether the money is genuinely available to you for the duration of your studies and whether you can prove where it came from . Who this is for
You are preparing a Canadian study permit application (study destination outside Quebec). Your funds will come from one or more of these:
Personal savings in your own name.
A sponsor — usually a parent or guardian — funding tuition and living costs.
A Guaranteed Investment Certificate (GIC) at a participating Canadian financial institution.
An education loan, often from a bank or government agency.
A scholarship, fellowship, or assistantship from the DLI or a third party.
You want to know how IRCC reads each of those, and what evidence converts a bank balance into "proof."
Who this is not for
Applicants whose destination is Quebec . Quebec's CAQ has its own financial requirements.
Applicants who are already inside Canada and renewing — proof of funds at renewal is judged on the remaining period, not the full program.
Sponsorship-based PR applications (Family Class). Different evidence framework.
The decision this page helps you make
Will an IRCC officer reading your funds documents conclude that:
The minimum required amount is shown.
The money is genuinely available (not borrowed for the application).
The source is plausible given the sponsor's life and work.
If any of those three is shaky, you are in refusal territory.
The controlling source
The controlling source is IRCC's guidance on proof of financial support for study permit applicants. IRCC publishes a per-year minimum for living expenses outside Quebec, plus first-year tuition, plus return travel. That minimum is updated periodically, so confirm the current figure directly on IRCC's official proof-of-financial-support page before you rely on it. 
GIC-based proof under the framework formerly known as the Student Direct Stream is a defined sub-route with its own rules. The participating-institution list and the eligible GIC amount are also published by IRCC and have changed over time — check both against IRCC's current published guidance before relying on this route.
Documents that prove the case
In reviewer order:
The minimum threshold check. 
First-year tuition (from the LOA).
Living expenses for the applicant for one year, at the per-year minimum IRCC currently publishes.
Plus living expenses for each accompanying family member, at IRCC's current published per-person amount.

01 Step 1 — read the refusal letter: It will cite the specific legal provision (e.g. R216(1)(b) for purpose of visit, R220 for funds). This tells you which category of evidence was insufficient. 
02 Step 2 — order GCMS notes: The refusal letter is a summary. The GCMS notes reveal the officer's actual reasoning, what specific evidence was missing, and which documents were given weight. 
03 Step 3 — assess the gap: Once you know the real reason, determine whether you can fix it with new evidence. A funds refusal that you can fix with better documentation is a reapplication case. A refusal based on a legal error may warrant judicial review. 
04 Step 4 — reapply with new evidence: Every new application must address the specific refusal grounds and include evidence that was not in the refused file. Reusing the same documents is a waste of a filing fee. 
05 Alternate path — judicial review: If the officer made a legal error (misapplied the test, ignored material evidence, made an unreasonable finding), a lawyer can seek leave for judicial review at the Federal Court. This is slow and expensive — reserve it for cases where the decision was genuinely wrong, not just disappointing. 
What a refusal means — and what it does not mean
A study permit refusal is a decision by an IRCC officer that your application did not satisfy the requirements of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act and Regulations. The officer must state the legal ground for refusal, but the level of detail varies. Most refusals cite section 216(1) of the Regulations (purpose of visit — the officer was not satisfied you will leave Canada at the end of your authorised stay) or the financial requirements in section 220.
A refusal is not a ban. It does not prevent you from reapplying, and it does not create a permanent record of inadmissibility. What it does is put you on notice that your next application must be materially stronger. IRCC officers can see the previous refusal in the system and will check whether you have addressed the stated concerns. A second application with the same evidence as the first is almost always refused for the same reason — the officer is looking for what changed.
Who this guide is for
International students whose Canadian study permit application was refused and who want to understand the specific refusal reason before deciding their next step. Students who received a Procedural Fairness Letter and need to prepare a response before the deadline. Education agents helping students assess whether to reapply or seek legal review.
If you have not yet applied, this guide helps you understand the common refusal grounds so you can avoid them in your initial application. For the full document checklist, read the study permit document checklist . For financial proof requirements, read the proof of funds guide .

02 If the permit expires without a renewal, you have 90 calendar days to apply for restoration of status and a new study permit. You cannot study during the restoration period. 
03 GCMS notes (free, ~30 days through ATIP) reveal the case officer's specific refusal reasons. Without them, reapplying is guesswork. 
04 Key renewal documents: updated letter of enrolment, proof of funds covering tuition plus living expenses at the level confirmed on the IRCC website, passport, and transcripts showing academic progression. 
05 A renewal refusal while you are inside Canada leaves you without status from the date of the decision. A restoration application or departure must follow within 90 days. 
Who this is for — and who it isn't
This guide is for international students in Canada whose study permit is approaching its expiry date and who need to extend their authorisation to complete their program. It covers the renewal process, maintained status, restoration of status after an expiry, GCMS notes for understanding a refusal, and the documents you need for a renewal application. It also applies to students who changed programs or institutions and need a new permit to reflect the change.
This guide is not for students applying for a study permit from outside Canada for the first time — that is an initial application with different documentary requirements. It is not for students applying for a post-graduation work permit (PGWP) — a PGWP is a separate application with its own eligibility rules and is not a study permit renewal. It is not for students whose DLI has permanently lost its designation — you need a new study permit tied to a new DLI, not a renewal of the existing permit.
Maintained status: the rule that keeps you studying
Under section R183(5) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations, if you apply to renew your study permit before it expires, your existing authorisation to study continues under the same conditions until a decision is made on the renewal application. This is called maintained status. It applies automatically upon filing — you do not receive a separate document confirming it. You continue to hold the same study rights, work authorisations (if applicable), and conditions that were on your expiring permit. Maintained status ends when IRCC issues a decision. If the renewal is approved, your new study permit takes effect. If refused, you are out of status from the date of the decision and must either apply for restoration within 90 days or leave Canada.

01 Up to 5 years per entry at the CBSA officer's discretion — not automatic; limited by passport validity and insurance coverage period. 
02 The child or grandchild must meet LICO (Low Income Cut-Off) for the most recent tax year. LICO depends on family size including the visiting parent(s). 
03 The parent must purchase Canadian medical insurance from a Canadian provider (not travel insurance from a home-country insurer) with at least $100,000 coverage, valid for at least 1 year from entry. 
04 The Super Visa is a temporary resident visa (V-1) — it does not authorize work, grant access to provincial health coverage, or create a path to permanent residence independently. 
05 An Immigration Medical Examination (IME) is required as part of the application. The parent must be admissible on health grounds. 
Who this is for — and who it isn't
This guide is for Canadian citizens and permanent residents who want to bring their parents or grandparents to Canada for extended stays of up to 5 years per entry. It is also for parents and grandparents who have been invited to apply and need to understand the documentary requirements from their side: medical insurance, medical exam, and proof of ties to the home country.
This guide is not for parents who want to work in Canada (the Super Visa does not authorize employment), parents who need immediate permanent residence (use PGP sponsorship or explore Humanitarian and Compassionate grounds), or parents who are inadmissible on criminality or health grounds. If the parent has a prior visa refusal or removal order from Canada, consult an immigration lawyer before applying — the Super Visa does not override existing inadmissibility findings.
Super Visa vs PGP sponsorship: which one fits now
The choice between Super Visa and PGP sponsorship is usually about timing. PGP grants permanent residence, but the annual intake is capped, selection is not guaranteed, and processing takes 12-24 months. The sponsor must demonstrate MNI (Minimum Necessary Income) for three consecutive taxation years — not just one. Super Visa only requires LICO for the most recent tax year and is generally processed within a few months.
Most families use the Super Visa as a bridge: the parent visits for extended periods under Super Visa while the PGP application is in progress. The two processes can run in parallel. A Super Visa application does not prejudice a PGP application, and vice versa. The key distinction is that Super Visa is a visitor status — the parent must maintain genuine temporary intent even while a PR application is pending. At the port of entry, the CBSA officer may ask about the PR application and assess whether the parent genuinely intends to leave at the end of the authorized stay. A pending PR application is not, by itself, grounds to refuse entry, but it is a factor the officer weighs in the overall temporary intent assessment.

02 Open employer: Both visas allow you to work for any employer, in any role, without sponsorship or job offer requirements. 
03 Study requirement: Australia requires 2 academic years (92 weeks) of CRICOS-registered study. Canada requires a program of at least 8 months at an eligible DLI. 
04 Family: Both visas allow dependent partners who can work full-time. Children can attend local schools. 
05 PR pathway: Australia uses a points-tested system; Canada uses Express Entry CRS. Both reward local education and work experience with points. 
How the two post-study work visas compare
The Australia Temporary Graduate visa (subclass 485) and the Canada Post-Graduation Work Permit (PGWP) serve the same purpose: giving international graduates time-limited, open work rights after completing their studies. Both are open-employer visas, meaning you can work for any employer in any role without sponsorship. Both are also key stepping stones to permanent residence in their respective countries.
This comparison covers the five factors that matter most for graduates choosing between Australia and Canada: eligibility requirements, visa duration, work rights, family options, and the pathway to permanent residence.
Eligibility requirements
Both visas require completion of a qualifying program of study, but the specific requirements differ.
For the Australia 485 visa (Temporary Graduate stream), you must: hold an eligible recent student visa (usually the subclass 500), be under 50 years of age (under 36 for the Graduate Work stream), have completed at least 2 academic years (92 weeks) of study at a CRICOS-registered institution, meet the Australian Study Requirement, and show competent English (IELTS 6.0 or equivalent). The study must have been completed in Australia within the last 6 months.
For the Canada PGWP, you must: have completed a study program of at least 8 months at a Designated Learning Institution (DLI), hold a valid study permit, and apply within 180 days of receiving your completion letter or transcript. The program must have been pursued full-time during each academic session (with limited exceptions for final semester part-time status).
Key difference: Australia requires a minimum of 2 academic years of study; Canada requires a minimum of 8 months. Australia has an age limit (under 50 for the main stream); Canada has no age limit. See the Australia 485 checklist and the Canada PGWP checklist for detailed document requirements.
Visa duration
How long you can work on each visa depends on your qualification level and, in Australia, where you studied.
Australia's 485 visa duration by qualification: 2 years for bachelor's degrees, 2 years for master's by coursework, 3 years for master's by research, and 4 years for PhD graduates. Students who study and work in designated regional areas can receive an additional 1–2

How the two visa systems compare
The Australian Subclass 500 student visa and the UK Student Route visa serve the same purpose — allowing international students to study at a registered institution — but they differ in structure, evidence requirements, and post-study options. This guide compares both systems across the five factors that matter most: cost, work rights during study, post-study work, family and dependant rules, and refusal risk.
Neither country is universally better. The right choice depends on your academic goals, budget, family situation, and long-term immigration plans. A student with a spouse and children may prefer Australia's more generous dependant rules. A master's applicant who wants a shorter program may prefer the UK's one-year degrees.
Cost: tuition, living expenses, and hidden fees
The total cost of studying in either country is tuition plus living expenses plus health coverage plus visa fees. However, the way these costs are structured differs.
In Australia, undergraduate degrees typically cost AUD 30,000–45,000 per year. Most bachelor's programs run 3 years. Master's programs cost AUD 35,000–50,000 per year and run 1.5–2 years. The Overseas Student Health Cover (OSHC) is mandatory for the entire visa period and costs approximately AUD 600–1,000 per year for single coverage. The student visa application fee is AUD 1,600.
In the UK, undergraduate degrees cost GBP 20,000–38,000 per year for 3 years. Master's programs cost GBP 25,000–45,000 per year and typically run 1 year. The Immigration Health Surcharge (IHS) is approximately GBP 776 per year and is paid upfront for the full visa period. The Student Route visa application fee is GBP 490.
A key difference: UK master's programs are shorter, which means lower total living costs even when annual tuition is higher. Australia's longer programs mean more total living expenses, but OSHC is cheaper than the UK's IHS for longer visa periods. § Key takeaways

02 The UK Immigration Health Surcharge (IHS) covers NHS hospital care but NOT dentistry, optical, or prescription costs. You still need a top-up or private plan for full coverage.

International student health insurance: the systems at a glance
Every major study destination requires international students to have health insurance, but the mechanism differs fundamentally. In the United States , health insurance is typically purchased through the university or from a private insurer, and costs vary widely by state, school, and coverage tier. In the United Kingdom , international students pay the Immigration Health Surcharge as part of the visa application, which grants access to the NHS. In Canada , the system is provincial: some provinces cover international students under the public health plan; others require private insurance through the university or an insurer. Australia requires Overseas Student Health Cover for the entire duration of the student visa, with minimum coverage standards set by the Department of Home Affairs.

05 Work rule: Do not start paid work until your program has officially begun and your permit explicitly authorises it. 
The first week: what actually matters
The first week is not for sightseeing. It is for establishing your legal presence, your financial infrastructure, and your housing safety net. The order matters because some steps block others: you cannot open a UK bank account without proof of address, and you cannot get proof of address without a signed tenancy agreement or a university hall confirmation.
In the US, the first step is SEVIS check-in with your DSO. Without it, your F-1 record is not activated, and you cannot work on campus, apply for a Social Security Number, or remain in status. The second step is updating your US address in SEVIS within 10 days. The third step is opening a bank account with your passport, I-20, and university ID. Health insurance enrolment is usually handled through the university portal but has a hard deadline.
In the UK, BRP collection is time-sensitive: you have 10 days from arrival to collect it from the post office or university collection point. Council tax exemption must be registered with your local council — international students in full-time education are exempt, but you must apply for the exemption; it is not automatic. GP registration should happen in the first two weeks because appointment waiting times near universities can be long.
In Canada, study permit validation happens at the port of entry. The officer stamps your passport and issues the permit. Check the permit immediately for work-authorisation wording and the DLI name. The SIN can be applied for online or at a Service Canada centre and is required for on-campus employment and tax filing. Provincial health insurance enrolment varies: some provinces cover international students immediately; others have a waiting period during which you need private insurance.
Research local transportation options before you arrive so you know how to get from the airport to your accommodation. Many cities offer student transit passes with significant discounts — for example, most US and Canadian universities provide subsidised bus or rail passes, and UK cities offer student-rate monthly travelcards. If you live within walking or cycling distance of campus, you may not need a transit pass at all, saving hundreds of dollars per semester. Reliable transportation options are esse

01 Categories: Home-country loans, school-certified loans, direct private loans, and family or sponsor financing each have different visa implications. 
02 Visa rule: Visa officers prefer liquid, available funds. Conditional loan letters — disbursed only after visa approval — usually create a circular problem. 
03 Currency risk: Borrowing in one currency and repaying from earnings in another exposes you to exchange-rate movements that can raise the real cost of repayment. 
04 Co-signer risk: If a co-signer withdraws support, the lender may freeze disbursements. Read the release terms before signing. 
05 Borrower defense: US federal student loan borrowers may seek discharge through the Department of Education if their school misrepresented the program. 
The four categories of international student financing
Most international students use one or more of four financing categories. Understanding the differences is the first step to choosing a combination that satisfies both your university and your visa officer.
Home-country loans. These are loans from banks or government agencies in your country of citizenship. They often have lower interest rates than international private loans and may not require a co-signer. The downside is currency risk: if your home currency depreciates against the currency of your study destination, the real cost of your program rises. Home-country loans also may not be recognised by foreign universities or visa officers unless the lender has an international presence.
School-certified loans. These are private loans that your university's financial aid office certifies. The school confirms your enrollment and cost of attendance, and the lender disburses funds directly to the school. School certification adds credibility with visa officers because the university has verified the loan amount against actual costs. The downside is that not all universities certify loans for international students, and the certification process can add weeks to your timeline.
Direct private loans. These bypass the university. The lender sends funds to your bank account, and you pay the university yourself. Direct loans are faster to arrange but carry higher scrutiny from visa officers because there is no institutional verification. They also tend to have higher interest rates and stricter co-signer requirements.
Family or sponsor financing. This is the most common source of funding for international students in many countries. A parent, relative, or family business provides the funds. The key requirement is documentation: the visa officer needs to see where the money came from, how long it has been available, and whether it is genuinely accessible. Large unexplained deposits are a common refusal trigger.

02 Content rule: A strong LoR replaces adjectives with evidence. "Hardworking" is weak; "reduced server latency by 40% in Q2 2025" is strong.

Who should write your letter of recommendation
The best recommender is not the most famous person you can find. It is the person who supervised your work most closely and can describe specific outputs with dates, metrics, and context. A professor who taught you in a 200-person lecture hall where you never spoke cannot write a credible letter. A research supervisor who met with you weekly for eight months and reviewed your code, data, or drafts can.
For professional applicants — those with work experience between degrees — a direct manager who can cite project deadlines, team size, budget, and outcomes is usually stronger than a distant executive. For academic applicants, a thesis or dissertation supervisor who can describe your research question, methodology, and contribution is ideal.
Family members should not write LoRs unless they were also your direct supervisor, and even then the conflict of interest weakens the letter. Peer letters — from classmates or colleagues at the same level — are rarely useful unless the program specifically requests them.
Choose your purpose
The LoR that wins a scholarship is not the same LoR that supports a visa application after a refusal. Match the letter's emphasis to the decision-maker's risk framework.
University admission
Emphasize academic readiness, research ability, leadership, and professional impact. Cite specific courses, projects, or publications. Link to the SOP guide for how to align the LoR with your program fit argument.
Visa supporting evidence
Emphasize home-country ties, career progression, and credibility. A supervisor who confirms your post-study employment plan strengthens non-immigrant intent. See the US , UK , or Canada student FAQ for jurisdiction-specific credibility rules.
Scholarship or fellowship
Emphasize impact, leadership, and alignment with the funder's mission. Cite awards, community work, or policy outcomes. The recommender should explain why you, specifically, are a better investment than other qualified applicants.

01 Two audiences: Admissions committees care about fit and potential; visa officers care about non-immigrant intent, funds, and ties to your home country. 
02 Structure: Background, program fit, country rationale, funding, career plan, and honest explanation of weaknesses. 
03 Evidence rule: Every date, amount, and institution name in the SOP must match your CV, transcripts, and financial documents exactly. 
04 Refusal recovery: A reapplication SOP must name the refusal ground by statute — INA §214(b), Appendix V, or IRPA s.11 — and show what has changed. 
05 Cross-use risk: Do not copy an admissions SOP into a visa application without revising for the visa officer's risk framework. 
The two-audience problem
Admissions officers read your SOP to answer one question: will this student succeed in our program and strengthen our cohort? Visa officers read the same document to answer a different question: will this student leave our country when their visa expires? The two officers look at the same paragraph and see different risks.
A paragraph about wanting to work at a Silicon Valley startup after graduation helps admissions at a US computer-science program. It hurts a visa application because it signals immigrant intent under INA §214(b). A paragraph about wanting to bring your spouse and children helps a Canadian DLI understand family context. It can hurt a study-permit application if it shifts the officer's focus from study-plan credibility to family settlement under IRPA s.11.
The fix is not to hide your ambition. The fix is to align each paragraph with the decision-maker who will read it. Use the admissions SOP to show academic depth. Use the visa SOP to show time-bound, home-country-specific career plans and documented financial capacity.
Choose your jurisdiction
The SOP that works for a US F-1 interview will not work for a UK Student Route credibility assessment, and neither will work for a Canadian study permit review under IRPA s.11. Pick the path that matches your current application.
US F-1 applicant
Focus on non-immigrant intent under INA §214(b). Name specific home-country ties, dated employment offers, or property evidence. See the F-1 refusal-recovery template and the US student visas FAQ.
UK Student Route applicant
Focus on financial maintenance under Appendix V and CAS consistency. Show the 28-day balance history and explain any large deposits. See the UK refusal-recovery template and the UK student route FAQ.
Canada study permit applicant
Focus on study-plan specificity and ties under IRPA s.11. Name the exact program, faculty, or research facility, and show why this training is not available in your home country. See the Canada refusal-recovery template and the Canada study permit FAQ.

Side-by-side: who qualifies, how long it lasts, what employer rules apply, and which one builds a clearer path to permanent residence.
One-sentence answer: the most important structural difference is not duration — it is the link to permanent residence. Canada's PGWP feeds directly into a defined PR pathway (the Canadian Experience Class). US post-study work does not. Who this is for
You are a prospective international student choosing between the United States and Canada. Cost, ranking, and city all matter — but the decision you may be putting off is the one this page handles: what happens to your work authorization after graduation, and what does it lead to? 
Who this is not for
Students already enrolled and now choosing employers — talk to your DSO (US) or DLI (Canada) and to licensed counsel.
Applicants comparing pure visitor or tourist routes — different question entirely.
Spouses or dependants comparing accompanying work permits — different rules; out of scope here.
The decision this page helps you make
Which country's post-study work pathway better fits your career trajectory and PR goals ? Cost of living and program quality are real considerations but they sit outside the work-authorization question this page settles.
The controlling sources
Canada side: IRCC's PGWP program delivery instructions and eligibility page.
US side: USCIS guidance on Optional Practical Training (OPT) for F-1 students, including the STEM OPT extension.
Cite each country's official source; do not generalize across them.
How tuition and cost-of-living interact with work authorization
The post-study work permit is only one part of the financial equation. The cost of your degree and the city you study in create different breakeven points depending on which work authorization you get. Canada's international tuition is generally lower than comparable US private and public out-of-state tuition, though the gap narrows for in-state public tuition in the US. Living costs in major Canadian cities (Toronto, Vancouver) are comparable to US tech hubs (San Francisco, New York). However, the Canadian PGWP allows graduates to work for any employer from day one at market rates in Canadian dollars — salaries in Canadian tech and finance hubs are competitive but typically lower in nominal terms than US equivalents.
The US STEM OPT extension provides up to 36 total months of work authorization, which is longer than the standard 3-year PGWP maximum — but OPT employment must be in a role related to the field of study and, during STEM OPT, at an E-Verify employer with a formal training plan. The PGWP has no employer restrictions or training plan requirements, so graduates can take any job, switch employers freely, and do not need employer sponsorship to remain in status. Corrections Policy
We aim for accuracy in every article, but law changes quickly and errors can slip through. This policy explains how we handle mistakes once we know about them.
1. How we learn about errors
Errors reach us through three channels: reader emails, attorney review during quarterly updates, and our own monitoring of government announcements. We treat every report seriously, regardless of source.
2. Error severity levels
Critical: A wrong deadline, fee, or legal requirement that could cause a reader to miss a filing or lose a right. Corrected within 4 hours. Affected readers are notified by email if we have their address.
Significant: A wrong statute citation, outdated procedure, or missing step. Corrected within 48 hours. Noted at the bottom of the article.
Minor: A typo, broken link, or formatting issue. Corrected within 5 business days.
3. Correction process
When we confirm an error, the reviewing attorney drafts the correction. An editor applies it to the article, updates the "Updated" date, and adds a correction note. The note includes the date of the correction and a brief description of what changed. We do not remove the original text without explanation.
4. How to report an error
Email legal@yousafeconsultancy.com with the article URL, the incorrect text, and what you believe is correct. If you can, include a link to the primary source (statute, regulation, or government guidance). We reply within 48 hours to confirm receipt and tell you the expected resolution timeline.
5. No retaliation
We do not retaliate against readers, attorneys, or staff who report errors. Anonymous reports are accepted, though we may need to follow up for source verification.

Editorial Policy
MyCaseworks publishes legal-topic guides to help international students and immigrants understand their rights and obligations. This policy explains how we produce, review, and maintain that content.
1. Purpose and scope
Our articles explain law and procedure in plain language. They are not legal advice and do not create an attorney-client relationship. Every article includes a disclaimer to that effect. The purpose is education: to help readers know what questions to ask, what documents to gather, and what deadlines to watch.
2. Research standards
Writers base every article on primary sources: statute, regulation, government guidance, and court decisions. We cite those sources with direct links where possible. We do not rely on news articles, forums, or unverified social-media posts as primary authority. When a source is behind a paywall or available only in print, we say so.
For immigration content, primary sources include USCIS policy manuals, Federal Register notices, UKVI guidance, IRCC operational bulletins, and the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act. For tenancy content, sources include the Renters' Rights Act 2025, Housing Act 2004, and relevant local authority guidance.
3. Attorney review
Every article is reviewed by a licensed attorney admitted in the relevant jurisdiction before publication. The reviewer checks for legal accuracy, clarity, and completeness. The reviewer's name and bar affiliation appear on the article. If an article has not yet been attorney-reviewed, we label it "Editorial-only" and do not claim it has been vetted by counsel.
We do not publish articles that contain unresolved verification markers or placeholder text. If a fact is uncertain or likely to change, we say so explicitly and give the reader a way to check the current status (for example, linking to the official government page).
4. Update and freshness
We review articles quarterly or whenever the underlying law changes. The "Updated" date at the top of each article reflects the last review. Major legislative changes trigger an immediate review. Minor procedural changes are batched into the next quarterly cycle unless they affect a current filing deadline.
When we update an article, we note what changed in the page metadata. We do not silently rewrite articles without updating the date.
5. Independence and conflicts
MyCaseworks does not accept payment for article placement, favorable coverage, or backlink inclusion. We do not let advertisers or partner organizations influence editorial content. Affiliate links, if any, are disclosed inline and do not affect our recommendations.

02 F-2 children may attend public K-12 full-time at no extra cost beyond regular enrolment.

01 Understand F-2 for Children Know the rules for children on F-2 status

Public K-12 schools accept F-2 children without tuition. You need: proof of residence in the school district, the childs I-20 and F-2 visa, immunization records, and school records from their home country. Contact the school district enrollment office before arrival.

F-2 status ends at age 21. Before this age, your child must: change to F-1 status for college, transfer to another visa category, or leave the US. Start college planning early — F-1 applications, standardized tests, and financial documentation take 12-18 months.

Your childrens F-2 status depends entirely on your F-1 status. If you drop below full-time, violate status, or graduate without OPT, their F-2 status ends. Plan your academic timeline with your childrens schooling in mind.
Overview
Bringing your family to the US while studying on an F-1 visa involves a separate immigration process for each dependent. This guide provides detailed information about bringing-children-to-study-in-us, covering requirements, timelines, and financial considerations.
For families from India

01 Check Eligibility Verify who qualifies as a dependent

01 Canadian study experience adds 15–30 CRS points; 1 year of skilled Canadian work adds another 35–80. 
02 Canadian Experience Class (CEC) is the fastest route — 1 year of NOC TEER 0/1/2/3 Canadian work. 
03 Language scores (IELTS / CELPIP / TEF) move CRS more than almost any other factor — push for CLB 9+.

Online, free. Submit language scores, ECA reference number, work history, education. The system calculates your CRS score immediately.

01 Check Provincial Coverage Determine if your province covers international students

If your province does not cover international students (or during the waiting period), purchase private international student health insurance. Plans cost $500-$1,500 per year. Ensure coverage includes: doctor visits, hospitalization, prescription drugs, dental, and emergency evacuation.

Keep your insurance card with you at all times. For medical visits, present your card before treatment. For prescriptions, pay upfront and submit receipts for reimbursement. Maintain digital copies of all claims and approvals. Know the emergency contact number for your insurance provider.

01 Understand Work Rules Know the work rules for study permit holders
Full-time students at designated learning institutions (DLIs) can work up to 24 hours per week during academic sessions and full-time during scheduled breaks. No separate work permit is needed. Work must stop if you drop to part-time status or take a break from studies.

Only students at DLIs with a valid designation on IRCCs list can work off-campus. Check your schools DLI status before accepting employment. Schools that lose DLI designation trigger loss of work authorization for their students.

The 24-hour cap applies during academic sessions — this is a hard limit across all employers. During scheduled breaks (summer, winter), you can work full-time. Exceeding the 24-hour limit can jeopardize your study permit and future immigration applications.

Work authorization ends when you complete your program. PGWP (Post-Graduation Work Permit) provides a transition, but you should apply before your study permit expires. Maintain accurate records of your work hours and employer information.

The process at a glance
01 Step 1 Confirm tax residency
Most international students with a study permit, Canadian address, and ties (bank, lease, SIN) are deemed tax residents. CRA Form NR74 confirms — your university tax clinic can advise.
02 Step 2 Gather slips
T4 from employers (wages), T4A from scholarships, T2202 from your school (tuition), bank tax slips, and rent receipts (for provincial benefits).
03 Step 3 Pick a filing method
CRA-certified free software (Wealthsimple Tax, TurboTax Free, StudioTax) or a university CVITP volunteer tax clinic for simple returns.
04 Step 4 File by 30 April
Submit via NETFILE for fastest processing. Direct-deposit refunds in 1–2 weeks; paper takes 6–8 weeks.
05 Step 5 Claim GST/HST + provincial credits
These are automatic once you file. The GST/HST credit is paid quarterly (Jul/Oct/Jan/Apr) — typically $300–$500/year for students.

Use your school’s portal. Attach offer letter, course registration, and any required academic-advisor approval. Allow 1–2 weeks processing.

Your DSO updates SEVIS and prints a new I-20 with CPT authorisation on page 2. The dates on the I-20 are the legal employment window — no day earlier, no day later.

Arrive no earlier than 30 days before your programme start date. Attend the mandatory international student orientation where you will learn about SEVIS compliance, health insurance requirements, campus safety, and available support services. Open a US bank account (checking and savings) using your passport and I-20. Get a US phone number — prepaid plans are available without a Social Security Number. If living on campus, confirm your housing assignment and move-in date. If off campus, finalise your lease, set up utilities, and arrange transportation to campus.

§ Key takeaways
01 Regular CPT requires one full academic year of US enrolment before authorisation; Day 1 CPT does not. 
02 Day 1 CPT schools authorise work from the first day of enrolment — high USCIS scrutiny, high audit risk. 
03 CPT must be integral to your curriculum and tied to academic credit, regardless of which model your school uses. 
04 12 months or more of full-time CPT eliminates your post-completion OPT eligibility — permanently.

01 Understand CPT Know the difference between Day 1 CPT and regular CPT
Day 1 CPT allows immediate work authorization from day one of a program, while regular CPT requires one academic year of study. Day 1 CPT is legal but high-risk — USCIS scrutinizes these programs closely. Only use it at universities with legitimate in-person curricula, not CPT mills.
02 Check Eligibility Verify your academic program qualifies for CPT
CPT must be an integral part of your curriculum. You need a job offer letter, a signed CPT recommendation from your DSO, and enrollment in a CPT-authorized course. Day 1 CPT requires your employer to certify the work is directly related to your field of study.
03 Assess Risks Evaluate the visa and immigration risks
Day 1 CPT carries higher RFE risk during H-1B or green card processing. USCIS may question whether you entered the program primarily for work authorization. Maintain full-time enrollment, attend classes in person, and keep all CPT documentation for future applications.
04 Apply Strategically Submit CPT application through your DSO
Submit your CPT application with your job offer, employer letter, and academic justification. Day 1 CPT requires special authorization — ensure your DSO understands your program structure. Processing takes 5-10 business days. Renew CPT each semester.
Overview

For students from India
Indian-cohort applicants are over-represented in Day 1 CPT programmes — and over-represented in subsequent USCIS denials. If you go this route, do a US in-person residency for at least the first term, keep boarding passes, lecture notes, and graded assignments as evidence.

The process at a glance
01 Check Eligibility Verify you can bring dependants
Only PhD/research postgraduate students and government-sponsored students can bring dependants in 2026. Check your CAS Tier field: it must show "PGR" (Postgraduate Research) or your scholarship letter must confirm government sponsorship.
02 Prepare Funds Proof of maintenance for each dependant
UKVI expects £845/month outside London or £1,083/month inside London for each dependant, multiplied by up to 9 months. Funds must have been in your account for 28 consecutive days. Scholarships or official sponsorship letters can substitute.
03 Apply Online Submit separate dependant application
Each dependant submits their own online application via gov.uk. They need: valid passport, relationship proof (marriage/birth certificate with certified translation if needed), tuberculosis test results if from a listed country, and biometric appointment. Pay the visa fee (£490) and IHS surcharge (£1,035/year per dependant).
04 Receive Visa Travel and register in the UK
Dependant visa processing typically takes 3-8 weeks. Priority processing (£500) cuts this to 5 working days. Dependants can arrive before or after the main applicant. Upon arrival, the spouse dependant can work full-time in any role immediately — no skill threshold.

01 No direct F-1 → green card path; almost everyone goes F-1 → OPT/STEM-OPT → H-1B → I-140 → I-485 or consular processing. 
02 EB-1A (extraordinary ability) and EB-1B (outstanding researcher) allow self- or employer-petition without labour cert. 
03 Most graduate students take EB-2 (advanced degree) or EB-3 (skilled worker) — both require labour certification. 
04 EB-2 NIW (National Interest Waiver) skips the labour cert if you can prove your work is in the US national interest. 
05 India and China face decades-long EB-2/EB-3 backlogs due to per-country quotas; EB-1 is the only realistic relief.

Most EB-2/EB-3 cases need a US employer willing to sponsor. Choose roles and companies with proven I-140 history.
02 Step 2 PERM labour certification
Employer files ETA-9089 with DOL. Prevailing wage determination + recruitment campaign + final filing. Usually 6–12 months.
03 Step 3 File I-140
Employer files Form I-140 (Immigrant Petition for Alien Workers). Approval establishes your priority date.
04 Step 4 Wait for visa availability
Check the monthly Visa Bulletin. For India/China EB-2/EB-3, expect 6–15+ year waits as of 2026.
05 Step 5 File I-485 or consular processing
Adjustment of status (I-485) inside the US, or DS-260 consular processing abroad. Final step to permanent resident.

For students from India
Indian-born applicants face the worst EB-2/EB-3 backlogs of any country. Strategy: file the I-140 ASAP for the priority date, then continue building the EB-1B case (citations, peer reviews, original contributions). Cross-chargeability to a non-Indian-born spouse can shave years.

To be eligible, F-1 students must maintain valid immigration status throughout the process. This means full-time enrollment, no unauthorized employment history, and SEVIS compliance. Your DSO plays a crucial role in verifying eligibility and initiating work authorization applications.
