§ Key takeaways
01 F-1 students may work on-campus up to 20 hours/week during term and full-time during breaks — no separate authorisation. 
02 Off-campus work requires CPT, OPT, severe economic hardship, or international-organisation employment authorisation. 
03 Self-employment, freelance gigs, and "side hustles" are off-limits unless an EAD specifically permits it. 
04 Unauthorised employment terminates F-1 status retroactively and triggers unlawful-presence accrual. 
05 Reinstatement after unauthorised work is discretionary and rarely granted — prevention is far cheaper. 
The process at a glance
01 Know the Rules Understand F-1 employment categories
F-1 students have three work authorization paths: on-campus (20 hrs/week during semesters), CPT (authorized internship during studies), and OPT (pre/post-completion work authorization). Each has specific rules, timelines, and application procedures. Working outside these categories violates your status.
02 On-Campus Work Apply for on-campus employment
On-campus jobs (library, dining, research assistant) are automatically authorized with your F-1 status — no separate application needed. You can work up to 20 hours/week during the academic year and full-time during breaks. Find positions through your universitys career portal.
03 Apply for CPT Get Curricular Practical Training authorization
CPT requires one academic year of study (except grad programs requiring immediate CPT). You need a job offer, a signed CPT recommendation from your DSO, and CPT course enrollment. CPT can be part-time or full-time. Over 12 months of full-time CPT eliminates OPT eligibility.
04 Plan for OPT Apply for Optional Practical Training
OPT allows 12 months of work authorization (36 months for STEM). Apply up to 90 days before your program end date. USCIS processing takes 3-5 months. You need a job in your field of study. STEM OPT requires an employer enrolled in E-Verify.
Overview
Navigating work authorization as an F-1 student requires careful attention to regulations and deadlines. This guide covers the key aspects of f1-visa-employment-restrictions, helping you understand your options, obligations, and compliance requirements.
For students from Nigeria
Currency volatility means tuition bills look impossible some semesters. Severe-economic-hardship EAD is a real (if narrow) option — but never take cash hustles to bridge the gap; one unauthorised week can void four years of investment.

§ Key takeaways
01 Marrying a US citizen as an F-1 student is legal — but the immigration consequences require careful planning. 
02 Marriage to a US citizen makes you "immediate relative" with no visa quota — adjustment via I-485 typically 6–18 months. 
03 Marrying another non-immigrant (F-1, H-1B) does NOT automatically grant work authorisation or green card. 
04 F-1 status continues until programme completion or change; F-1 enrolment is not interrupted by marriage. 
05 USCIS scrutinises bona-fide-marriage evidence heavily — joint accounts, joint lease, family photos, shared health insurance. 
The process at a glance
01 Understand Marriage Rules Know how marriage affects F-1 status
Getting married while on F-1 status does not automatically change your immigration status. F-1 students remain on F-1 after marriage. Your spouse can apply for F-2 dependent status. Marrying a US citizen or green card holder opens the door to green card sponsorship.
02 Apply for F-2 Spouse Get F-2 status for your new spouse
Your spouse needs their own I-20 and F-2 visa application. Request an F-2 I-20 from your DSO showing sufficient financial support for two people. If your spouse is already in the US, they may be able to file a change of status rather than leaving for a visa interview.
03 Consider Adjustment If marrying a US citizen, explore green card options
Marriage to a US citizen allows the F-1 student to apply for a marriage-based green card. This is a separate process from F-1 status — consult an immigration attorney. Filing I-130 and I-485 (adjustment of status) while maintaining F-1 status requires careful planning.
04 Maintain F-1 Compliance Keep your F-1 status valid during and after marriage
Marriage does not excuse you from F-1 requirements. Continue full-time enrollment, maintain valid I-20, and follow all F-1 rules. If pursuing a green card through marriage, do not assume F-1 rules no longer apply until the green card is approved.
Overview
International students who wish to bring their family to the US need to understand the dependent visa process thoroughly. 04 F-2 dependents cannot work in the US — there is no F-2 EAD pathway.

01 Check Eligibility Verify requirements for F-2 dependent status
F-2 status is available to the spouse and unmarried children under 21 of F-1 students. You must prove the F-1 student has sufficient financial resources to support dependents. Each dependent needs their own Form I-20 and SEVIS record.
02 Apply for Status Submit the F-2 visa application
The F-1 student requests an F-2 I-20 from their DSO for each dependent. Dependents apply for F-2 visas at a US consulate with the I-20, proof of relationship (marriage certificate, birth certificates), financial documents, and valid passports. Processing times vary by consulate.
03 Understand Restrictions Know what F-2 status allows and prohibits
F-2 dependents cannot work in the US under any circumstances. Spouses can study part-time recreationally (not toward a degree). Children can attend public K-12 school full-time. Full-time degree study requires changing to F-1 status. Plan financially assuming one income.
04 Maintain Status Keep your F-2 status valid
F-2 status is dependent on the F-1 student maintaining their status. If the F-1 student drops below full-time, graduates, or violates status, F-2 status ends simultaneously. File for a change of status or plan departure before the F-1 program ends.

01 F-2 spouses may study only part-time (vocational, recreational, or under part-time enrolment). 
02 F-2 children under 21 may study K-12 full-time AND higher education part-time. 
03 For full-time degree study, F-2 spouses must change status to F-1 — typically via Form I-539. 
04 No SEVIS fee is paid by F-2 dependents — they share the F-1 student’s SEVIS record. 
05 Universities issue separate F-2 I-20s; some schools list dependents on the F-1 student’s portal. 
The process at a glance
01 Understand F-2 Study Limits Know what study is allowed on F-2
F-2 dependents can study part-time for recreation or enrichment, but cannot pursue a full-time degree program. Recreational study includes individual courses, language classes, and non-credit certifications. Full-time degree study requires changing to F-1 status.
02 Explore Part-Time Options Find study options within F-2 rules
Look for: non-credit certificate programs, language learning courses, online classes, community education, and auditing university courses. Many universities allow F-2 spouses to audit classes or take non-degree courses that do not lead to a full degree.
03 Plan F-1 Transition Prepare to change from F-2 to F-1 for degree study
To pursue a full degree, you must change status from F-2 to F-1. This requires: admission to a SEVP-certified school, proof of financial support, a new I-20, and filing Form I-539 with USCIS. Processing takes 3-8 months — plan ahead and maintain valid status during the transition.
04 Time Your Transition Coordinate with the F-1 students program timeline
Changing to F-1 means both you and your spouse are on separate F-1 statuses. Plan the transition so it does not conflict with your spouses graduation or OPT timeline. Consider consulting an immigration attorney for complex family situations.
Overview
For F-1 students planning to bring their spouse and children to the United States, understanding the dependent visa process is essential. This guide covers f2-visa-study-options, from initial application through maintaining status and financial planning.
For families from India
Many Indian-cohort spouses arrive intending to "wait it out" on F-2. Use the time productively — part-time English, professional certifications, GMAT prep — so the F-1 change-of-status case looks like a clear academic plan, not a workaround.

D Only J-1 status allows MBA study

§ Key takeaways
01 F-2 dependents cannot work in the US — paid or unpaid, on-campus or off, remote or in person. 
02 There is no F-2 EAD pathway — unlike H-4 dependents of H-1B holders. 
03 Self-employment, freelance, gig work, and remote work for non-US clients are all banned on F-2 status. 
04 To work, F-2 must change status to F-1 (and use CPT/OPT) or to a working visa like H-1B/L-1. 
05 Volunteering at a true non-profit in unpaid-norm roles is the only exception — same test as for F-1 students. 
The process at a glance
01 Understand F-2 Rules Know that F-2 dependents cannot work
F-2 visa holders are strictly prohibited from working in the US — there is no exception for remote work, freelance, or unpaid positions. Any work, including for a foreign employer while physically in the US, violates F-2 status. Even volunteering at a for-profit company may be considered work.
02 Explore Alternatives Consider changing to work-authorized status
If you need work authorization, options include: changing to F-1 status (study), H-1B (if sponsored by employer), or green card through family sponsorship. F-2 to F-1 change of status is common but requires admission to a school and proof of funds.
03 Avoid Violations Recognize activities that violate F-2 work rules
Remote work for a foreign company, freelance consulting, gig economy work, selling products online, and unpaid internships at for-profit companies all violate F-2 status. Even one paycheck or one day of work can trigger status violation and future inadmissibility.
04 Plan Ahead Build financial independence within the rules
F-2 spouses should plan for no work income during the F-1 students program. Explore: part-time recreational study (build skills), volunteer at non-profits, prepare for future F-1 or H-4 EAD eligibility. Keep skills current through online courses and certifications.
Overview
For F-1 students planning to bring their spouse and children to the United States, understanding the dependent visa process is essential. This guide covers f2-visa-work-authorization-rules, from initial application through maintaining status and financial planning.
For families from India
Many Indian-cohort families assume remote work for a Bangalore-based employer is fine because it does not "show up" in the US. USCIS audits at H-1B/H-4 transitions routinely catch this. If you must earn, change to F-1 or wait for an H-4 EAD when the spouse hits H-1B.

H-1B Visa Guide Guide

§ Key takeaways
01 H-1B is the main bridge from F-1/OPT to long-term US work — but it is gated by an annual cap and a lottery. 
02 Standard cap is 65,000 + 20,000 US master’s. Selection is random; registration opens each March. 
03 Cap-exempt employers (universities, affiliated non-profits, government research) skip the lottery entirely. 
04 A registered H-1B start date of 1 October triggers the "cap-gap" — F-1 status is auto-extended until then. 
05 Only your employer can file the H-1B petition (Form I-129). You cannot self-petition. 
The process at a glance
01 Year 1 of OPT Find a sponsor early
Begin applying to H-1B sponsors before your post-completion OPT begins. Filter job boards by "H-1B sponsor" or check the USCIS H-1B Employer Data Hub.
02 Early March Employer registers you
Your employer creates a USCIS online registration ($10 fee) listing your passport details. Selection results are released by 31 March.
03 April–June Employer files Form I-129
If selected, the employer has a 90-day window to file the full petition with LCA from the Department of Labor, fees, and your evidence (degree, transcripts, passport).
04 June–September Wait for approval
Standard processing runs 2–4 months; premium processing (extra fee) returns a decision in 15 calendar days. Cap-gap protects your F-1 status if your OPT expires in this window.
05 1 October Start H-1B employment
You can begin H-1B work on 1 October of the same year, even if your OPT EAD expired earlier. Your DSO will not issue a new I-20 — your H-1B approval notice (I-797) is your proof of status.
Overview
For F-1 international students, understanding work authorization rules is critical to maintaining lawful status. This comprehensive guide explains h1b-visa-guide-international-students in detail, covering eligibility, application procedures, and compliance obligations.
For students from India
Indian nationals make up roughly 70% of all H-1B selections — but country-of-birth EB green card backlogs run decades. Treat the H-1B as the beginning of a 6-year clock to file an I-140 (EB-2/EB-3), not the end of the process.
Languages: English · Hindi · Tamil · Telugu
§ Test your knowledge
Who is allowed to file an H-1B petition for you?
A You can self-petition once you have a job offer 
B Only a US employer who agrees to sponsor you 
C Your university’s international student office 
D Any licensed US immigration attorney 
Eligibility and Key Requirements
To be eligible, F-1 students must maintain valid immigration status throughout the process. This means full-time enrollment, no unauthorized employment history, and SEVIS compliance. Your DSO plays a crucial role in verifying eligibility and initiating work authorization applications.
For students from China
Chinese applicants face additional 221(g) administrative-processing review for STEM roles in sensitive fields (semiconductors, AI, aerospace). Schedule the visa stamping interview at least 4 weeks before your 1 October start.

§ Key takeaways
01 H-4 is the dependent visa for spouses and children under 21 of H-1B (and certain other H-category) workers. 
02 H-4 EAD is available ONLY to H-4 spouses whose H-1B partner has an approved I-140 OR is in AC21 extension territory. 
03 Apply for H-4 EAD via Form I-765 — typical processing 6–10+ months, biometrics often required. 
04 Standard H-4 (no EAD) status forbids all employment, same as F-2 — including remote and freelance work. 
05 H-4 EAD ends when the H-1B principal’s status ends, when the I-140 is revoked, or upon EAD expiry — no auto-renewal. 
The process at a glance
01 Step 1 Confirm H-1B principal eligibility
Your H-1B spouse needs an approved I-140 OR an AC21-extended H-1B (extended past year 6 due to backlogs). Without either, no H-4 EAD path.
02 Step 2 Gather evidence
I-140 approval notice, current H-1B I-797, marriage certificate, your I-94, passport biopage, current H-4 I-797.
03 Step 3 File Form I-765
Category code (c)(26). Online filing preferred. Filing fee + (often) biometrics fee. File concurrently with H-4 extension if relevant.
04 Step 4 Biometrics + processing
Most applicants attend a biometrics appointment. Processing typically 6–10 months as of 2026 — premium processing not available for (c)(26).
05 Step 5 Receive EAD and notify employer
EAD card arrives by mail. Work can begin on the start date listed; document your status with Form I-9 at any new employer.
Overview
H-4 is a dependent classification for certain family members of H-1B workers. Unlike F-2, some H-4 spouses may apply for employment authorization if the H-1B principal meets AC21 or I-140-based criteria. This guide focuses on eligibility, Form I-765 filing, and practical compliance. Always confirm the current USCIS H-4 EAD rules before you quit a job or file.
For families from India
The H-4 EAD is essentially designed for the Indian-cohort backlog — most beneficiaries are Indian-born spouses awaiting decades-long EB-2/EB-3 visa bulletins. Renew the EAD aggressively (180+ days before expiry) and keep employment records continuous to support the eventual I-485.
Languages: English · Hindi · Tamil · Telugu
§ Test your knowledge
Who can apply for H-4 EAD?
A Any H-4 spouse, immediately upon arrival 
B H-4 spouses whose H-1B partner has an approved I-140 OR is on AC21 H-1B extension 
C Only H-4 children, not spouses 
D Anyone with an SSN 
Eligibility Requirements
H-4 status requires a qualifying relationship to an H-1B principal in valid status. For H-4 EAD, the principal generally needs an approved I-140 or H-1B status extended under AC21 past the sixth year. Not every H-4 spouse qualifies for an EAD. Gather marriage evidence, status documents for both spouses, and the principal’s I-140 or AC21 proof before filing I-765.
For families from China
Chinese-cohort H-4 EAD applicants also benefit, though EB queues are shorter than Indian. Be aware: H-4 EAD does not currently cover children — H-4 children must change to F-1 to study full-time after high school and use CPT/O

§ Key takeaways
01 Most universities require F-1 students to carry health insurance and auto-enrol them in a university plan. 
02 US healthcare is expensive — an ER visit without insurance can cost $3,000+; an inpatient stay $20,000+. 
03 University plans typically cover students for the academic year; OPT students often need separate post-graduation coverage. 
04 Waivers to use external insurance require a plan that meets the university’s minimum coverage thresholds. 
05 Plans must usually meet SEVP guidance: medical evacuation, repatriation, and minimum deductible thresholds. 
The process at a glance
01 Understand Requirements Know your mandatory health insurance obligations
Most US universities require F-1 and J-1 students to carry health insurance that meets minimum coverage standards: at least $100k per accident, $50k per illness, $25k medical evacuation, and $10k repatriation. Some schools auto-enroll you in their plan; others let you waive with proof of comparable coverage.
02 Compare Plans Evaluate university vs. private insurance options
University plans cost $1,500-$4,000 per year but are the simplest option. Private international student plans ($500-$2,000/year) may be cheaper but must meet your schools waiver criteria. Compare deductibles, coverage limits, prescription benefits, and network access before deciding.
03 Check Coverage Verify what your plan covers for your needs
Ensure your plan covers: doctor visits, hospitalization, emergency care, prescription drugs, mental health services, and pre-existing conditions after a waiting period. Some plans exclude sports injuries or adventure activities. Read the policy details carefully before purchasing.
04 Plan for Gaps Handle coverage transitions and gaps
If you graduate, change status, or travel, ensure continuous coverage. OPT students often lose university coverage and need private plans. Short gaps (under 3 months) may be acceptable, but longer gaps can affect future visa applications. Consider catastrophic coverage as a minimum.
Overview
For F-1 international students, understanding work authorization rules is critical to maintaining lawful status. This comprehensive guide explains health-insurance-requirements-f1-students in detail, covering eligibility, application procedures, and compliance obligations.
For students from India
Indian-cohort families often assume US student insurance is generous like ESI/health cards at home. It is not — copays, deductibles, and out-of-network bills add up fast. Save copies of every Explanation of Benefits (EOB) and dispute surprise bills within 60 days.

International Student Tax Treaties: Tax Treaty Guide

§ Key takeaways
01 The US has 60+ income-tax treaties; many include student/trainee articles that exempt income from US tax. 
02 Common student exemptions: wages up to a dollar cap, scholarships, fellowships, training compensation. 
03 You must affirmatively claim the treaty — submit Form 8233 (wages) or W-8BEN (passive income) to the payer. 
04 India is special: Article 21(2) lets F-1 students claim the US standard deduction on Form 1040-NR. 
05 Treaty benefits often have a "look-back" clause — they can be revoked if you stay too long or change purpose. 
The process at a glance
01 Check Eligibility Determine if your country has a tax treaty with the US
The US has tax treaties with over 60 countries that reduce or eliminate withholding on certain types of income for residents of those countries. Check IRS Publication 901 for the full list. Common treaty benefits include tuition waivers and research grants being tax-exempt.
02 Claim the Benefit File Form 8233 with your employer or payer
To claim a tax treaty benefit, file Form 8233 (Exemption From Withholding) with your employer or the payer of your scholarship. You must have a valid SSN or ITIN. Submit the form before the payment is made — retroactive claims require amended returns.
03 File Correctly Report treaty benefits on your tax return
Even if income is exempt under a treaty, you must still report it on your tax return (Form 1040-NR). Attach Form 8833 (Treaty-Based Return Position Disclosure) to explain the exemption. Failure to file correctly can result in IRS notices and lost benefits.
04 Renew Annually Update your treaty claim each year
Tax treaty benefits must be claimed each year. Some treaties limit benefits to a specific number of years (e.g., 5 years for student exemptions). Track your treaty years carefully. When your treaty benefit expires, the income becomes taxable.
Overview
Work authorization is one of the most important topics for F-1 students planning to gain professional experience in the US. This guide walks through international-student-tax-treaties step by step, from eligibility to maintaining compliance after approval.
For students from India
Two big wins for Indian-cohort F-1s: (1) standard deduction via Article 21(2); (2) no separate $5,000 wage cap because the standard deduction structure is more generous overall. Use Sprintax or a non-resident-aware preparer — most US tax-prep tools miss this.

A Form W-2 
B Form 8233 
C Form 1040-NR 
D Form 8843 
Eligibility and Key Requirements
F-1 work eligibility begins after completing one academic year. Your DSO must confirm your status and recommend you in SEVIS. Each work option has specific requirements: CPT needs a job offer, OPT needs a completed degree, and STEM OPT needs an E-Verified employer.
For students from China
US-China Article 20(c) exempts $5,000/year of wages for the entire duration

§ Key takeaways
01 Canadian Computer Science Master's programmes offer a clear path to permanent residence through Express Entry CRS points for Canadian education and work experience. 
02 PGWP (Post-Graduation Work Permit) provides up to 3 years of open work authorisation. Canadian CS work experience counts toward Express Entry eligibility. 
03 Top programmes: University of Toronto (MScAC/MSc), UBC, University of Waterloo (MMath), McGill, and University of Alberta. Tuition: CAD $15,000-$45,000/year for international students. 
04 STEM-designated CS programmes in Canada also qualify for the Global Talent Stream, accelerating work permit processing for tech roles. 
The process at a glance
01 Choose Programme Select MSc, MEng, or professional Master's
Thesis-based MSc (2 years, research-focused, funding often available). MEng/MSc (course-based, 1-2 years, industry-focused). Professional Master's (waterloo MMath, UofT MScAC with internship). Longer programmes (2+ years) yield 3-year PGWP.
02 Meet Requirements Prepare academic credentials
IELTS 6.5-7.0 overall or equivalent. GRE may be required for thesis-based programmes at top universities. Indian students typically need 70%+ (first-class) for competitive programmes.
03 Apply Strategically Target PR-friendly provinces
Ontario (UofT, Waterloo, Western), British Columbia (UBC, SFU, UVic), and Alberta (UofA, UofC) offer strong PNP streams for Master's graduates. Quebec (McGill, Concordia) has its own immigration system (PEQ).
04 Fund Your Studies Seek funding and plan finances

§ Key takeaways
01 Post-completion OPT gives 12 months of US work authorisation after graduation — tied to your major field of study. 
02 File Form I-765 up to 90 days before and no later than 60 days after your programme end date. 
03 Total unemployment during the 12-month OPT period cannot exceed 90 days — every day counts. 
04 You can change employers freely on OPT, as long as each job is directly related to your degree field. 
05 Travel during OPT requires a valid I-20 with DSO travel signature (6 months), a valid F-1 visa stamp, and your EAD card. 
The process at a glance
01 90 Days Before Request OPT recommendation from your DSO
Ask your DSO for an OPT recommendation I-20. They will enter the request in SEVIS and print an I-20 with "OPT request pending" on page 2. This I-20 is valid for 30 days for filing purposes.
02 File I-765 Submit the OPT application to USCIS
Complete Form I-765 online or by mail with filing fee. Include: OPT I-20, passport photos, copies of previous EADs, I-94 record, and prior I-20s from your current degree level. Filing online is faster for tracking.
03 Wait for Receipt Receive the I-797 receipt notice
USCIS mails or emails your I-797 receipt within 2–4 weeks. This notice is your proof of pending status — you cannot work until the EAD is approved. Check USCIS processing times for I-765 (c)(3)(B).
04 EAD Arrives Begin working once the EAD card is in hand
Your Employment Authorisation Document (EAD) arrives 3–6 months after filing. You can start work any day on or after the start date listed on the card. Keep a digital copy at all times.
05 Stay Compliant Report employment within 10 days via SEVP Portal
Log into the SEVP Portal and enter your employer name, address, supervisor, and start date. Report any change of employer, address, or name within 10 days. Track unemployment days — the 90-day clock never stops.

§ Key takeaways
01 F-1 students get an SSN only when they have authorised employment — a job offer or CPT/OPT EAD. 
02 Apply in person at a Social Security office using Form SS-5, your I-20, I-94, passport, and employment letter. 
03 Allow 2–6 weeks for the card. You can start work without the card if employer accepts Form I-9 alternatives. 
04 An SSN is not a work permit — it is just a number. The work permit is your I-20 (on-campus) or EAD (off-campus). 
05 Your SSN is permanent and lifetime — same number even if your status changes to H-1B, green card, or citizen. 
The process at a glance
01 Step 1 Secure a job offer or CPT/OPT authorisation
You cannot apply for an SSN without one. On-campus jobs need only an offer letter; off-campus needs CPT on the I-20 or an OPT EAD card.
02 Step 2 Get a DSO support letter
Your DSO writes a letter confirming F-1 status, full-time enrolment, and employment authorisation. Many offices have a standard template.
03 Step 3 Wait 10+ days after US arrival
SEVIS records sync to the Social Security Administration roughly 10 days after your last port-of-entry. Apply before that and you will be told to come back.
04 Step 4 Visit a Social Security office
Bring Form SS-5 (printed), passport, I-94 printout, I-20, EAD or employer letter, and the DSO letter. SSA staff do not mail forms — bring originals.
05 Step 5 Receive your card by mail
Cards arrive at the US address listed on Form SS-5 in 2–6 weeks. Store the card securely; carrying it daily is discouraged.
Overview
International students on F-1 visas must follow specific rules when seeking employment. This guide provides detailed information about social-security-number-f1-students, including eligibility criteria, application timelines, and compliance requirements.
For students from India
Your US SSN is not equivalent to an Indian Aadhaar or PAN — it ties only to US tax and employment records. Do not share the 9-digit number on social media or with anyone calling about your "student account" — there is no such thing.

§ Key takeaways
01 STEM OPT adds 24 months on top of standard 12-month post-completion OPT — but only for DHS-listed STEM CIP codes. 
02 Your employer must be enrolled in E-Verify and sign a Form I-983 training plan tied to your degree. 
03 File Form I-765 up to 90 days BEFORE your current OPT EAD expires — and you can keep working for 180 days while pending. 
04 Self-employment, agency placements, and unpaid roles are not allowed on STEM OPT. 
05 Reporting cadence is heavier: every 6 months you confirm employment; every 12 months you self-evaluate the I-983. 
The process at a glance
01 Day −90 Confirm STEM eligibility
Your I-20 CIP code must appear on the DHS STEM Designated Degree Program List. The employer must be E-Verify-enrolled at the worksite you will be at.
02 Day −60 Draft Form I-983
You and your employer complete the I-983 training plan: goals, supervision, evaluation cadence, prevailing wage attestation. Your DSO reviews and updates SEVIS.
03 Day −45 Receive STEM I-20
DSO issues a new I-20 with STEM OPT recommendation on page 2. This replaces your standard OPT I-20 in your evidence packet.
04 Day −30 to −1 File Form I-765
Include I-983 (employer copy), STEM I-20, prior EAD copy, photos, fee. Online filing is preferred. You may keep working under the 180-day rule once USCIS receipts the application.
05 Every 6 months Report and evaluate
Validate employment in SEVP Portal at 6, 12, 18, 24 months. Submit a self-evaluation on the I-983 at 12 and 24 months.
Overview
International students on F-1 visas must follow specific rules when seeking employment. This guide provides detailed information about stem-opt-extension-requirements-2026, including eligibility criteria, application timelines, and compliance requirements.
For students from India
STEM OPT gives Indian-cohort graduates three lottery shots at the H-1B (one per fiscal year). Treat each I-983 6-month report as a chance to document promotion and wage-progression evidence — useful later for the I-140 prevailing-wage case.

§ Key takeaways
01 Renting in a new city as an international student requires understanding neighbourhoods, public transit, rental costs, and your tenant rights. 
02 Start your housing search 2-3 months before arrival — popular student neighbourhoods near universities fill quickly, and early searches give you more options and better rates. 
03 Budget for rent plus utilities ($100-$300/month), transportation ($50-$200/month), groceries ($300-$500/month), and other living costs — the total monthly student budget in most cities ranges from $1,500-$3,500 depending on location. 
04 Never send money before viewing a property or verifying the landlord's identity — rental scams targeting international students are common in every city. Use your university's off-campus housing portal or verified platforms. 
The process at a glance
01 Research Neighbourhoods Identify student-friendly areas near your campus
Research neighbourhoods within walking distance or along public transit routes to campus. Consider safety ratings, grocery store access, cost of living, and nightlife/ social options. University housing offices and student forums are excellent resources for honest neighbourhood reviews from current international students.
02 Set Budget Calculate your monthly housing budget
A general rule is to spend no more than 30% of your monthly income (or total budget if not working) on rent. Include utilities, internet, renters insurance, and commuting costs in your total housing budget. Using the university's off-campus housing portal can help you compare rents in different neighbourhoods.
03 Search & View Search for rentals and verify listings
Use the university housing portal, established rental platforms, and local real estate agents. Never pay a deposit before viewing or having someone verify the property. Verify the landlord's identity — legitimate landlords will have a rental license or property registration number if required locally. Ask about the lease renewal terms, increase caps, and whether early termination is allowed.
04 Sign & Move In Review the lease and document condition
Read every clause in the lease — check the rent amount, due date, late fee, term length, subletting policy, maintenance procedures, and termination notice period. Take timestamped photos or video of every room before moving in to support your security deposit return. Keep a copy of the signed lease, rent receipts, and all correspondence with the landlord.
Overview of Student Housing in Albuquerque
The student housing landscape in Albuquerque offers something for every budget. From modern apartment complexes near campus to charming older homes in residential areas, the variety means you can find housing that fits your lifestyle. International students typically spend $1,000–$2,500 per month on rent.

02 Set Budget Calculate your monthly housing budget

Using the university's off-campus housing portal can help you compare rents in different neighbourhoods.

US Tax Guide: Tax Filing

Home

§ Key takeaways
01 Every F-1 student must file Form 8843 every year — even with zero US income. 
02 F-1 students are non-resident aliens for the first 5 calendar years (substantial presence test exemption). 
03 Non-resident aliens file Form 1040-NR — NOT the standard 1040 that resident citizens use. 
04 Tax treaty benefits can wipe out US tax on scholarship or wages — but you must claim them on Form 8233 / W-8BEN. 
05 Filing deadline is 15 April. Form 8843 alone (no income) is due 15 June. 
The process at a glance
01 Step 1 Determine your tax residency
F-1 students are "exempt individuals" for the substantial-presence test for their first 5 calendar years on F-1. Year 6 onward, you may flip to resident alien.
02 Step 2 Gather your tax documents
W-2 (wages), 1042-S (treaty-exempt income, scholarships), 1099 forms (gig income), and 1098-T (tuition — informational only for non-residents).
03 Step 3 Pick the right form
Form 8843 (no-income, mandatory). Add Form 1040-NR if you had US-source income. Free filing tools include Sprintax, Glacier, and IRS Free File for some forms.
04 Step 4 Apply treaty benefits if eligible
India, China, South Korea, and 60+ countries have tax treaties. File Form 8233 with your employer for wage exemptions; W-8BEN for passive income.
05 Step 5 File by the deadline
15 April for returns with income; 15 June for Form 8843-only filers. Sign physical returns in ink and mail to the address on the form (most non-resident returns cannot e-file).
Overview
Work authorization is one of the most important topics for F-1 students planning to gain professional experience in the US. This guide walks through tax-guide-international-students-us step by step, from eligibility to maintaining compliance after approval.
For students from India
India is the ONE country with a treaty article (Article 21(2)) allowing F-1 students to claim the US standard deduction on 1040-NR. This is worth roughly $14,600 in 2026 — do not skip it. Cite the treaty article on your return.
Languages: English · Hindi · Tamil · Telugu
§ Test your knowledge
Your first calendar year on F-1 you earned zero US income. Do you still need to file anything with the IRS?
A No — no income means no filing requirement 
B Yes — Form 8843 is mandatory for every F-1 student 
C Yes — but only if you also have a UK or Canadian income 
D Only if your DSO requests it 
Eligibility and Key Requirements
F-1 work eligibility begins after completing one academic year. Your DSO must confirm your status and recommend you in SEVIS. Each work option has specific requirements: CPT needs a job offer, OPT needs a completed degree, and STEM OPT needs an E-Verified employer.
For students from China
The US-China treaty Article 20(c) exempts up to $5,000/year of personal-services wages from US tax for Chinese F-1 students. File Form 8233 with your employer at the start of the year to stop withholding upfront, rather than chasing a refund.

§ Key takeaways
01 You need a UK bank account to receive wages, set up direct debits, and avoid forex fees on rent. 
02 Required documents: passport, visa/BRP, proof of UK address, and a university enrolment letter. 
03 High-street banks (Barclays, HSBC, Lloyds, NatWest) offer student accounts; Monzo/Starling/Revolut open in minutes via app. 
04 Most accounts are fee-free with no minimum balance — switch if yours starts charging. 
05 Build a UK credit footprint by using the account regularly, paying rent on time, and avoiding overdrafts. 
The process at a glance
01 Step 1 Gather your documents in one folder
Passport (with visa vignette), BRP card, enrolment letter from your university (must show your UK address), and a recent utility bill or tenancy agreement if you have one.
02 Step 2 Decide: app-only vs high-street
Monzo/Starling/Revolut open in 5 minutes via app — useful while you wait for a high-street appointment. High-street banks offer interest-free overdrafts on student accounts but require a branch visit.
03 Step 3 Book your appointment
For high-street banks, book online or via the app. Allow 2–4 weeks in September/October peak season. Bring originals — most banks no longer accept scans.
04 Step 4 Set up direct debits and add to your phone
Once the account is open, set up direct debits for rent and utilities, link to Apple Pay/Google Pay, and download the bank app. Your debit card arrives by post within 5–7 days.
Overview
Navigating UK immigration regulations requires careful attention to visa conditions and deadlines. This guide covers the key aspects of uk-bank-account-international-students, helping international students understand their options and obligations while studying in the United Kingdom.
For students from India
Indian-cohort students typically receive parental forex remittance for living costs. Use Wise or Revolut for the first inbound transfer (mid-market FX, ~£3 fee), then route everything else via your UK Faster Payments-enabled account. Avoid Western Union for rent — the FX margin alone covers a month of groceries.

§ Key takeaways
01 Full-time students are EXEMPT from council tax — but you must apply with proof; it is not automatic. 
02 Get a council tax exemption letter from your university registry, then submit it to your local council. 
03 Halls of residence are usually 100% exempt by default — private rentals require you to apply. 
04 In a mixed household (e.g. student + working partner), council tax is still owed but at a 25% single-occupier discount. 
05 Ignoring a council tax bill leads to enforcement action — pay or apply for exemption within 14 days of any bill. 
The process at a glance
01 Step 1 Request your council tax exemption certificate
Go to your university registry or student services portal — most have a self-service "council tax letter" download. It confirms full-time enrolment, course dates, and your address.
02 Step 2 Find your local council via gov.uk/find-local-council
Type your postcode; the site directs you to the correct council’s tax page. Avoid third-party "council tax exemption" sites — go direct.
03 Step 3 Submit the exemption application online
Most councils have a "Student Exemption" form. Upload the university letter, your name, address, course dates. Processing: 2–4 weeks.
04 Step 4 Update the council when you graduate or move
Your exemption ends the day your course ends. Notify the council within 21 days, or you risk a backdated bill. Same applies when moving address mid-course.
Overview

UK Graduate Route Visa Guide 
Skip to main content MyCaseworks 
Home

Following

§ Key takeaways
01 The Graduate Route gives 2 years post-study work (3 for PhDs) — no sponsor, no salary floor. 
02 Apply from inside the UK before your Student visa expires; you cannot apply from abroad. 
03 The visa cannot be extended — switch to Skilled Worker, Innovator Founder, or another route before it ends. 
04 You can work in any job, at any level, including self-employment — but not as a professional sportsperson. 
05 Time on the Graduate Route does NOT count toward Indefinite Leave to Remain (ILR). 
The process at a glance
01 Before course end Wait for your university to confirm course completion
Your institution must notify UKVI you have successfully completed your eligible course (passed all components). Until they do, you cannot apply — and they will not confirm before the official course end date.
02 Inside UK only Apply online from inside the UK
Submit the application before your Student visa expires. If you leave the UK before applying, you lose eligibility — there is no overseas Graduate Route application.
03 Application step Pay the visa fee and IHS in full upfront
In 2026: application fee £822 plus IHS £776 per year × 2 years (£1,552). Total roughly £2,374 — paid as one upfront sum, no instalments.
04 Biometrics Provide biometrics via the UKVCAS app or appointment
Most applicants reuse biometrics from their Student visa via the UK Immigration: ID Check app. A small minority must attend a UKVCAS service point.
05 Decision Receive your eVisa decision (usually within 8 weeks)
Outcome arrives by email and is linked to your UKVI account. From 2025 the Graduate Route is digital-only — no BRP card is issued.
Overview
For international students in the UK, understanding visa rules is critical to maintaining lawful status. This comprehensive guide explains uk-graduate-route-visa-guide in detail, covering eligibility, application procedures, and compliance obligations specific to the UK immigration system.
For students from India
Indian-cohort graduates are the largest single user of the Graduate Route. Pay the application fee and IHS from your own UK account where possible — if you must use parental forex remittance, keep the conversion receipt, and ensure the bank account holder name on the card matches your application.

UK IHS Guide for Students 
Skip to main content MyCaseworks 
Home

§ Key takeaways
01 IHS gives you access to NHS care just like a UK resident — no insurance claims, no co-pays at point of use. 
02 Students pay the discounted rate of £776/year; full rate is £1,035/year on most other routes. 
03 Pay the FULL multi-year amount upfront — there are no instalments or refunds for early departures. 
04 Dependants pay their own IHS at the same rate; family of four = four separate payments. 
05 Prescriptions, dental, and optical care are NOT free under IHS — they have their own fees. 
The process at a glance
01 Step 1 Calculate your total IHS in advance
Multiply £776 by the years of your visa, rounded up. A 3-year course with 4 months "wrap-up" = 4 × £776 = £3,104. Half-years count as a full year; never round down.
02 Step 2 Pay during the online visa application
IHS is paid in the same flow as the visa fee, before biometrics. The system generates an IHS reference number — screenshot it; you will need it if you query NHS access later.
03 Step 3 Register with a GP within the first month
IHS gives access, not auto-registration. Walk into a local GP surgery with your passport, visa/BRP, and proof of address (university letter works). Registration is free.
04 Step 4 Keep your IHS reference for any disputes
NHS staff occasionally challenge international students at non-GP services. Show the IHS reference + visa; you should never be charged. Report wrongful invoices to the NHS Trust’s overseas patient team.
Overview
International students in the UK must follow specific rules regarding their visa conditions. This guide walks through uk-health-surcharge-ihs-guide step by step, from understanding your entitlements to maintaining compliance after approval.
For students from India
Indian-cohort families often arrange private medical insurance "in case the NHS is slow". You do not need it for visa purposes — IHS is mandatory and covers you. Save the premium and put it toward a dental check-up or optical care, which IHS does not cover.

§ Key takeaways
01 A National Insurance (NI) number is your unique HMRC tax identifier — required for any paid work in the UK. 
02 You can START work without an NI number — show your visa/BRP, then apply within the first 30 days. 
03 Apply online at gov.uk/apply-national-insurance-number; the process is FREE. 
04 You will receive your NI number by letter or in the HMRC app within 2–8 weeks. 
05 Once issued, your NI number is yours for life — store it safely; you will never get a new one. 
The process at a glance
01 Step 1 Wait until you have a UK address
Your NI letter will be posted to the UK address you list. Apply only after you have moved into halls or rented accommodation — applying with a temporary or hotel address risks lost post.
02 Step 2 Apply online at gov.uk/apply-national-insurance-number
The form takes 15–20 minutes. You will need passport details, BRP/visa, UK address, and a current email + UK phone number.
03 Step 3 Wait for the identity verification email
HMRC may email asking for a video call or a photo upload of your passport/BRP. Respond quickly — delays here add weeks to the timeline.
04 Step 4 Tell your employer your NI is "pending"
You can legally start work without an NI number. Give the employer your start date and explain it is pending. They will use a temporary tax code (often emergency tax) until your NI arrives.
05 Step 5 Update HMRC and your employer once issued
When the NI letter arrives, give it to payroll. Any emergency-tax overpayment is refunded via your next paycheque or at the tax-year end through a P800.
Overview
Studying in the UK as an international student comes with specific rights and responsibilities. This guide provides detailed information about uk-national-insurance-number-students, including eligibility criteria, application timelines, and ongoing requirements.
For students from India
Indian-cohort students sometimes share family Aadhaar-style stories with classmates and assume the UK NI is the same — it is similar in function but only for tax and benefits, not ID. You do not need to show your NI letter to landlords, banks, or universities; keep it private.

A No — you must wait for the letter

D Only after 3 months in the UK 
Key Information
As a Student visa holder in the UK, you must study full-time at a licensed sponsor institution, make satisfactory academic progress, and comply with all visa conditions. Reporting obligations include address changes and any gaps in enrollment to your university.
For students from Nigeria
Nigerian-cohort students are heavily targeted by WhatsApp "NI fast-track" scams charging £30–£100. The application is free; processing time is the same for everyone. Forward suspicious messages to 7726 (the UK spam-text reporting line) and report scam sites to ncsc.gov.uk.

On-campus jobs (library, student union, research assistant), retail, hospitality, tutoring, and university ambassador roles are popular with international students. You pay income tax on earnings above £12,570 per year (2026/27 personal allowance) and National Insurance on earnings above £242 per week. Students can claim a tax refund if they overpay. Many employers offer student-friendly contracts with flexible hours around class schedules.

§ Key takeaways
01 Degree-level Student visa holders can work 20 hours/week in term time, full-time in vacations. 
02 Below-degree-level students (foundation, language schools) are capped at 10 hours/week. 
03 A "week" is Monday to Sunday — every minute of paid work counts, even unpaid trial shifts. 
04 You cannot be self-employed, fill a permanent full-time role, or work as a sportsperson/entertainer. 
05 Breaching the 20-hour cap can void your visa, end your degree, and trigger a 10-year ban from re-entry. 
The process at a glance
01 Understand Tier 4 Rules Know the work rules for Student visa holders
Tier 4 (Student) visa holders can work up to 20 hours per week during term time and full-time during official holidays. This limit applies to both paid and unpaid work. Work must stop if you drop below full-time enrollment or your visa conditions change.
02 Check Your Visa Verify your specific work conditions
Your BRP (Biometric Residence Permit) shows your work conditions. Most Student visas allow 20 hrs/week during term time. Some short-term study visas allow only 10 hrs/week. Government-sponsored students may have additional restrictions. Always check the specific conditions on your BRP.
03 Find Permitted Work Know what types of work are allowed
Most work is permitted within the hour limit: retail, hospitality, tutoring, internships, and on-campus positions. Some roles are restricted: professional sportsperson, entertainer, doctor/dentist in training (unless on a recognized foundation program), and self-employment/business.
04 Avoid Violations Stay compliant with work conditions
Exceeding 20 hours/week even by one hour is a visa violation. Keep accurate records of your work hours. If you change programs or extend your visa, verify your work conditions remain the same. Violating work rules can affect future UK immigration applications.
Overview
Navigating UK immigration regulations requires careful attention to visa conditions and deadlines. This guide covers the key aspects of uk-student-visa-work-rules, helping international students understand their options and obligations while studying in the United Kingdom.
For students from India
Indian-cohort students often supplement parental remittance with part-time work. Use a payslip tracker (free apps work) and reconcile each Monday — Indian families used to monthly aggregation can underestimate how strictly the UK weekly cap is enforced.

§ Key takeaways
01 The Skilled Worker visa (formerly Tier 2) is the main route from study to long-term UK settlement. 
02 You need a sponsor on the Home Office register and a Certificate of Sponsorship (CoS) before applying. 
03 From April 2024, the general salary threshold is £38,700/year — or the role’s "going rate", whichever is higher. 
04 New entrant rates (within 4 years of graduation) can be ~20% lower — a critical concession for recent graduates. 
05 Five continuous years on Skilled Worker → eligible to apply for Indefinite Leave to Remain (ILR). 
The process at a glance
01 Step 1 Find a sponsor-licensed employer
Search the Home Office register of licensed sponsors (updated monthly on gov.uk). Filter by sector and tier. Not every company on the register actively hires graduates — confirm before investing in the application.
02 Step 2 Secure a Certificate of Sponsorship (CoS)
Once hired, the employer assigns you a CoS — a digital reference number, not a paper certificate. The CoS lists job title, SOC code, salary, and start date. It is valid for 3 months.
03 Step 3 Check salary against the going rate
Your salary must beat both the general threshold (£38,700) AND the SOC-code going rate. New entrants get ~20% off both. Software developers (SOC 2136), for example, have specific going rates published.
04 Step 4 Apply online and pay fees + IHS
Application fee ~£719 (in-country, 3+ years) or ~£827 (out-of-country). IHS £1,035/year. English language proof (or CAS exemption) required. Application can be made inside or outside the UK.
05 Step 5 Track the ILR clock from day one
5 continuous years on Skilled Worker counts toward ILR. Absences over 180 days in any rolling 12-month period reset the clock — keep a travel log from the first trip.
Overview
Navigating UK immigration regulations requires careful attention to visa conditions and deadlines. This guide covers the key aspects of uk-tier-2-visa-after-study, helping international students understand their options and obligations while studying in the United Kingdom.
For students from India
Indian-cohort graduates are the largest single source of Skilled Worker switchers from study. The £38,700 threshold is a hard ceiling in non-London tech and finance hubs — line up the offer letter before your Graduate Route year 2, and verify the SOC-code going rate (not just the general threshold) for the role.

§ Key takeaways
01 Unpaid internships still count as employment for F-1 visa purposes — even with no paycheck, you need authorisation. 
02 Volunteer work is only safe if it is at a charity, not in a role that would normally be paid. 
03 Unpaid roles in your field of study require CPT or OPT authorisation — the same as paid roles. 
04 Department of Labor "primary beneficiary" test determines whether an unpaid intern is legally an employee. 
05 An unpaid internship without authorisation can be cited as unauthorised employment — terminating F-1 status. 
The process at a glance
01 Check Legality Determine if the internship qualifies for F-1 work authorization
Unpaid internships for F-1 students require proper authorization — either CPT (during studies) or OPT (during or after). Volunteering for a genuine non-profit is different from an unpaid internship at a for-profit company. Without authorization, even unpaid work violates F-1 status.
02 Verify Academic Connection Ensure the internship is tied to your curriculum
For CPT-authorized unpaid internships, the work must be an integral part of your academic program. You need a signed CPT recommendation from your DSO, a letter from the employer confirming the role, and enrollment in a CPT-authorized course. Unpaid positions still require the same paperwork as paid ones.
03 Document Everything Maintain proper records of your internship
Keep your CPT authorization form, employer letters, timesheets, and academic records. Without proper documentation, USCIS may rule that you worked without authorization — even if the internship was unpaid. This can trigger F-1 status violations and future immigration complications.
04 Avoid Common Mistakes Know what F-1 students cannot do
You cannot volunteer at a for-profit company without authorization. You cannot work without CPT/OPT even if the position is unpaid. You cannot retroactively authorize past work. If in doubt, consult your DSO before starting any work.
Overview
For F-1 international students, understanding work authorization rules is critical to maintaining lawful status. This comprehensive guide explains unpaid-internship-rules-f1-students in detail, covering eligibility, application procedures, and compliance obligations.
For students from India
Indian-cohort students often accept unpaid "training" arrangements at Indian-owned US start-ups because the framing feels familiar from internships back home. The US rule is different — if the work would normally be paid, it needs CPT/OPT, regardless of community ties.

A Canada study permit application requires a complete file: a Letter of Acceptance, a study plan or Statement of Purpose, financial evidence, and — for most provinces — a Provincial Attestation Letter. MyCaseworks provides flat-fee document review services mapped to the stages of the study-permit journey, so you can address gaps before an officer sees them.

SOP review — Tracked changes, structure check, and edit flags for your Statement of Purpose or study plan. We verify that it addresses program choice, career goals, and home-country ties.

If your study permit is refused
A refusal under IRPA section 11 means the officer was not satisfied that you meet the requirements of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act. I-765 OPT application review for F-1 students
A single error on Form I-765 can delay your OPT start date or trigger a rejection that costs months. MyCaseworks reviews your form field-by-field against current USCIS instructions, verifies your eligibility-category code against your I-20 OPT recommendation, and checks that your supporting evidence — photos, filing fee, prior EADs, and I-94 — meets intake requirements.
Form I-765 review is performed by US-licensed attorneys. Lead reviewer is Denise Platter Cabrera (CA Bar #298948). This is document review against USCIS instructions, not retained legal representation.
The review focuses on the fields and evidence that USCIS checks first: eligibility category, I-20 recommendation date, photo specification, fee amount, and prior EAD history. Catching these errors before filing avoids the most common rejection triggers and reduces the risk of a Request for Evidence that delays your work authorization.
Students often assume the form is straightforward because it looks like a standard government document. In practice, the I-765 has category-specific requirements that change with USCIS policy updates. A photo that was acceptable two years ago may no longer meet the specification. A fee that was correct last semester may have changed. Our review catches these policy-level details that are easy to miss when filing on your own.
The I-20 OPT recommendation date is especially critical. USCIS requires that the recommendation be dated within 30 days of your I-765 filing. If you file on day 31, USCIS may reject the application regardless of everything else being correct. We verify this date window as part of every review.

The cap-gap extension allows an F-1 student on OPT to continue working legally between the expiration of OPT and the October 1 start date of an approved H-1B petition. The extension is automatic upon a timely filed H-1B petition, but the student's SEVIS record must be updated by the DSO, and the employer must provide a letter confirming the H-1B filing and the continued employment relationship. This template structures that employer confirmation letter.

Employers who filed an H-1B petition for a current F-1 OPT employee and need to confirm cap-gap status.

Deposit dispute letter for UK tenants
Under the Housing Act 2004 and the Renters' Rights Act 2025, most tenancy deposits in England must be protected in a government-approved scheme (TDS, DPS, or MyDeposits) within 30 days of receipt. If the landlord fails to protect the deposit, refuses to return it, or proposes unreasonable deductions, the tenant has specific legal routes: free ADR for protected deposits, and a county court compensation claim of one to three times the deposit for unprotected deposits. This template is for tenants in the protected-but-disputed or protected-but-withheld cases. For the full legal context, see our deposit dispute guide .
Who this template is for
Tenants whose deposit was protected but the landlord has not returned it or has proposed unreasonable deductions.
Tenants who have completed the tenancy, returned the keys, and left the property in the condition required by the tenancy agreement.
International students in England who need a formal letter to escalate a deposit dispute.
Tenants who have already tried informal negotiation and need a written record for ADR or court.
Annotated template
Send by email and recorded delivery. Keep proof of postage. Replace bracketed fields.
DEPOSIT DISPUTE LETTER
[Your full name]
[Your forwarding address]
[Email]
[Phone]
[Landlord / agent full name]
[Address as on tenancy agreement]
[DATE]
Dear [Name],
Tenancy at: [property address]
Tenancy start date: [DD MMM YYYY]
Tenancy end date: [DD MMM YYYY]
Deposit amount: £[amount]
Deposit protection scheme: [TDS / DPS / MyDeposits]
Deposit protection certificate number: [number]
RE: RETURN OF DEPOSIT
1. TENANCY END AND PROPERTY CONDITION
I vacated the property on [date], returned all keys on [date], and left the property in the condition recorded in the move-out check-out report dated [date]. I have attached photographs of the property on departure.
2. DEDUCTIONS DISPUTED
You have proposed deductions of £[amount] for:
• [Deduction 1: e.g., cleaning] — I dispute this because [reason: e.g., the property was professionally cleaned on [date]; invoice attached].
• [Deduction 2: e.g., damage to item] — I dispute this because [reason: e.g., the item was noted as worn in the check-in inventory; see page [X] of the attached inventory].
3. LEGAL POSITION
Under the Housing Act 2004, a deposit protected in an approved scheme must be returned promptly after the tenancy ends, less only reasonable deductions supported by evidence. The Renters' Rights Act 2025 abolished fixed-term tenancies and strengthened tenant rights to challenge deductions.
4. REQUEST FOR ACTION
I request that you:
(a) Release the full deposit of £[amount] to me within 14 days of this letter; or
(b) Provide written evidence and cost estimates for each deduction you maintain.
If I do not receive a satisfactory response within 14 days, I will:
• Open a free ADR case with [scheme name] using the certificate number above; and
• If ADR does not resolve the matter, fil

Financial sponsor letter for Canada study permit
IRCC requires proof that a Canadian study permit applicant has enough money to pay tuition and living expenses for the first year. A sponsor letter is one way to show that a parent, guardian, or spouse will provide those funds. Unlike the US F-1 process, IRCC places heavy emphasis on the source of funds—officers want to see that the money was earned or saved lawfully, not borrowed temporarily for the application. This template structures a sponsor letter around IRCC's published requirements.
Who this template is for
Students whose first-year costs will be covered partly or fully by a family member.
Applicants who have purchased a GIC and need the sponsor letter to explain its source.
Sponsors with documented employment income, business income, or documented savings.
Students applying under the Student Direct Stream or the regular study permit stream.
Annotated template
The sponsor should sign this letter in ink. A notarised signature is recommended if the sponsor is self-employed or if the funds come from a business. Replace bracketed fields.
FINANCIAL SPONSOR LETTER
[Sponsor full name]
[Sponsor address]
[Sponsor phone]
[Sponsor email]
[Date]
To: Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada
Re: Financial support for [Student full name] — study permit
1. SPONSOR DETAILS
I, [Sponsor name], am the [relationship: father / mother / legal guardian / spouse] of [Student name]. I am a citizen of [country] and reside at [address]. I am employed as [job title] at [Employer name] / I am the owner of [Business name], a [type of business] registered in [country] since [year].
2. COMMITMENT
I commit to providing CAD $[amount] to cover [Student name]'s first-year costs at [DLI name]:
• Tuition: CAD $[amount]
• Living expenses: CAD $[amount] (based on IRCC minimum of $[1,334 or 1,023]/month for [number] months)
• Total first-year commitment: CAD $[amount]
This support will continue for the duration of the program or until [Student name] completes the credential, whichever comes first.
3. SOURCE OF FUNDS
The funds are sourced as follows:
• Annual income: CAD $[amount] from [salary / business profit / rental income]
• Savings: CAD $[amount] held at [Bank name], account [number]
• GIC (if applicable): CAD $[amount] purchased from [Canadian bank name] on [date], certificate [number]
The funds have been accumulated over [number] years through [employment / business / savings]. Attached are my [employment letter / business registration / tax returns] and bank statements.
4. RELATIONSHIP TO THE STUDENT
[Student name] is my [son / daughter / ward / spouse]. I have supported [his / her] education since [year]. I have attached [birth certificate / marriage certificate / guardianship order] as proof of relationship.
5. DECLARATION
I declare that the information in this letter is true and accurate. I understand that IRCC may verify these documents with the issuing institutions.
Sincerely,

Financial sponsor letter for US F-1
A financial sponsor letter is a formal declaration that a third party will pay some or all of the costs of a US education. Consular officers read this letter alongside the sponsor's bank statements, tax returns, and employment letter. The letter must be specific about the relationship, the income source, the amount committed, and the duration of support. Generic or overly broad letters are a common reason for F-1 delays and refusals.
Who this template is for
Students whose education will be funded partly or fully by a parent, guardian, or spouse.
Sponsors who are salaried employees with documented tax returns and bank statements.
Students applying to programs where the I-20 cost estimate exceeds their personal savings.
Applicants who need a standardised format that consular officers recognise.
Annotated template
The sponsor should write this letter on official letterhead if employed, or on plain paper with a notarised signature if self-employed. Replace bracketed fields.
FINANCIAL SPONSOR LETTER
[Sponsor full name]
[Sponsor address]
[Sponsor phone]
[Sponsor email]
[Date]
To: US Consulate / USCIS
Re: Financial support for [Student full name] — F-1 student visa
1. SPONSOR DETAILS
I, [Sponsor name], am the [relationship: father / mother / legal guardian / spouse] of [Student name]. I am a citizen of [country] and currently reside at [address]. I am employed as [job title] at [Employer name], where I have worked since [start date]. My gross annual income is [currency and amount], as documented by my employment letter and tax returns.
2. COMMITMENT
I commit to paying the following costs for [Student name]'s education at [University name]:
• Tuition and fees: [currency and amount] per [year / semester / program]
• Living expenses: [currency and amount] per [month / year]
• Health insurance and other required costs: [currency and amount]
• Total commitment: [currency and amount] for the [duration] of the program
This support is unconditional and will continue for the duration of the program or until [Student name] completes the degree, whichever comes first.
3. SOURCE OF FUNDS
The funds will come from:
• My salary at [Employer name]: [currency and amount] per year
• Savings held at [Bank name], account [number], balance [currency and amount] as of [date]
• [Other source, if any: property rental, investment income, etc.]
4. RELATIONSHIP TO THE STUDENT
[Student name] is my [son / daughter / ward / spouse]. I have supported [his / her] education since [year]. Attached are copies of [birth certificate / marriage certificate / guardianship order] proving the relationship.
5. DECLARATION
I declare that the information in this letter is true and accurate. I understand that providing false information may result in visa denial and legal consequences.
Sincerely,
[Sponsor signature]

I-983 training plan for STEM OPT
Form I-983 is the training plan required for a 24-month STEM OPT extension. Both the student and the employer must sign it, and the employer must be enrolled in E-Verify. USCIS and SEVP auditors review I-983s for compliance. A deficient training plan is one of the most common reasons for STEM OPT RFEs (Requests for Evidence) and denials. This template structures the I-983 Section 5 training plan with specific, measurable objectives that satisfy 8 CFR §214.2(f)(10)(ii)(C).
Who this template is for
F-1 students applying for a 24-month STEM OPT extension with an E-Verify employer.
Employers who need a compliant training plan format for their HR or legal files.
Students who received an RFE on a prior I-983 and need to resubmit with stronger objectives.
DSOs who want a standardised template to recommend to students and employers.
Annotated template
This template covers Section 5 of Form I-983 (Training Plan for STEM OPT Students). Sections 1–4 are administrative and should be filled directly on the USCIS form. Replace bracketed fields.
FORM I-983 — SECTION 5: TRAINING PLAN FOR STEM OPT STUDENT
Student name: [Full name]
SEVIS ID: [NXXXXXXXX]
Employer name: [Company name]
E-Verify number: [XXXXXXXX]
Site of activity: [Address where student will work]
Training start date: [DD MMM YYYY]
Training end date: [DD MMM YYYY] (24 months later)
5.1 STUDENT ROLE
Title: [Job title]
Department: [Department name]
Full-time status: Yes / No (must be at least 20 hours/week)
5.2 TRAINING PLAN — LEARNING OBJECTIVES
The student will receive practical training in the following areas:
Objective 1: [Specific technical skill]
Description: The student will learn [specific technique, tool, or methodology] by completing [specific project or task].
Measurement: [How success is measured: e.g., completion of module, passing score on internal assessment, delivery of working code].
Supervisor oversight: [Name], [title], will review progress weekly / bi-weekly.
Objective 2: [Specific technical skill]
Description: The student will apply [academic knowledge] to [industry problem] using [specific technology or process].
Measurement: [Specific deliverable or metric].
Supervisor oversight: [Name], [title], will review progress [frequency].
Objective 3: [Specific technical skill]
Description: The student will gain proficiency in [specific competency] through [specific activity].
Measurement: [Specific deliverable or metric].
Supervisor oversight: [Name], [title], will review progress [frequency].
5.3 EMPLOYER COMMITMENTS
The employer commits to:
• Provide structured and guided work-based learning related to the student STEM degree.
• Assign a supervisor with expertise in [field] and the capacity to train and mentor the student.
• Not replace a full-time or part-time US worker with the student.
• Provide compensation and benefits comparable to similarly situated US workers.

SOP after Canada study permit refusal
Canadian study permit refusals are typically issued under section 11 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA), which gives officers broad discretion to refuse if they are not satisfied the applicant will leave Canada at the end of their stay. The most common sub-grounds are an unclear study plan, insufficient financial proof, weak ties to the home country, and a mismatch between the applicant's academic history and the chosen Canadian program. This template structures a reapplication around those discretionary factors.
Who this template is for
Applicants refused under IRPA s.11 for an unclear or generic study plan.
Students whose financial documents did not show a clear path from income to savings to the GIC or first-year funds.
Applicants with weak ties to their home country who can now demonstrate employment, property, or family obligations.
Students reapplying to the same or a different DLI with a more specific academic and career rationale.
Annotated template
Replace bracketed fields. Each annotation explains what IRCC expects for that section.
STATEMENT OF PURPOSE
[Your full name]
[Passport number]
[Date]
To: Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada
Re: Study permit reapplication — [Program name] at [DLI name]
Prior refusal date: [DD MMM YYYY]
UCI: [UCI from prior application]
1. THE REFUSAL GROUND
My previous study permit application was refused on [date] under section 11 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act. The refusal letter indicated that the officer was not satisfied that [study plan / financial capacity / ties to home country / purpose of visit] was genuine. I have taken the following steps to address those concerns.
2. THE STUDY PLAN — WHY THIS PROGRAM, WHY CANADA, WHY NOW
I am applying to the [program name] at [DLI name] because [specific course, faculty member, research facility, or industry partnership that is unique to this institution].
This program is not available in [home country] because [specific reason: lack of specialisation, different curriculum, no accredited equivalent]. After completing the [credential], I will return to [home country] to [specific job, professional licence, or family business role].
My prior education in [field] at [institution] prepared me for this program by [specific skills]. The gap between my current knowledge and the requirements of my target role is [specific competency], which this program addresses through [module or project name].
3. FINANCIAL CAPACITY
Total first-year cost: CAD $[tuition + living expenses].
Funds available:
• GIC: CAD $[amount] with [Canadian bank name], certificate number [number], purchased on [date].
• First-year tuition balance: CAD $[amount] held at [bank name] in [country].
• Living expenses: CAD $[amount] from [source].

SOP after UK Student Route refusal
UK Student Route refusals fall into four main categories: financial requirement failure, CAS credibility doubts, English language concerns, and genuineness under Appendix V. Unlike US §214(b) refusals, which centre on immigrant intent, UK refusals often focus on whether the funds are genuinely available and whether the course fits the applicant's academic history. This template structures a reapplication SOP around those specific doubts.
Who this template is for
Applicants refused under Appendix V for failing the financial maintenance requirement.
Students whose CAS details conflicted with their financial documents or academic record.
Applicants whose bank statements did not meet the 28-day rule or whose funds were not genuinely accessible.
Students reapplying to the same or a different UK institution with corrected documentation.
Annotated template
Replace bracketed fields. Each annotation explains what UKVI expects for that section.
STATEMENT OF PURPOSE
[Your full name]
[Passport number]
[Date]
To: UK Visas and Immigration
Re: Student Route visa reapplication — [Course name] at [University name]
Prior refusal date: [DD MMM YYYY]
1. THE REFUSAL GROUND
My previous Student Route application was refused on [date]. The refusal notice cited [specific paragraph — e.g., Appendix V para 320(2), financial requirement, CAS mismatch, or English language]. I have reviewed the refusal grounds and taken the following corrective steps.
2. CORRECTIVE STEPS TAKEN
Since the refusal:
• [Financial fix: new bank account with 28-day balance history, corrected sponsor letter, or removed unclear large deposits]
• [CAS fix: obtained corrected CAS from the university with matching course title, fee, and start date]
• [English fix: new SELT result at CEFR B2 or above from an approved provider]
• [Academic fit fix: explained the progression from prior degree to this course with a clear skills gap]
3. FINANCIAL MAINTENANCE

The funds have been held continuously for 28 days. There are no unexplained large deposits. The source of the funds is [salary / savings / property sale / family gift — with supporting document reference].

SOP after F-1 visa refusal
Most F-1 refusals are issued under INA §214(b), which presumes every visa applicant intends to immigrate permanently. The consular officer found your ties to your home country insufficient to overcome that presumption. This template helps you write a new Statement of Purpose that directly addresses the doubted elements—ties, finances, and post-study plans—without contradicting your prior application.
Who this template is for
Students refused under INA §214(b) who are reapplying for the same or a different US program.
Applicants whose financial documents or family ties have changed materially since the first interview.
Students who can show a specific, time-bound post-graduation plan that returns them home.
Applicants whose first SOP was generic and did not address the officer's specific doubt.
Annotated template
Copy the text below into your own document. Replace bracketed fields. Each annotation explains why the field matters and what the consular officer is looking for.
STATEMENT OF PURPOSE
[Your full name]
[Passport number]
[Date]
To: US Consulate [City]
Re: F-1 visa reapplication — [Program name] at [University name]
Prior refusal date: [DD MMM YYYY]
1. THE REFUSAL GROUND
My previous F-1 application was refused under INA §214(b) on [date]. I understand that the consular officer was not satisfied that I have strong enough ties to [home country] to ensure my departure from the United States after my studies.
2. WHAT HAS CHANGED SINCE THE FIRST APPLICATION
Since my last interview, the following material facts have changed:
• [New or strengthened tie — e.g., property ownership, employment offer, family business role]
• [Updated financial evidence — e.g., higher sponsor balance, new scholarship, reduced loan burden]
• [Academic clarity — e.g., changed to a more specific program, added a defined research topic]
3. TIES TO [HOME COUNTRY]
I intend to return to [home country] because:
• [Specific post-graduation role: job title, employer name, expected start date]

• [Professional licensing requirement: name of license, issuing body, requirement that it be obtained domestically]

Study plan for Canada study permit
IRCC officers use the study plan to assess whether an applicant is a "genuine student" under section 11 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act. A strong study plan explains why the specific Canadian program was chosen, how it fits the applicant's academic and career history, and why the applicant will return home after graduation. Generic plans are one of the most common refusal grounds. This template structures the plan around IRCC's published criteria.
Who this template is for
Applicants whose first study permit was refused for an unclear or generic study plan.
Students applying to a program that is not an obvious next step from their prior degree.
Applicants with a gap between their last education and the Canadian program.
Students who can show a direct link between the Canadian credential and a specific home-country job or licence.
Annotated template
The study plan is typically 1–2 pages. Replace bracketed fields. Each annotation explains what IRCC expects.
STUDY PLAN
[Your full name]
[Passport number]
[Date]
To: Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada
Re: Study plan for [Program name] at [DLI name]
1. CURRENT EDUCATION AND WORK BACKGROUND
I hold a [prior degree] in [field] from [Institution name] in [country], completed in [year]. Since [year], I have worked as [job title] at [Employer name], where I [brief description of responsibilities].
2. WHY THIS PROGRAM
I am applying to the [Program name] at [DLI name] because:
• The program offers [specific course, module, or research group] that is not available in [home country].
• The faculty includes [Professor name], whose work on [topic] aligns with my career goal of [specific role].
• The program includes a [co-op / internship / capstone project] with [industry partner type], which will provide practical experience in [specific skill].
3. WHY CANADA
Canada is the right place for this study because:
• [Specific reason: regulatory environment, research funding, industry concentration, or academic specialisation that does not exist at home.]
• The credential is recognised by [professional body or employer in home country].
• The program duration and cost are structured to allow completion without unnecessary delay.
4. CAREER GOAL AND RETURN PLAN
After completing the [credential] in [expected month/year], I will return to [home country] to:
• [Specific job title] at [Employer name] — offer letter attached.
• [Professional licence requirement] — the Canadian credential is a prerequisite for [licence name] issued by [issuing body].
• [Family business role] — my [family member] has confirmed that my return is required by [date] to [specific responsibility].
