title: UK Graduate Route 2026 Changes: What Students Need to Know
body:
Source repository: kylemwalkerpr-ship-it/caseworks
Source site: https://legal.yousafeconsultancy.com
Source URL: https://legal.yousafeconsultancy.com/uk/blog/graduate-route-2026-changes/

UK Graduate Route 2026 Changes: What Students Need to Know 
Skip to main content MyCaseworks 
Home 
Library 
Profile 
Your stats 
Following 
Discover 
Get weekly immigration updates
Join 
In 60 seconds
01 Current duration: 2 years for bachelor's/master's, 3 years for PhD. No changes implemented as of July 2026. 
02 MAC recommended retaining the route in May 2026 with tighter compliance checks rather than a duration cut. 
03 Timing: apply before your Student permission expires. Section 3C leave covers pending in-time applications. 
04 No restrictions on job type or salary level during the Graduate Route — you can work in any role, be self-employed, or be unemployed for a reasonable period. 
05 Graduate Route time does not count toward settlement. You must switch to Skilled Worker or another qualifying route for ILR eligibility. 
What the Graduate Route currently offers
The Graduate Route was introduced in July 2021 as the replacement for the former Post-Study Work visa. It allows international students who have successfully completed a UK degree at a Home Office-licensed sponsor to remain in the UK for two years (bachelor's and master's) or three years (PhD) to work or look for work. There are no restrictions on the type of work, no minimum salary requirement, and no employer sponsorship is needed. You can work as an employee, be self-employed, run a business, or take time to find a role that matches your career plan.
The route is uncapped — there is no annual limit on the number of Graduate Route visas granted. You must have valid Student Route permission at the time your university reports your course completion to UKVI. The application is made from inside the UK, and the visa fee and Immigration Health Surcharge must be paid at the time of application. Dependants who were already in the UK as your dependants during your Student Route can also apply to stay.
What the 2026 proposals would have changed
In early 2026, the Home Office consulted on several proposed changes to the Graduate Route, including: reducing the duration from two years to 18 months for non-PhD graduates; requiring a job offer at or above a minimum salary threshold before the visa could be granted; and restricting the route to graduates of specific universities or courses deemed to have high employability outcomes. These proposals generated significant opposition from universities, business groups, and the Migration Advisory Committee.
The MAC published its formal review in May 2026. It recommended retaining the current two-year/three-year duration structure but strengthening compliance checks to ensure universities are monitoring attendance and course completion. The MAC explicitly advised against introducing a salary threshold or restricting the route by institution type, finding that the route had not been associated with significant abuse and that its economic benefits to the UK outweighed the risks. As of July 2026, the government has not announced whether it will accept or reject the MAC recommendations in full.

01 Primary authority: GOV.UK BRP guidance, UKVI eVisa guidance, UKVI account guidance, and travel/status-sharing guidance 
02 Core rule: A Biometric Residence Permit (BRP) is the physical proof of your UK immigration status. If it is lost, stolen, or damaged, you are legally required to report it to UKVI within three months. Who this is for — and who it isn't
This guide is for EU, EEA, and Swiss nationals who are resident in the UK and need to regularise their immigration status under the EU Settlement Scheme. It is also for family members of those nationals — spouses, partners, children, and dependent relatives — who need to apply in their own right. If you are an Irish citizen, you do not need to apply, but this guide explains your optional application route if you want formal documentation of your UK residence rights.
This guide is not for non-EEA nationals who have no family connection to an EU/EEA/Swiss citizen — those applicants should use the relevant points-based or family visa route (Skilled Worker, Student Route, or Appendix FM partner visa). It is also not for EU nationals who arrived in the UK after 31 December 2020 and do not have a family connection to a qualifying EU citizen — those applicants will need a visa under the new points-based system rather than the EUSS.
How the EU Settlement Scheme works in practice
The EU Settlement Scheme was established by Appendix EU of the Immigration Rules, implementing the UK's obligations under the Withdrawal Agreement with the European Union. The scheme grants two forms of immigration status: settled status (indefinite leave to enter or remain) and pre-settled status (limited leave to remain for five years). To qualify for settled status, an applicant must show five continuous years of qualifying residence in the UK, where each 12-month period contains no more than six months of absence from the UK (subject to specific exceptions for childbirth, serious illness, study, or overseas posting). An applicant who can show less than five years receives pre-settled status, which is valid for five years from the date of grant. Family visa parent route: the rule in plain English
Appendix FM is the part of the Immigration Rules that covers family visas. Within it, the parent route (paragraphs E-ECPT.2.1–2.4) allows a parent outside the UK to join a child who is living in the UK, where that child is British, settled, or has pre-settled status.
The route has two possible grounds for eligibility — you need to meet one of them:
Sole parental responsibility. You alone make all major decisions about the child. The other parent has no role — by choice, death, or court order. This must be proven with contemporaneous records, not just a statement.
Seven-year child residence. The child has lived in the UK continuously for at least 7 years, and it would not be reasonable to expect the child to leave the UK if the application were refused.
Additionally, the applicant must show adequate maintenance (enough income to support the family without public funds), suitable accommodation, and English at CEFR level A1.

06 Pitfalls include applying before completion is reported, applying outside the UK, travelling while pending, assuming every dependant can join, and missing the 2027 duration change. 
The rule in plain English
The Graduate Route lets international students who have successfully completed an eligible UK degree stay in the UK for post-study work. Non-doctoral grants last 2 years if applied for by December 31, 2026, reducing to 18 months from January 1, 2027. Doctoral grants last 3 years regardless of when applied. The route is unsponsored  you do not need a job offer to apply.
Key requirement: Your education provider (sponsor) must have reported your successful completion to the Home Office before you apply. If they have not yet submitted the report, your application will be refused, even if you have physically graduated. The sponsor report is submitted electronically through the Home Office sponsor management system, and your university may have a specific process and timeline for submitting these reports after the results are finalised. Ground 4A in context: why this ground exists
Ground 4A was inserted into Schedule 2 of the Housing Act 1988 by the Renters' Rights Act 2024 specifically to fill a gap created by the abolition of Section 21 evictions. § Key takeaways
01 On 1 May 2026 every assured shorthold tenancy in England converted to an assured periodic tenancy; fixed terms no longer have legal effect. 
02 A tenant can end a periodic tenancy by serving two months' written notice ending on a rent day, at any time. 
03 A landlord can only end the tenancy on a Section 8 ground; there is no 'no-fault' eviction route anymore. 
04 Rent can only rise once per year via a Section 13 notice in the prescribed form; an informal email is not sufficient. 
05 A tenant can challenge a Section 13 rent increase at the First-tier Tribunal within one month of receiving the notice. 
06 Scotland has used the private residential tenancy (PRT) since December 2017; Wales uses the Renting Homes (Wales) Act 2016. 
Last updated 2026-05-14 · Editorial review by MyCaseworks Editorial 
In 60 seconds
On 1 May 2026 every assured shorthold tenancy in England converted to an assured periodic tenancy.
No more fixed terms — old "12-month minimum" clauses have no legal effect.
You can leave on two months' written notice ending on a rent day, at any time.
Your landlord can only end the tenancy on a Section 8 ground — no "two months without a reason" anymore.
Rent can only rise once per year via a Section 13 notice; challengeable at the First-tier Tribunal within one month.
One-sentence answer
On 1 May 2026 every assured shorthold tenancy converted to an assured periodic tenancy — there is no longer a fixed term, you can leave on two months' written notice at any time, your landlord must use a Section 8 ground to end it, and rent can only rise once a year via a Section 13 notice you can challenge.
What "periodic" means now
A periodic tenancy is a rolling tenancy with a period (almost always one month, matching the rent cycle). It continues period by period until one side ends it lawfully.
What this changes in practice:
You are no longer locked in to a 6-month, 12-month, or any other fixed term. Old contracts that said "12-month minimum" have no effect on the new structure.
The landlord cannot make you sign a new fixed term as a condition of continuing.
A "break clause" is meaningless — you don't need one to leave.
The tenancy ends only when a tenant serves notice, both sides agree, or the landlord obtains possession on a Section 8 ground.
Notice you give to leave (two months, in writing)
As a tenant, you can end a periodic tenancy by serving the landlord two months' written notice at any time, ending on a rent day. The notice must be:
In writing. Email is usually fine but check what the contract says about service.
Signed. On a joint tenancy, any one joint tenant's notice ends the whole tenancy for everyone — check all housemates agree before you use it.
Dated. 
Served on the landlord at the contractual address (or at the agent if the contract says so).
If you need to leave faster, you can ask the landlord to accept an earlier surrender — that requires the landlord's written agreement. Don't move out

01 The standard ILR qualifying period for Skilled Workers is 5 years of continuous lawful residence. Time on Tier 2 General, Skilled Worker, Global Talent, and some other work visas counts toward the 5 years. 
02 You must not exceed 180 days outside the UK in any rolling 12-month period. All absences count — business travel, holidays, family visits. The 12-month window rolls backward from the ILR application date. 
03 Salary requirement: at or above the going rate for your SOC occupation code, or the general threshold — whichever is higher. Check current thresholds on the GOV.UK Skilled Worker page at the date of application. 
04 Life in the UK test (£50, 24 questions, 75% pass mark) and English language at B1 level are required. The test result never expires — take it early to avoid delays. 
05 Your employer must provide a sponsor letter confirming your job title, SOC code, salary, ongoing need, and dates of employment. The letter must be dated within one month of the ILR application. 
Who this is for — and who it isn't
This guide is for Skilled Worker visa holders (and former Tier 2 General visa holders) approaching the 5-year mark and preparing to apply for Indefinite Leave to Remain. It covers the continuous residence requirement, the 180-day absence rule, the salary threshold at the date of application, the Life in the UK test and English language requirement, and the employer letter that your sponsor must provide. It also covers applicants who changed employers during the 5-year period and need to confirm their residence was continuous across multiple sponsors.
This guide is not for ILR applicants on the 10-year long residence route, the family route (spouse/partner of a British citizen or settled person), the Global Talent route (which has a 3-year accelerated path), or the Innovator Founder route. It is also not for applicants who have exceeded 180 days of absence in a rolling 12-month period — if your continuous residence is broken, the 5-year clock resets and this guide's timeline does not apply to you. If your absence record is marginal (175-185 days in any 12-month window), consult an immigration adviser before applying — a refusal on absence grounds resets your qualifying period.
The 180-day absence rule: how it works and how to calculate it
The continuous residence requirement for ILR is broken if you have been outside the UK for more than 180 days in any rolling 12-month period during the 5-year qualifying period. Every full day outside the UK counts. The day of departure and the day of arrival in the UK are not counted as absences — only full days spent entirely outside the UK count. The 12-month period is rolling: start from the date of your ILR application and count backward in 12-month blocks, checking each block for a total that exceeds 180 days. Repeat the exercise for each overlapping 12-month period throughout the 5 years.

UK Skilled Worker visa guide
The UK Skilled Worker visa is the main route for non-UK nationals who have a job offer from a licensed sponsor at or above the salary threshold. It replaced the Tier 2 (General) route in December 2020 and now covers a broad range of occupations, from software engineers and healthcare workers to construction managers and academics. This guide orients you to the cluster: how the two-test salary system works, what a Certificate of Sponsorship is, how to switch employers without breaking your visa, how to bring dependants, and what employers must do to obtain a sponsor licence. If you are a software engineer, healthcare worker, or tech professional, start here and follow the path that matches your situation. Every article in this cluster links back to this guide, so you can navigate depth-first without losing context.
Last updated 2026-05-19 · Editorial review by MyCaseworks Editorial 
Reviewer programs for UK matters are under development; until those programs launch, UK content is editorial-only.
How the Skilled Worker route works
The Skilled Worker visa is a points-based immigration route. Applicants must score a minimum of 70 points under the Home Office tradeable points system. All applicants must score 20 points for a job at the appropriate skill level (RQF 3 or above), 20 points for English language proficiency at B1 level, and 20 points for salary meeting the minimum threshold (currently GBP 38,700 per year for most applicants). The remaining 10 points can be earned through tradeable attributes: a PhD relevant to the job (10 points), a job in a shortage occupation (10 points), or new entrant status (10 points, which also reduces the salary threshold to approximately 70% of the going rate). Understanding the points system is essential before preparing an application — the tradeable points can make the difference between a qualifying and non-qualifying salary offer.
The application process begins with the employer. Before a worker can apply, the employer must assign a Certificate of Sponsorship through the Sponsor Management System. The CoS confirms the job title, occupation code (SOC 2020), salary, and that the employer holds a valid A-rated sponsor licence. Once the CoS is assigned (it is valid for 3 months), the worker can submit the visa application online, pay the fee and Immigration Health Surcharge, attend a biometric appointment (or use the UK Immigration: ID Check app), and submit supporting documents. The processing time from inside the UK is approximately 8 weeks; from outside the UK, approximately 3 weeks after biometrics.
The Skilled Worker visa is typically granted for up to 5 years, with extensions available. Settlement (indefinite leave to remain) is available after 5 years of continuous residence, provided the applicant meets the continuous residence requirement (no more than 180 days absences from the UK in any rolling 12-month period) and passes the Life in the UK test. How much money do I need to show for a UK Student Route visa?
You must show enough money to cover your first year of course fees plus living costs. The living cost amount is £1,529 per month if studying in London, or £1,171 per month outside London, for up to 9 months. If your course is 9 months or longer, you show 9 months of living costs. If your course is shorter, you show the full course length. The funds must have been in the account for the required evidence period ending no more than 31 days before you apply. If you are using a student loan, the loan letter must confirm the amount, that it is available to you, and the disbursement schedule. Verify the exact figures on GOV.UK before applying, as they are updated periodically.

Renting as a student in the UK means navigating different legal regimes depending on whether your university is in Scotland or England. From 1 May 2026, the Renters' Rights Act 2025 fundamentally changed the tenancy landscape for students in England, while Scotland has operated under its own Private Residential Tenancy (PRT) framework since December 2017. This guide explains which legal regime applies to you, what protections you have in Glasgow, Edinburgh, Bristol, Leeds, Liverpool, Manchester and Nottingham, and what to check before signing a tenancy agreement in 2026.
If you are an international student also navigating visa requirements, our Student visa document checklist covers the immigration documentation you need alongside your housing arrangements. For broader coverage of how the Renters' Rights Act affects all tenants, see our guide to renters' rights in 2026 .
Which legal regime applies to your city
The UK does not have a single national tenancy law for students. Your rights depend on which side of the border your university sits:
City Legal regime Tenancy type (private rentals) Glasgow Scotland Private Residential Tenancy (PRT) Edinburgh Scotland Private Residential Tenancy (PRT) Bristol England Assured periodic tenancy (from 1 May 2026) Leeds England Assured periodic tenancy (from 1 May 2026) Liverpool England Assured periodic tenancy (from 1 May 2026) Manchester England Assured periodic tenancy (from 1 May 2026) Nottingham England Assured periodic tenancy (from 1 May 2026) If you rent directly from your university (on-campus halls), you will typically hold a licence to occupy rather than a tenancy, and the rules below may not apply. Purpose-built student accommodation (PBSA) operated by private providers may fall under separate codes of practice. The guidance here covers private rentals with landlords or letting agents — the sector most international and UK students enter when moving off-campus in their second or third year.
For city-by-city deep dives, MyCaseworks also maintains dedicated pages for Glasgow , Edinburgh , Bristol , Leeds , Liverpool , Manchester and Nottingham .
Part 1: Scotland — Glasgow and Edinburgh
The Private Residential Tenancy (PRT) framework
Since 1 December 2017, all new private tenancies in Scotland have been Private Residential Tenancies (PRTs) under the Private Housing (Tenancies) (Scotland) Act 2016. A PRT has no fixed end date. Your landlord cannot include a minimum term or expected end date in your agreement, and you can give notice to leave at any point after the tenancy begins. This is confirmed by the Scottish Government's private residential tenancy guidance for tenants and the enacted legislation on legislation.gov.uk.

In 60 seconds
01 Admin review deadline: 14 days from refusal receipt (in-country) or 28 days (out-of-country). The clock starts on the date the refusal notice was issued, not the date you opened it. 
02 Admin review examines caseworking errors only — no new evidence allowed. If the decision was correct based on the evidence submitted, admin review will not overturn it. 
03 A fresh application allows corrected evidence (new bank statements, new CAS, new English test). It resets the clock but requires a new application fee and Immigration Health Surcharge. 
04 A Pre-Action Protocol (PAP) letter is a pre-litigation step alleging unlawful decision-making — procedural unfairness, failure to follow published guidance, or irrationality. 
05 Common Student Route refusal grounds: maintenance shortfall (including the 28-day rule), credibility interview failure, CAS withdrawn or expired, English test not on SELT list, academic progression not demonstrated. 
Who this is for — and who it isn't
This guide is for international students whose Student Route (formerly Tier 4) visa application has been refused by UKVI. It covers the three options available after refusal: admin review, fresh application, and PAP letter. It explains the deadlines, what each process can and cannot achieve, and how to read a refusal notice to identify the correct next step.
This guide is not for refusals of Skilled Worker, Graduate Route, family visas, or visit visas — each has its own refusal and review framework. It is also not a substitute for immigration legal advice when the refusal involves complex grounds such as deception allegations, general grounds for refusal under Part 9, or a previous adverse immigration history. If your refusal notice cites paragraph 9.4.1 (false representations) or 9.7.1 (previous breach of immigration laws), consult a regulated immigration adviser before responding — the consequences of an adverse finding on these grounds extend beyond the current application.
Read the refusal notice first: what the paragraph numbers mean
The UKVI refusal notice is structured around Immigration Rules paragraphs. The key paragraphs for Student Route refusals are:
ST 1.1-ST 1.5 (valid application): The application was not validly made — fee not paid, biometrics not enrolled, form incomplete, or passport not provided. Usually a correctable error in a fresh application rather than an admin review issue.
ST 3.1-ST 3.3 (entry clearance requirements): Eligibility under the Student Route was not demonstrated. This is the most common refusal paragraph and covers the substantive requirements.
ST 12.3-ST 12.4 (financial requirement): Maintenance funds were not demonstrated at the required level, for the required period, or in the required format. Often involves the 28-day rule — the funds must have been held for 28 consecutive days ending no more than 31 days before the application date. A one-day breach results in refusal.

UK Renters' Rights Act 2025 FAQ
Clear answers for tenants and students renting in England. This FAQ covers the Renters' Rights Act 2025, Section 21 abolition, deposit disputes, rent increases, and how to leave a tenancy safely. For deeper guidance, see our cluster articles below.
The Renters' Rights Act 2025, which took full effect on 1 May 2026, represents the most significant reform of English private rented sector law in a generation. It abolished the Section 21 no-fault eviction procedure, converted all existing assured shorthold tenancies to periodic tenancies, introduced new mandatory and discretionary possession grounds under Section 8, and strengthened rent increase protections by requiring landlords to use a prescribed Section 13 form with a one-month tribunal challenge window. The Act also introduced the Decent Homes Standard for the private rented sector, established a new Private Rented Sector Database, and created a new Ombudsman scheme for tenant complaints. These changes apply to all assured shorthold tenancies in England, regardless of when they were signed, and they affect every tenant currently renting from a private landlord in the English jurisdiction.
For international students renting in England, understanding the post-May 2026 framework is particularly important because the abolition of Section 21 and the transition to periodic-only tenancies removes the previous flexibility that some landlords relied on to manage academic-year turnover outside the Ground 4A student-HMO framework. You now have stronger procedural protections against eviction, but you also need to be more careful about how you give notice when you want to leave, how you respond to possession notices, and how you challenge unlawful rent increases or deposit deductions. The answers below address the most common questions we receive from tenants navigating these new rules, with cross-references to the detailed cluster articles where each topic is covered in full.
If you have received a possession notice from your landlord, start by identifying whether it is a valid Section 8 notice. A valid notice must use Form 3 (not the old Form 6A which was used for Section 21), name a specific ground from Schedule 2 of the Housing Act 1988 as amended, state the date after which possession proceedings can begin (which varies by ground), and include the prescribed information about where the tenant can get advice. If the notice does not meet these requirements, it is likely invalid and the landlord must serve a corrected notice before they can proceed to court. 02 Key requirement: The visitor must satisfy UKVI they are a genuine visitor who will leave the UK at the end of their visit, can support themselves without working, and will not live in the UK for extended periods through frequent visits.

The Standard Visitor route: what it covers
The Standard Visitor visa (Appendix V of the Immigration Rules) is a single route covering tourism, visiting family and friends, attending events, short study, and certain business activities. For family members of international students, the most common purposes are: attending a graduation ceremony, visiting during a holiday period, and helping the student settle in at the start of a course. There is no separate category for parents or family — the same application form and evidence requirements apply regardless of the visit purpose.
The Standard Visitor visa does not permit work (paid or unpaid), access to public funds, marriage or civil partnership registration, or long-term study. A visitor who stays beyond the permitted period becomes an overstayer with consequences for future UK immigration applications. The maximum stay on a Standard Visitor visa is 6 months per visit. Long-term visitor visas (2, 5, or 10 years) allow multiple entries but each individual stay remains limited to 6 months.

What 0300 number eligibility means
0300 numbers are UK non-geographic numbers. They are not tied to a particular city or area code, so callers can reach an organisation without knowing its physical location. Ofcom, the UK communications regulator, reserves the 0300 range for specific categories of organisations.
The range is associated with public services and organisations that operate without distributing profits to owners or members. Eligible users can include government departments, local authorities, emergency-related services, registered charities, and other qualifying not-for-profit bodies. The precise category depends on the organisation’s legal status and the service it provides.
Ofcom’s numbering rules are the starting point. The relevant rules appear in the National Telephone Numbering Plan and Ofcom’s guidance for 03 numbers:

Ofcom guidance on 03 numbers: https://www.ofcom.org.uk/phones-and-broadband/phone-numbers 
The term “eligibility” has two parts. First, your organisation must fall within an allowed user category. Second, your intended use must comply with the provider’s service terms and Ofcom’s numbering conditions. Meeting one part does not automatically settle the other.

§ Key takeaways
01 Many F, J, M, and Q visa students file as nonresident aliens for federal tax until the substantial-presence counting rules make them residents for tax purposes. 
02 Teach tax residence before form selection; the wrong residency status can make the whole return wrong. 
03 Core documents include W-2, 1042-S, 1099 if any, passport, visa history, I-20 or DS-2019, SSN or ITIN, treaty article details, Form 8843, and state tax documents if required. 
04 Sequence the file in the order a reviewer will test it: eligibility first, deadline second, evidence third, and payment or submission last. 
05 Pitfalls include using resident-only software, skipping Form 8843, claiming treaty benefits without evidence, ignoring state tax, and using SSN/ITIN incorrectly. 
How international student tax filing works
International students on F, J, M, or Q visas have specific tax filing obligations. Determine whether you are a resident or nonresident alien using the substantial presence test from IRS Publication 519. Students are generally exempt for the first 5 calendar years. File Form 8843 annually regardless of income.
The substantial presence test counts the number of days you have been present in the United States over a three-year period using a weighted formula. You are considered a resident alien if you were present in the US for at least 31 days during the current calendar year and 183 days during the three-year period that includes the current year and the two preceding years. The 183-day total is calculated by adding all the days you were present in the current year, one-third of the days you were present in the first preceding year, and one-sixth of the days you were present in the second preceding year.
F-1 and J-1 students are classified as exempt individuals for the substantial presence test if they substantially comply with the requirements of their visa status. The exemption applies for a maximum of 5 calendar years. Students who have been in the United States for more than 5 calendar years must apply the substantial presence test to determine their tax residency status. If you had US-source income including wages or scholarships, file Form 1040-NR. Use nonresident-specific software like Sprintax. The IRS provides full guidance in Publication 519 and Form 1040-

What is the cap-gap extension?
The cap-gap extension is an automatic benefit for F-1 students whose OPT or STEM OPT expires between April 1 and September 30 of the H-1B fiscal year. If your employer filed a timely cap-subject H-1B petition requesting change of status, your F-1 status and (if applicable) work authorization extend automatically through September 30.
No separate application to USCIS is required. Your DSO issues an updated I-20 noting the cap-gap extension, and your SEVIS record is updated to reflect the bridge period. The key requirement is that the H-1B petition was timely filed (received by USCIS during the filing window) and requests a change of status — consular processing does not qualify for cap-gap.
The cap-gap extension is not guaranteed. If USCIS selects your registration but the petition is never filed, or if the filing is rejected as improperly filed, cap-gap does not apply. Your DSO will confirm eligibility once they receive proof of filing from your employer.
Eligibility timeline and key dates
Understanding the timeline is critical. Here is how the cap-gap calendar works by scenario:
OPT expires May 30, H-1B filed April 1: Cap-gap starts May 31, runs through September 30. You can continue working for the petitioning employer during this period.
STEM OPT expires August 15, H-1B filed April 1: Cap-gap starts August 16, runs through September 30. STEM OPT benefits (including the 180-day automatic extension) apply until cap-gap takes over.
OPT expires March 15 (before April 1): No cap-gap available because OPT expired before the filing window. You must maintain lawful status through other means (e.g., starting a new degree program or departing).
Your DSO must issue the cap-gap I-20 within 30 days of receiving the H-1B receipt notice. If your OPT expires before the DSO issues the I-20, your work authorization pauses until the I-20 is issued — but your F-1 status remains valid as long as the petition was timely filed.
What your DSO needs from you to issue the cap-gap I-20
Your Designated School Official (DSO) cannot issue the cap-gap I-20 automatically — they need proof that your H-1B petition was actually filed. The most common mistake students make is assuming the DSO will know about the filing through SEVIS or the H-1B registration system. In reality, the DSO relies entirely on evidence that you or your employer provide.

How service center assignment affects your timeline
One of the biggest variables in marriage-based green card processing is which USCIS service center adjudicates your I-130 petition. While applicants can influence their timeline by filing comprehensively the first time, the center itself — its current backlog, staffing, and case complexity mix — often determines whether you wait 8 months or 18 months.
As of mid-2026, USCIS operates five service centers that handle family-based I-130 petitions: Texas (TSC), Nebraska (NSC), California (CSC), Vermont (VSC), and Potomac (PSC). The National Benefits Center (NBC) processes most I-485 adjustment of status applications, but the I-130 timeline is the primary driver of the overall wait.
Service center processing time comparison (2026)
Based on USCIS published processing times, historical case data, and recent applicant reports, here is how each center compares for marriage-based I-130 petitions:
Texas Service Center (TSC): 8–12 months. TSC is the fastest center for straightforward marriage-based petitions. Cases filed by US citizens for spouses living in the US or abroad both benefit from TSC's relatively lighter backlog.
Nebraska Service Center (NSC): 10–14 months. Nebraska handles a mix of family and employment petitions. Its marriage-based I-130 times are moderate, with recent improvements in efficiency.
Vermont Service Center (VSC): 11–15 months. Vermont processes a significant volume of international adoption and humanitarian cases, which can slow family-based I-130 adjudication during peak periods.
Potomac Service Center (PSC): 12–16 months. Potomac handles online filings and complex cases, including those with waivers or prior immigration violations. Initial evidence quality heavily impacts speed here.
California Service Center (CSC): 14–18 months. California has the longest backlog for marriage-based petitions, partly due to its geographic jurisdiction (high-volume west coast districts) and complex caseload mix.
How to prepare for service center delays
Regardless of which service center handles your case, proactive preparation can prevent unnecessary delays. The most common holdup is not the service center itself but incomplete or inconsistent evidence that triggers a Request for Evidence (RFE). An RFE can add 2–4 months to your timeline regardless of which center is adjudicating your petition.

The 2025 naturalization civics test applies to N-400 applications that USCIS received on or after October 20, 2025. What it is: DACA renewal extends your deferred action and work permit for two years by re-filing Form I-821D with USCIS.
When to file: Submit your application 150 to 120 days before your current DACA and Employment Authorization Document (EAD) expire.
What you need: Form I-821D, Form I-765, filing fees, two passport-style photos, and evidence you still meet DACA guidelines.

Next step: Gather your documents and confirm your eligibility against the official USCIS checklist before mailing your packet.
Common mistakes that delay or reject DACA renewals
USCIS rejects Form I-821D packages for reasons that are almost always preventable.
A rejected application does not stop the clock on your expiration date, and you lose weeks while you refile.
Knowing the top rejection triggers helps you avoid them.
Incorrect fee amount. USCIS updates fee schedules periodically. Sending a check for the wrong amount results in an immediate rejection.
Verify the current fee on the official USCIS fee page before you write your check or money order.
Missing signature on Form I-765. The work authorization application requires your signature in the designated field.
An unsigned form gets rejected at the lockbox facility. Check every signature block before you seal the envelope.
Expired passport photos. USCIS requires two identical color photos taken within the last 30 days. Submitting older photos triggers a Request for Evidence (RFE), which adds weeks to your processing time.
Filing outside the 150-day window. Filing too early or too late creates problems. USCIS may reject packages filed more than 150 days before expiration, and filing inside 120 days risks a lapse in work authorization.
Note: A rejection differs from a denial. Rejections happen at the lockbox for procedural errors like missing fees. Denials happen after an officer reviews your case on the merits.
Review every page of your packet against the USCIS filing checklist before you mail your package. A 20-minute self-audit can save you a month of delays.
Preparing your DACA renewal packet before you file
Preparation reduces errors and stress. Gather your documents and review your forms in the weeks before your filing window opens.
A prepared applicant files confidently and avoids last-minute scrambling.

How the E-2 treaty investor visa works
The E-2 nonimmigrant visa under INA 101(a)(15)(E)(ii) allows treaty-country nationals to enter the US to develop and direct a business enterprise in which they invested substantial capital. Unlike H-1B, E-2 does not require employer sponsorship. The investor controls the enterprise, making it popular for entrepreneurs and business buyers from eligible countries.
E-2 is renewable indefinitely with no annual lottery or prevailing wage requirement. It is one of the most flexible nonimmigrant categories for eligible nationals who want to build or acquire a US business. Status is available through consular processing abroad or change of status within the US.
The E-2 visa is governed by 8 CFR 214.2(e) and the State Department's Foreign Affairs Manual at 9 FAM 402.9. USCIS adjudicates change-of-status applications while the State Department adjudicates visa applications at consular posts. Before committing capital, verify that your country of nationality maintains a qualifying treaty with the United States.
Who qualifies for E-2
This guide is for nationals of E-2 treaty countries who have invested or plan to invest substantial capital in a US business and intend to develop and direct the enterprise. This includes founders, business buyers, franchise investors, and current nonimmigrant holders wanting to change status.
This guide is not for nationals of non-treaty countries (India, China, Brazil, Russia, South Africa), passive investors, or those whose business will only support themselves without creating US jobs. Treaty-country citizens by naturalization or descent may qualify but face additional requirements about the source of investment funds.
Consular processing versus change of status
Decide whether to apply through consular processing abroad or change of status within the US. Consular processing requires a visa interview at a US embassy in the treaty country and results in a visa stamp allowing free travel. Change of status through Form I-129 to USCIS does not produce a visa stamp, so travel requires a separate E-2 visa application before re-entry.

How the EB-1A self-petition pathway works

Unlike other employment-based categories, EB-1A does not require a job offer or labor certification. The applicant may file Form I-140 on their own behalf without employer sponsorship.
To qualify, the applicant must demonstrate sustained national or international acclaim through extensive documentation. USCIS evaluates petitions using a two-part framework: first, whether the applicant meets at least 3 of the 10 regulatory criteria at 8 CFR 204.5(h)(3), and second, whether the totality of the evidence shows that the applicant is among the small percentage at the very top of the field.
The self-petitioning aspect means the applicant controls the filing timeline, evidence selection, and legal argument. This flexibility is valuable for individuals whose work does not fit a traditional employer-employee relationship, such as freelance artists, independent researchers, founders of startups, and consultants with international recognition.

This guide is not for individuals whose work is primarily local or regional in scope, those who have not received awards beyond their immediate employer, or applicants who cannot document at least 3 of the 10 criteria with objective evidence. EB-2 NIW: the rule in plain English
An NIW is a petition that asks USCIS to waive the standard job offer and labor certification requirements because the applicant's work benefits the United States in a way that makes the labor certification process unnecessary. The waiver is discretionary — USCIS evaluates each case under the three-prong Dhanasar framework.
Step one: Prove EB-2 eligibility. You must show either that you hold an advanced degree (master's or higher, or a bachelor's plus five years of progressive experience) or exceptional ability in the sciences, arts, or business.
Step two: Prove the waiver is warranted. Under Dhanasar, you must show: (1) the proposed endeavor has substantial merit and national importance, (2) you are well positioned to advance it, and (3) on balance, waiving the labor certification benefits the United States.
Who this guide is for
Professionals with advanced degrees or exceptional ability whose work has a credible U.S. benefit. The NIW is available to self-petitioners and employer-sponsored applicants across virtually every field.
Who this guide is not for
Applicants who do not meet the EB-2 threshold — the NIW does not waive this.
EB-1 applicants — different standards apply under Matter of Kazarian.
Applicants considering priority date portability from an earlier I-140 — consult an attorney.

Prong one: Substantial merit and national importance. Substantial merit is broadly defined — USCIS has found substantial merit in fields as varied as biotechnology, education technology, business consulting, and the arts. 01 PERM requires the employer to demonstrate no qualified US worker is available for the position through a structured, DOL-supervised recruitment process. 
02 Average PERM timeline: 6-18 months including PWD (2-4 months), recruitment (2-3 months), and DOL processing (6-10 months). Audited cases add 4-8 months. 
03 About 30% of PERM applications are audited. Audit requires submission of all recruitment documentation within 30 days. 
04 Once certified, PERM is valid for 180 days — the I-140 must be filed before the certification expires. If it expires, a new PERM is required. 
05 EB-3 requires a bachelor's degree, two years of experience, or (for unskilled workers) less than two years. EB-3 visa wait times vary significantly by country of birth. 
Who this is for — and who it isn't
This guide is for US employers who are sponsoring a foreign national employee for an EB-3 green card and need to understand the PERM labor certification requirements, timeline, and documentation. It is also for foreign national employees who want to understand what their employer must do to obtain a labor certification on their behalf and how the process works from start to finish.
This guide is not for applicants who qualify for a PERM exemption such as EB-1A (extraordinary ability), EB-2 NIW (national interest waiver), or EB-5 (investor) — those categories do not require labor certification. It is also not for applicants pursuing EB-2 PERM — while the PERM process is the same, the education and experience requirements differ. EB-3 applicants should also be aware that the annual visa quota for EB-3 is shared across three subcategories (skilled workers, professionals, and unskilled workers), and waiting times depend on the applicant's country of birth and the current Visa Bulletin priority date cut-offs.
Step one: the prevailing wage determination from DOL
The PERM process begins with the employer requesting a prevailing wage determination from the DOL National Prevailing Wage Center. The employer submits ETA Form 9141, which specifies the job title, SOC occupation code, job duties, education and experience requirements, geographic area of intended employment, and proposed wage. The NPWC reviews the submission against the Occupational Employment Statistics wage data and issues a determination that establishes the minimum wage the employer must pay for the position.
Common PWD issues include: selecting the wrong SOC code (which changes the prevailing wage because each occupation has a different wage range), requesting the wrong wage level (Level I is entry level, Level IV is fully competent — the level must match the job requirements), or submitting an incomplete form. The PWD is valid for 90 days (extendable to 180 days with documentation). The employer must begin recruitment before the PWD expires, and the offered wage must be at least 100% of the prevailing wage for the SOC code and level.

An eviction notice is a legal warning, not an immediate lockout — you have time to respond.
Your F-1 or J-1 status requires a current residential address, so housing loss can affect your SEVIS record.
Deadlines and defenses vary by state — check your state's landlord-tenant statute and local housing court rules.
Document every notice, payment, and communication in writing from the moment you receive the papers.
Free legal aid, university housing offices, and HUD-certified counselors can help at no cost.
What an eviction notice means
An eviction notice is a landlord's written warning that they intend to start a court case to remove you. It is not a court order, and it does not allow the landlord to lock you out, remove your things, or shut off utilities. In most states, the landlord must serve a formal notice and then file a case in local housing court.
The notice must state a reason, such as unpaid rent or a lease violation. The required form, delivery method, and minimum response time vary by state — check your state's landlord-tenant statute. Some states require specific language; missing details can sometimes invalidate the notice.
Keep the original and make a copy the same day. Write the date and time you received it on your copy. This date starts the clock for your response, so an accurate record protects you if the landlord claims you had more time.
How eviction can affect your F-1 or J-1 status
Your SEVIS record must list a current residential address. If you lose housing and cannot provide a new address to your Designated School Official quickly, your record may show a compliance problem. Email your DSO within a few days of any change, even if the address is temporary.
Eviction itself does not automatically end your visa or OPT. However, an arrest during a dispute, failure to update your address, or an inability to maintain a full course load because you are homeless can trigger a status review. Universities report address changes to SEVIS, so delays matter.

01 Primary authority: USCIS H-1B guidance and ICE SEVIS program 
02 Core rule: Cap-gap extends F-1 status through September 30 when a timely filed cap-subject H-1B change-of-status petition requests an October 1 start date. The extension is automatic in the sense that no separate USCIS application is required, but it is not automatic in the practical sense — the student must take specific steps to benefit from it. First, the student must confirm with the employer that the H-1B petition requests change of status rather than consular processing, because only change-of-status petitions qualify for cap-gap protection. Second, the student must obtain an updated I-20 from the DSO showing the cap-gap endorsement after USCIS receipts the H-1B petition. Without that I-20, the employer may not accept proof of continued work authorization, and the student may be placed on unpaid leave until the H-1B start date on October 1. Third, the student must ensure that their OPT EAD was still valid on the date USCIS received the H-1B petition — if the OPT expired before the filing date, the student qualifies for the status extension but cannot work during the cap-gap period. 
03 Documents: H-1B receipt notice (Form I-797), cap-gap I-20 endorsed by DSO, OPT EAD, passport, I-94, SEVIS record, and denial or withdrawal notices if any. 
04 Timing: Request the cap-gap I-20 from your DSO immediately after USCIS receipts the H-1B petition, not after approval. 
05 Main risk: Travel abandons change of status, denial ends cap-gap immediately, and consular-processing petitions do not qualify for cap-gap. 
06 Review status: Basic review for F-1 cap-gap available now; attorney-review tiers coming soon. 
What the cap-gap rule does for F-1 students
The cap-gap rule at 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(vi) addresses the timing problem between the April H-1B filing season and the October 1 H-1B start date. F-1 students on OPT whose OPT expires between April 1 and September 30 face a gap in status and work authorization. The rule bridges that gap automatically for students whose employers file cap-subject H-1B petitions requesting change of status.
Cap-gap extends the F-1 status and, in some cases, the OPT work authorization through September 30 of the fiscal year. The extension is not automatic in the sense that no separate application is required, but it does require the student to obtain an updated I-20 from the Designated School Official showing the cap-gap endorsement. Without that I-20, an employer may not accept proof of continued work authorization.
The rule applies only to cap-subject H-1B petitions that request change of status rather than consular notification. If the employer files for consular processing, cap-gap does not apply, and the student must maintain valid status through other means or depart and activate the H-1B abroad.

F-1 visa stamp: unless you are a Canadian citizen exempt from the visa requirement. Form I-20: signed by you and your DSO, with a travel signature within the last 12 months (for returning students; first-time students should have the original signed I-20). Skip to main content MyCaseworks

In 60 seconds
01 214(b) is the most common F-1 refusal ground — it is not a finding of ineligibility, only that the officer was not persuaded on nonimmigrant intent or funding. 
02 There is no mandatory waiting period to reapply, but you must demonstrate changed circumstances with new evidence. 
03 Each reapplication requires a new DS-160 form and visa fee; the SEVIS I-901 fee remains valid as long as the I-20 is active. 
04 A cover letter explaining what changed — and what new evidence you are submitting — helps the second officer focus their review. 
05 214(b) refusals do not trigger bars or penalties. A pattern of refusals without changed circumstances, however, can raise credibility concerns in future applications. 
What 214(b) actually says — and what it means for your application
Section 214(b) of the Immigration and Nationality Act states that every nonimmigrant visa applicant is presumed to be an intending immigrant unless they convince the consular officer otherwise. For F-1 applicants specifically, this means you must demonstrate: (1) you intend to pursue a full course of study at an accredited US institution, (2) you have sufficient funds to cover your first year of tuition and living expenses (with a credible plan for subsequent years), and (3) you maintain a residence abroad that you have no intention of abandoning.
When a consular officer refuses a visa under 214(b), the refusal notice does not specify which element was not satisfied — it simply states that the officer was not persuaded. The officer may have said something during the interview that hints at the reason (“your ties to Nigeria are not strong enough” or “I am not satisfied your sponsor has sufficient income”), but the written notice will not include this detail. Reconstructing the refusal reason requires analyzing what you presented and what the officer focused on during the interview.
A 214(b) refusal is not a bar. It does not trigger a period of inadmissibility, does not need to be waived, and does not prevent you from travelling to the US on other visa categories (though the new application will also be evaluated under 214(b) for that category). The refusal becomes part of your visa record and must be disclosed on all future visa applications. Multiple 214(b) refusals without changed circumstances can make future applications harder, but a single 214(b) refusal followed by a successful application with stronger evidence is a common and non-prejudicial sequence.
Who this guide is for — and who it isn't
This guide is for international students whose F-1 visa application has been refused under INA 214(b) and who want to reapply with a stronger case. You may have received a verbal refusal at the interview window or a written refusal notice by email or post. Either way, the path forward is the same: identify the weakness, gather new evidence, and submit a fresh application that addresses it. US family-based immigration covers marriage green cards, K-1 fiancé visas, conditional permanent residence (I-751), and DACA renewal. The right path depends on where you are — inside the US or abroad, married or engaged, and whether your spouse is a US citizen or permanent resident. The 5 most important things to know
Adjustment of status (Form I-485) is for eligible applicants already inside the US; consular processing is for applicants abroad or those who cannot adjust. The wrong choice can trigger a 3-year or 10-year bar if unlawful presence or entry-history issues exist. See USCIS policy guidance.
A K-1 visa holder must marry the US citizen petitioner within 90 days of entry. After marriage, file I-485 to adjust status. The K-1 does not permit employment until the EAD or green card is issued, and the beneficiary cannot adjust through a different petitioner without leaving.
Form I-751 to remove conditions must be filed during the 90-day window before the 2-year conditional green card expires. Filing within this window extends conditional residence under the receipt rule. Late filings require a written explanation and USCIS discretion.
The most common financial sponsorship mistake is using the wrong household size on Form I-864. The household size includes the sponsor, spouse, dependents, other sponsored persons, and the intending immigrant. Using too small a household size makes the income requirement appear met when it is not.
DACA renewals are accepted and processed in 2026; initial requests are accepted but not processed due to ongoing litigation. File Forms I-821D, I-765, and I-765WS between 150 and 120 days before expiration to avoid a gap in work authorization.
Choose your path
Family-based immigration has several distinct routes. Pick the guide that matches your current situation. If you are already married to a US citizen or permanent resident, start with the marriage green card checklist. If you are engaged, the K-1 guide explains the 90-day rule and the AOS process. You attach civil records, status proof, and category evidence.
Building a complete i-485 adjustment of status document checklist before you pay any fee reduces the chance that routine identity or status gaps trigger a Request for Evidence.
This i-485 adjustment guide does not replace attorney advice or the official form edition on the USCIS forms page.
Keep originals safe; submit clear photocopies or scans unless instructions require originals.
Note the edition date on every blank form you download so your packet matches the version USCIS is accepting when you file.
A document checklist guide keeps copies, translations, and photos in one stack. Officers compare that stack to the current form instructions.
Use this i-485 adjustment guide as a planning tool. Confirm every item against USCIS Forms before you mail or upload.
For family or employment context, review the Green Card Process (Family & Employment) page after you finish this list.
Who qualifies under i-485 adjustment eligibility
In this case, i-485 adjustment eligibility is category-specific. Family, employment, asylee, and special programs use different underlying petitions.
You usually must be physically in the United States when you file.
An immigrant visa number must also be available, unless a concurrent filing rule applies.
i-485 adjustment eligibility is never only about having a passport and photos; the underlying immigrant basis must be valid, and you must remain admissible under the Immigration and Nationality Act.
Physical presence at filing, proper status history where required, and visa availability are core screens officers apply before they dig into every exhibit.
Family path: A qualifying relative’s approved or pending petition may support filing. See USCIS Family for relationship categories.

Form DS-160 — Online Nonimmigrant Visa Application
Form DS-160 is the online application that every nonimmigrant visa applicant must complete before scheduling a visa interview at a US consulate. The form collects biographical information, travel plans, employment history, educational background, and security-related questions. Once submitted, the form generates a confirmation page with a barcode that you must bring to your interview.
The DS-160 is not adjudicated on its own. It is a data-collection tool that gives the consular officer a structured overview of your background before the interview. The officer uses the DS-160 responses to ask targeted questions and to verify consistency between what you wrote and what you say in person. Discrepancies are one of the leading causes of visa refusal.
This guide explains what Form DS-160 is, who needs to file it, what information it collects, and how to avoid the most common mistakes that lead to interview problems or delays.
Who files this form
Form DS-160 is filed by anyone applying for a nonimmigrant visa to the United States. This includes F-1 students, J-1 exchange visitors, B-1/B-2 tourists, H-1B workers, and every other visa category except immigrant visas. Each applicant completes their own DS-160, including dependents. A parent may assist a minor child, but the responses must reflect the child's actual circumstances.
The form is completed online through the State Department's Consular Electronic Application Center. You do not mail a paper copy. After submission, you print the confirmation page and bring it to your visa interview. The DS-160 must be submitted before you can schedule the interview, and the information on the form should match your supporting documents exactly.
What this form is for
The purpose of Form DS-160 is to collect standardized biographical and background information from every nonimmigrant visa applicant. The State Department uses this information to screen applicants for security concerns, to verify identity, and to provide consular officers with a complete profile before the interview.
The form also serves as a legal record. By submitting the DS-160, you certify under penalty of perjury that the information is true and correct. Misrepresentation on the DS-160 can result in a permanent inadmissibility finding under INA §212(a)(6)(C)(i), which bars you from ever receiving a US visa. Accuracy is not optional — it is a legal requirement.
Key sections
Personal information: name, date and place of birth, passport details, and national ID number
Travel information: purpose of trip, intended dates of travel, and contact in the United States
Family information: parents, spouse, and children, including their US immigration status if applicable
Work and education: current and previous employers, schools attended, and field of study
Security and background: questions about criminal history, health, and prior immigration violations

Form DS-2019 — Certificate of Eligibility for Exchange Visitor (J-1) Status
Form DS-2019 is not a form you fill out and mail to a government agency. It is a certificate issued by a designated program sponsor — a US university, research institution, hospital, or cultural organization that has been authorized by the Department of State to administer exchange visitor programs. The DS-2019 certifies that you have been accepted into a legitimate exchange program and that the sponsor has the resources and structure to support your participation.
Every J-1 exchange visitor receives a DS-2019 before applying for a J-1 visa at a US consulate. The document is also what you present to the Customs and Border Protection officer when you enter the United States. Once you are in the country, your program sponsor updates your DS-2019 whenever your program end date changes, when you transfer to a different sponsor, or when you need a travel signature for re-entry after international travel.
Unlike forms filed with USCIS, the DS-2019 is not fee-based. The program sponsor issues it as part of their sponsorship duties. However, sponsors may charge program fees, administrative fees, or insurance fees that are separate from the visa application fee paid to the Department of State. This guide explains what Form DS-2019 is, who issues it, what information it contains, and the most common mistakes exchange visitors make.
Who files this form
Form DS-2019 is not filed by the exchange visitor. It is issued by the program sponsor's Responsible Officer or Alternate Responsible Officer after the visitor has been accepted into a designated exchange program. The sponsor enters the visitor's information into the Student and Exchange Visitor Information System and generates the DS-2019 from the system. The visitor then uses the DS-2019 to apply for a J-1 visa at a US consulate.
After the visitor enters the United States, the Responsible Officer is responsible for maintaining the accuracy of the DS-2019. Any change to the visitor's program, funding, or personal information must be reported to the Responsible Officer, who updates SEVIS and issues a new DS-2019 if necessary. The visitor does not file anything with USCIS to update their DS-2019 — the sponsor does this through SEVIS.
What this form is for
The purpose of Form DS-2019 is to certify that a nonimmigrant has been accepted into a bona fide exchange visitor program administered by a Department of State-designated sponsor. The document serves as the foundation for the visitor's J-1 visa application, entry into the United States, and maintenance of lawful J-1 status throughout their program.

Form I-129 — Petition for a Nonimmigrant Worker
Form I-129 is the petition an employer files with USCIS to bring a foreign national worker to the United States in a temporary nonimmigrant status. It is not filed by the worker — it is filed by the employer, who is called the petitioner. The worker is called the beneficiary. The form covers multiple visa categories including H-1B for specialty occupations, L-1 for intracompany transferees, O-1 for individuals with extraordinary ability, and several lesser-known categories.
Each visa category has its own classification supplement that accompanies the I-129 — the H Classification Supplement for H-1B petitions, the L Classification Supplement for L-1 petitions, and the O and P Classifications Supplement for O-1 petitions. These supplements ask for category-specific information such as the job description, wage level, and evidence that the beneficiary meets the requirements.
The I-129 process is employer-driven from start to finish. The employer must demonstrate that the position qualifies for the requested visa category, that the beneficiary meets the requirements, and that the employer will pay the required wage. This guide explains what Form I-129 is, who files it, what the process involves, and the most common mistakes employers make.
Who files this form
Form I-129 is filed by a US employer who wants to employ a foreign national in a temporary nonimmigrant worker status. The employer is the petitioner, and the foreign national is the beneficiary. The form cannot be filed by the worker themselves, although the worker may need to provide documents and information to the employer for inclusion in the petition.
The employer must be a legitimate US entity with a tax identification number and the ability to pay the required wage. For H-1B specialty occupation petitions, the employer must also file a Labor Condition Application with the Department of Labor before filing the I-129. For L-1 intracompany transferee petitions, the employer must demonstrate a qualifying relationship between the US entity and a foreign parent, subsidiary, affiliate, or branch office. For O-1 extraordinary ability petitions, the employer or an agent may file on behalf of the beneficiary.
What this form is for
The purpose of Form I-129 is to allow USCIS to evaluate whether a US employer has a legitimate temporary need for a foreign worker and whether the proposed position and beneficiary meet the statutory and regulatory requirements for the requested nonimmigrant visa category. If approved, USCIS issues a Form I-797 Approval Notice, which the beneficiary can use to apply for a visa at a US consulate or, if already in the United States, to change or extend their status.
The I-129 petition is specific to the employer, the position, and the location. If any of these change significantly, the employer may need to file an amended petition. For H-1B workers, a change in work location may require a new Labor Condition Application and

Form I-130 — Petition for Alien Relative
Form I-130 is the petition a US citizen or lawful permanent resident files to establish a qualifying family relationship with a relative who wants to immigrate to the United States. It is the first step in most family-based immigration cases, but filing the I-130 does not grant the relative any immigration status or permission to enter the country. It merely establishes that a valid family relationship exists under the Immigration and Nationality Act.
The form is filed with USCIS and requires evidence of the petitioner's status, evidence of the claimed relationship, and the filing fee. The required evidence varies significantly depending on the relationship — a spousal petition requires a marriage certificate and evidence of a bona fide marriage, while a parent petition requires a birth certificate showing the biological or legal relationship. Step-parent and adoptive relationships require additional documentation.
After USCIS approves the I-130, the case moves to either consular processing at a US embassy abroad or adjustment of status inside the United States via Form I-485, depending on where the beneficiary currently lives and whether a visa number is immediately available. This guide explains what Form I-130 is, who files it, what evidence is required, and the most common mistakes petitioners make.
Who files this form
Form I-130 is filed by a US citizen or lawful permanent resident who wants to sponsor a qualifying relative for immigration to the United States. US citizens can petition for a spouse, unmarried children under 21, married children of any age, siblings, and parents. Lawful permanent residents can petition for a spouse and unmarried children, but not for parents, married children, or siblings.
The person filing the petition is called the petitioner. The relative being sponsored is called the beneficiary. The petitioner must prove both their own US citizenship or permanent resident status and the claimed relationship to the beneficiary. If the petitioner is a US citizen by naturalization, they must include their naturalization certificate. If they are a lawful permanent resident, they must include a copy of their green card.
What this form is for
The purpose of Form I-130 is to establish that a qualifying family relationship exists between a US citizen or lawful permanent resident and a foreign national relative. USCIS reviews the petition to verify the petitioner's status, the beneficiary's identity, and the claimed relationship through documentary evidence. The form does not grant the beneficiary any immigration benefit on its own — it is a prerequisite step.
Once approved, the I-130 petition creates a place in line for the beneficiary. For immediate relatives of US citizens — spouses, unmarried children under 21, and parents — visa numbers are always available, so the case can proceed immediately to the next step. Form I-20 — Certificate of Eligibility for F-1 Student Status
Form I-20 is not a form you fill out and mail to USCIS. It is a certificate issued by your Designated School Official — a staff member at your US educational institution who is authorized by the Student and Exchange Visitor Program to manage international student records. The I-20 certifies that you have been admitted to a full-time program of study, that you have demonstrated sufficient financial resources, and that the school has reported your enrollment in the SEVIS database.
Every F-1 student receives an I-20 before applying for a visa at a US consulate. The document is also what you present to the Customs and Border Protection officer when you enter the United States. Once enrolled, your DSO updates your I-20 whenever your program end date changes, when you apply for OPT, when you transfer schools, or when you travel and need a signature for re-entry.
This guide explains what Form I-20 is, who issues it, what information it contains, and how it governs your status as an F-1 student.
Who files this form
Form I-20 is not filed by the student. It is issued by the school's Designated School Official after the student has been admitted to a SEVP-certified institution and has demonstrated the ability to pay tuition and living expenses. The student then uses the I-20 to apply for an F-1 visa at a US consulate and to enter the United States.
After enrollment, the DSO is responsible for maintaining the accuracy of the I-20. Any change to your program, your funding, or your personal information must be reported to the DSO, who updates SEVIS and issues a new I-20 if necessary. You do not file anything with USCIS to update your I-20 — the DSO does this through the SEVIS system.
What this form is for
The purpose of Form I-20 is to certify that a nonimmigrant student has been admitted to a full-time academic or vocational program at a SEVP-certified school and has the financial means to complete that program. The document serves as the foundation for the student's F-1 visa application, entry into the United States, and maintenance of lawful status throughout their studies.
The I-20 also governs specific permissions and restrictions. The program start and end dates on the I-20 define the boundaries of your authorized stay. The I-20 must be endorsed by your DSO before you travel outside the United States and seek re-entry. And the OPT recommendation printed on page 2 of the I-20 is what authorizes you to file Form I-765 for work authorization after graduation.

Page 1 — Student information: name, date of birth, country of citizenship, and SEVIS ID number
Page 1 — School information: name, address, and SEVP certification number
Page 1 — Program of study: degree level, major field, program start and end dates
Page 1 — Financial certification: estimated costs and funding sources
Page 2 — Employment authorization: DSO recommendation for OPT or CPT

Form I-485 — Application to Register Permanent Residence or Adjust Status
Form I-485 is the application you file when you are already in the United States and want to become a lawful permanent resident — commonly known as getting a green card. Unlike consular processing, which happens at a US embassy abroad, adjustment of status happens entirely within the United States through USCIS. You do not leave the country during the process, and if your case is pending, you may be eligible for work authorization and advance parole while you wait.
The form is filed after an immigrant visa petition — such as Form I-130 for family-based cases or Form I-140 for employment-based cases — has been approved and a visa number is available. For immediate relatives of US citizens, the visa number is always available, so the I-485 can be filed concurrently with the I-130. For everyone else, the priority date must be current on the Department of State Visa Bulletin before filing.
The I-485 is one of the most document-intensive forms in the immigration system. It requires biometrics, a medical examination by a USCIS-approved civil surgeon, extensive background information, and evidence that you are admissible to the United States. This guide explains what Form I-485 is, who can file it, what the process involves, and the most common mistakes applicants make.
Who files this form
Form I-485 is filed by foreign nationals who are physically present in the United States and eligible to adjust their status to lawful permanent resident. The most common categories are immediate relatives of US citizens, family-sponsored preference immigrants with an approved I-130 and a current priority date, employment-based immigrants with an approved I-140, asylees who have been granted asylum and have waited one year, and refugees who have been admitted and have waited one year.
To be eligible, you must generally have been inspected and admitted or paroled into the United States, and you must not be inadmissible under any ground listed in INA section 212. Certain grounds of inadmissibility can be waived with Form I-601 or I-602, but not all. If you entered the United States without inspection, you are generally not eligible to adjust status unless you fall under a narrow exception such as section 245(i) or the LIFE Act.
What this form is for
The purpose of Form I-485 is to allow a foreign national who is already in the United States to become a lawful permanent resident without leaving the country. USCIS reviews the application to confirm that the applicant is eligible for adjustment of status, that they are not inadmissible, and that all required documents are present and authentic.
The application process includes a biometrics appointment for fingerprinting and background checks, a medical examination to screen for communicable diseases and required vaccinations, and potentially an interview where the applicant answers questions under oath about their application and eligibilit

Form I-539 — Application to Extend/Change Nonimmigrant Status
Form I-539 is the document you file when you want to stay in the United States longer than your current nonimmigrant visa allows, or when you want to change from one nonimmigrant category to another without leaving the country. The most common filers are B-1/B-2 visitors extending a tourist stay, F-1 students requesting a program extension, and J-1 exchange visitors seeking a waiver or extension.
The form is filed with USCIS before your current authorized stay expires. Filing on time creates a period of authorized stay while the application is pending, but it does not guarantee approval. If you file after your status has already expired, you must demonstrate that the delay was due to extraordinary circumstances beyond your control.
This guide explains what Form I-539 is, who needs to file it, what the process involves, and the most common mistakes applicants make.
Who files this form
Form I-539 is filed by nonimmigrants who are already in the United States and need either an extension of their current status or a change to a different nonimmigrant category. Common filers include B-1/B-2 visitors whose travel plans have changed, F-1 students who need more time to complete their degree program, and J-1 exchange visitors who need additional time for research or training.
Dependents in certain visa categories also file Form I-539. For example, an F-2 dependent who wants to change status to F-1 student, or a B-2 dependent who needs to extend their stay along with the principal visa holder. Each category has different evidentiary requirements, and the burden of proof is on the applicant to show that they have maintained their current status and that the extension or change is warranted.
What this form is for
The purpose of Form I-539 is to request permission from USCIS to remain in the United States beyond the expiration date on your Form I-94, or to switch to a different nonimmigrant status without leaving the country and applying for a new visa at a consulate. If approved, USCIS updates your status in its records and issues a new I-94 with the extended or changed status.
For extensions, the key question is whether you still meet the requirements of your current visa category and whether your circumstances justify additional time. For changes of status, USCIS evaluates whether you are eligible for the new category and whether you have maintained lawful status up to the date of filing. A change of status is not available for every category — for example, changing from B-1/B-2 to F-1 is permitted but heavily scrutinized — you cannot begin studying until USCIS approves the change, and USCIS may deny it if your B visa was not annotated as a prospective student.
Key sections
Part 1 — Information about you: name, date of birth, country of birth, and passport information
Part 2 — Application type: extension of stay, change of status, or reinstatement
Part 3 — Processing information: current
