Form I-765 — Application for Employment Authorization
Form I-765 is the document you file when you need permission to work in the United States as a noncitizen. Most F-1 students first encounter it when applying for Optional Practical Training after graduation, but the form is also used for other categories including asylum applicants, adjustment-of-status applicants, and certain dependents. The form is filed with USCIS, and approval produces an Employment Authorization Document — the physical card commonly called an EAD.
The form itself is deceptively short, but the supporting evidence and timing rules are where most filers stumble. A single wrong eligibility-category code, an expired I-20 recommendation, or a missing prior EAD can trigger a rejection that delays work authorization by weeks or months. Understanding what the form asks for, and what USCIS verifies behind the scenes, is the best way to avoid those delays.
This guide explains what Form I-765 is, who needs to file it, how the process works, and the most common mistakes filers make. For field-by-field review of your completed form, see the I-765 OPT review service.
Who files this form
Form I-765 is filed by noncitizens who are in the United States and need work authorization. The largest group of filers are F-1 students applying for post-completion OPT or the STEM OPT extension. Other filers include applicants for asylum, applicants adjusting status to lawful permanent resident, certain spouses of visa holders, and refugees.
For F-1 students specifically, the filing is tied to your academic stage. Pre-completion OPT filers are still enrolled; post-completion OPT filers have graduated or are about to graduate; STEM OPT extension filers have already been approved for post-completion OPT and hold a degree in a designated STEM field. Each stage uses a different eligibility-category code on the form, and choosing the wrong code is one of the most common rejection triggers.
What this form is for
The purpose of Form I-765 is to request permission to work in the United States. USCIS reviews the form to confirm that you belong to a category eligible for employment authorization and that your supporting documents prove your eligibility. If approved, USCIS issues an Employment Authorization Document that lists your photo, name, alien registration number, and the validity period of your work authorization.
For OPT filers, the EAD is what you show employers to prove you are legally authorized to work. The card is also what you use to complete the I-9 verification process when you start a job. Without an approved I-765 and a valid EAD, you cannot legally begin employment in the United States, even if you have a job offer in hand.
Key sections
Part 1 — Reason for applying: new application, renewal, or replacement of a lost or damaged EAD
Part 2 — Information about you: name, address, alien registration number, and USCIS online account number
Part 3 — Applicant statement and signature: declara

Form I-864 — Affidavit of Support
Form I-864 is the legally binding contract that a financial sponsor signs to promise that an immigrant will not become a public charge. It is required in most family-based immigration cases and some employment-based cases where the petitioner is a relative. The form creates a legal obligation for the sponsor to support the immigrant at 125 percent of the federal poverty guidelines until the immigrant becomes a US citizen, has worked 40 qualifying quarters, dies, or permanently leaves the United States.
The sponsor is typically the same person who filed the immigrant petition — for example, the US citizen spouse who filed Form I-130. However, if the petitioner does not meet the income requirement, a joint sponsor can also file a separate I-864. The joint sponsor does not need to be related to the petitioner or the beneficiary, but they must be a US citizen or lawful permanent resident, domiciled in the United States, and meet the income requirement independently.
The I-864 is one of the most legally consequential forms in the immigration process because it is enforceable in court. The sponsored immigrant, a federal agency, or a state agency that provides means-tested benefits can sue the sponsor to recover costs. This guide explains what Form I-864 is, who must file it, how the income requirement works, and the most common mistakes sponsors make.
Who files this form
Form I-864 is filed by the petitioner who sponsors an immigrant for lawful permanent residence. In family-based cases, the petitioner is usually the US citizen or lawful permanent resident who filed Form I-130. In employment-based cases where the petitioner is a relative, the relative may also need to file an I-864. The sponsor must be at least 18 years old, domiciled in the United States, and a US citizen, national, or lawful permanent resident.
If the petitioner's household income does not reach 125 percent of the federal poverty guidelines for their household size, a joint sponsor can file a separate I-864. A joint sponsor must meet the same eligibility requirements as the primary sponsor and must demonstrate sufficient income or assets independently. The beneficiary's own income cannot be used to satisfy the sponsor's obligation unless the beneficiary is the petitioner's spouse and the income will continue from the same source after the beneficiary becomes a permanent resident.
What this form is for
The purpose of Form I-864 is to satisfy the public charge ground of inadmissibility under INA section 212(a)(4). By signing the affidavit, the sponsor contractually obligates themselves to provide financial support to the immigrant at a level equal to or exceeding 125 percent of the federal poverty guidelines. The obligation continues until one of the terminating events occurs: the immigrant naturalizes, dies, permanently leaves the United States, or is credited with 40 qualifying quarters of work.

Form I-94 — Arrival/Departure Record
Form I-94 is the official record of your admission to the United States. It is created electronically when you pass through Customs and Border Protection inspection at a port of entry — an airport, seaport, or land border crossing. The I-94 records your date of entry, the port of entry, your visa classification, and the date by which you must depart or change status. For most nonimmigrants, this date is what governs your authorized stay, not the visa expiration date in your passport.
You can retrieve your I-94 record online through the CBP I-94 website. The record is free to access and should be checked immediately after every entry to confirm that CBP recorded your admission correctly. Errors on the I-94 — such as the wrong visa class or an incorrect admission date — can cause problems with school enrollment, work authorization, and future visa applications.
This guide explains what Form I-94 is, how it works, why it matters, and what to do if the record contains an error.
Who files this form
Form I-94 is not filed by the traveler. It is created automatically by Customs and Border Protection when you are admitted to the United States. The CBP officer inspects your passport, visa, and supporting documents, determines your admissibility, and enters the admission data into the CBP system. The electronic I-94 record is then available for you to download and print.
Certain categories of travelers, including most F-1 and J-1 visa holders, are admitted for "duration of status" rather than a specific date. This means your I-94 shows "D/S" instead of a departure date. For these categories, your authorized stay is tied to your program end date on Form I-20 or DS-2019, not to a fixed date on the I-94.
What this form is for
The purpose of Form I-94 is to create an official record of every noncitizen's admission to the United States. The record documents when you entered, under what visa classification, and how long you are authorized to stay. USCIS, your school, and your employer all use the I-94 to verify that you were lawfully admitted and that you remain in valid status.
For F-1 students, the I-94 admission class should read "F1" and the admit-until date should read "D/S" for duration of status. If your I-94 shows a specific date instead of "D/S," or if the class of admission is incorrect, you must contact CBP to correct the record immediately. An incorrect I-94 can prevent you from enrolling in classes, applying for OPT, or changing status.

Admission number: a unique 11-digit identifier assigned to each entry
Date of entry: the calendar date you were admitted to the United States
Class of admission: your visa category — F1, J1, B1, B2, H1B, etc.
Admit until date: the expiration of your authorized stay, or D/S for duration of status
Port of entry: the specific airport, seaport, or land border where you were inspected

Form I-983 — Training Plan for STEM OPT Students
Form I-983 is the training plan that every STEM OPT extension applicant must complete with their employer. Unlike Form I-765, which is filed with USCIS, the I-983 is a bilateral agreement between you and your employer that documents how your practical training relates to your STEM degree. The form is signed by both you and your employer and is maintained in your school's records, not sent to USCIS.
The I-983 was introduced to ensure that STEM OPT employment is genuinely educational and not just a work permit. The form requires your employer to describe specific learning objectives, training methods, and supervision structures. It also requires the employer to commit to regular evaluations of your progress. These requirements are stricter than standard post-completion OPT and reflect the extended 24-month period that STEM OPT provides.
This guide explains what Form I-983 is, who needs to complete it, what the form requires, and how it fits into the STEM OPT extension process.
Who files this form
Form I-983 is completed by F-1 students who have been approved for post-completion OPT, hold a degree in a STEM field from a SEVP-certified institution, and are seeking a 24-month STEM OPT extension. The student and the employer must complete the form together. The student then submits the signed form to their Designated School Official, who creates a new I-20 with the STEM OPT recommendation.
The employer must be enrolled in E-Verify and must agree to the training plan's requirements, including the learning objectives, supervision structure, and evaluation schedule. The employer must also report any material changes to the training plan — such as a change in supervisor, a significant shift in duties, or termination of employment — to the student's DSO within five business days.
What this form is for
The purpose of Form I-983 is to document that your STEM OPT employment is a structured training experience that is directly related to your STEM degree. USCIS and SEVP use the form to verify that STEM OPT is being used for its intended purpose — practical training that enhances the student's academic knowledge — rather than as a generic work authorization.
The form creates accountability for both the student and the employer. The student must commit to the learning objectives and attend scheduled evaluations. The employer must provide supervision, training, and feedback, and must report material changes to the school. If the training plan is not followed, the DSO can terminate the student's STEM OPT recommendation, which invalidates the underlying I-765 and EAD.

Section 2 — Employer information: name, address, E-Verify number, and number of employees

Form N-400 — Application for Naturalization
Form N-400 is the application a lawful permanent resident files to become a naturalized US citizen. Naturalization is the legal process by which a noncitizen voluntarily becomes a citizen of the United States. It is the final step in the immigration journey for most permanent residents, and it confers the full rights and responsibilities of US citizenship, including the right to vote, the right to run for most public offices, the ability to sponsor a wider range of family members for immigration, and protection from deportation.
To qualify for naturalization, you must meet several statutory requirements established by Congress. You must have been a lawful permanent resident for a specific period — generally five years, or three years if you are married to a US citizen. You must demonstrate continuous residence and physical presence in the United States. You must be a person of good moral character. You must demonstrate an attachment to the principles of the US Constitution. And you must pass an English test and a civics test covering US history and government.
The N-400 is a detailed application that asks about your residence history, employment history, marital history, children, travel outside the United States, criminal history, and affiliation with organizations. USCIS reviews every answer carefully, and discrepancies between the N-400 and prior immigration filings can raise concerns. This guide explains what Form N-400 is, who qualifies, what the process involves, and the most common mistakes applicants make.
Who files this form
Form N-400 is filed by lawful permanent residents who meet the statutory requirements for naturalization. The general requirement is five years of permanent residence, but the period is reduced to three years if you have been married to and living with a US citizen spouse for those three years. Certain military service members and their families may qualify under special provisions with reduced or no residence requirements.
To be eligible, you must also demonstrate continuous residence in the United States, meaning you have not taken trips abroad that are so long they break the continuity of your residence. You must meet the physical presence requirement — at least half of the required residence period physically in the United States. You must have lived in the state or USCIS district where you file for at least three months. And you must be a person of good moral character during the statutory period leading up to your application.
What this form is for
The purpose of Form N-400 is to allow USCIS to evaluate whether a lawful permanent resident meets all the statutory requirements for naturalization. USCIS reviews the application for completeness, consistency with prior immigration records, and any grounds that might disqualify the applicant. What the Fair Housing Act covers
The federal Fair Housing Act prohibits discrimination in housing based on race, color, religion, national origin, sex, familial status, and disability. This law applies to most rental housing, including apartments, houses, and student housing. The Act covers every stage of the rental process: advertising, application, showing, lease terms, and eviction. It also prohibits harassment based on a protected characteristic, including unwanted comments, threats, or demands related to your national origin or immigration status.
National origin discrimination specifically includes treating applicants differently because of their country of birth, accent, or perceived foreign status. A landlord who imposes extra requirements on international students — such as demanding a larger deposit, requiring a US-based guarantor when US citizens are not asked for one, or refusing to accept foreign scholarship letters as proof of income — may be violating the Act. Direct statements like "We don't rent to international students" or "US citizens only" are clear violations of the Fair Housing Act's national origin protections.
The Act covers every stage of the rental process, including advertising language. An advertisement that says "perfect for American students" or implies a preference for English speakers may violate the law. Who this is for — and who it isn't
This guide is for people considering or already holding J-1 Exchange Visitor status: interns, trainees, research scholars, professors, summer work travel participants, au pairs, camp counselors, and graduate medical residents. If you are trying to decide between J-1 and F-1 for a study or training program in the US, this guide explains the tradeoffs — particularly the 212(e) home residency rule that does not exist in F-1.
This guide is not for F-1 students (see the F-1 rights guide), H-1B workers, or green card applicants. J-1 vs F-1: the decision that matters
The J-1 and F-1 visas both allow entry for educational and cultural exchange, but they serve different populations and impose different post-program restrictions. F-1 is for students enrolled in a full course of study at a US academic institution. J-1 is broader — it covers students, but also scholars, researchers, interns, trainees, camp counselors, physicians, and au pairs. The sponsoring organization, not the individual, initiates the J-1 process by issuing a DS-2019 through a Department of State-designated program sponsor.

The implied warranty of habitability
Every state in the US recognizes an implied warranty of habitability. This means landlords must maintain rental properties in a condition fit for human habitation, even if the lease does not explicitly say so. The warranty takes effect automatically when you move in — the landlord does not need to sign a separate agreement, and you do not need to request it. It is built into every residential lease, written or verbal, under common law adopted by state statutes across the country.
What counts as uninhabitable varies by state, but the category generally includes heating, plumbing, electricity, water, structural integrity, and pest control. Some states also include mold, lead paint, and security measures. Check your state landlord-tenant statute for the exact list that applies where you live. Most state statutes list specific conditions that qualify as uninhabitable, and comparing the list in the relevant statute to the conditions in your unit is the first step in building a repair rights case.
The warranty is automatic. A landlord cannot waive it in the lease, and attempting to do so is usually unenforceable. If your lease says the landlord is not responsible for repairs, that clause is likely invalid. Some landlords include clauses requiring tenants to perform minor maintenance tasks such as changing light bulbs or air filters — these are generally enforceable if they are reasonable. But any clause that shifts the burden for major habitability repairs from the landlord to the tenant is not enforceable in any state.

In 60 seconds
A green card gives you lawful permanent residence in the United States; eligibility comes through family, employment, refugee status, or other categories defined by USCIS.
Most applicants file a petition first (Form I-130 or I-140), then either adjust status with Form I-485 or complete consular processing.
Required permanent residence documents include a passport, birth certificate, medical exam, and proof of the qualifying relationship or job offer.
Permanent residence costs in 2026 range from roughly $1,000 to $5,000+, depending on category, and processing time varies from 6 months to several years.
A qualified immigration attorney can review your facts before you file; rules change, and an officer decides every case on its merits.
Article
Renewing or replacing a permanent resident card
A permanent resident card expires every ten years, and renewal requires Form I-90.
File well before the expiration date, since renewal processing can take several months.
Replacement for a lost, stolen, or damaged card also uses Form I-90, and you may need a temporary I-551 stamp in your passport if travel is urgent.
Renewal does not change your underlying status; it simply refreshes the physical document.
Conditional residents follow a different path through Form I-751, which you must file within the 90-day window before the card expires.
Missing that window can result in automatic termination of your status, so mark the date on your calendar the moment your conditional card arrives.
Travel and re-entry considerations
Leaving the U.S. while a green card application is pending can complicate your case, especially if you lack advance parole.
For approved permanent residents, short trips abroad are generally fine, but absences over six months may raise questions about your intent to reside permanently.
A re-entry permit, filed on Form I-131, protects extended travel of up to two years.
If you are in removal proceedings or have a criminal record, consult an attorney before any international travel, since re-entry may trigger secondary inspection or inadmissibility grounds.
Keep copies of your boarding passes and pay stubs from abroad to document that your U.S. residence remained your primary home.
Family members and derivative beneficiaries
Certain green card categories allow spouses and unmarried children under 21 to derive status from your application.
For employment-based petitions, derivatives file concurrently when a visa number is available, or later if priority dates differ.
Family-based petitions follow separate preference categories with their own waiting lists.
Keep each family member's biographical data consistent across forms, and note that children who turn 21 during processing may age out unless the Child Status Protection Act protects their priority date.
If you are unsure whether your child qualifies as a derivative, review the visa bulletin for your category and consult an immigration attorney

The N-400 interview is the stage after USCIS reviews the application and before the oath ceremony. How the O-1A extraordinary ability visa works
The O-1A nonimmigrant visa, authorized under INA 101(a)(15)(O)(i), allows individuals with extraordinary ability in science, education, business, or athletics to work in the United States temporarily. Unlike the H-1B visa, O-1A has no annual cap, no lottery, and no prevailing wage requirement. It requires meeting at least 3 of 8 regulatory criteria or evidence of a one-time major achievement such as a Nobel Prize.
The petition must be filed by a U.S. petitioner and include a consultation letter from an appropriate labor organization or peer group. USCIS reviews evidence under a two-part framework: whether the beneficiary meets at least 3 criteria, and a final merits review of whether the totality of evidence demonstrates extraordinary ability.
The O-1A is distinct from the O-1B category for artists and entertainers. Applicants in creative fields should verify which category matches their work. The evidence standards differ materially between the two, and filing under the wrong category can result in denial.
Who should apply under O-1A
This guide is for individuals with verifiable achievements seeking U.S. work authorization without H-1B cap constraints. It is relevant for researchers with strong publication records, technology founders with industry recognition, athletes with national competition achievements, and business professionals at organizations with distinguished reputations.
This guide is not for individuals whose achievements are primarily internal to their employer without external recognition. It is not for artists or entertainers who should apply under O-1B. Applicants who cannot document 3 of 8 criteria should explore H-1B, L-1, or E-2 as alternatives.
The key strategic decision: O-1A versus EB-1A timing
If you qualify for O-1A, decide whether to apply for the O-1A first and pursue a green card later, or file EB-1A directly. O-1A allows starting work within weeks under premium processing. EB-1A requires more evidence but, if current, allows concurrent adjustment of status.

When a rent increase is legal

These laws typically apply to older buildings and require landlords to register the unit with a local housing agency. These cities include New York, San Francisco, Los Angeles, Washington DC, and others. If you live in a rent-controlled jurisdiction, your landlord must follow the local formula. 01 Joint and several liability means you can be held responsible for your roommate's unpaid rent — the landlord can demand the full amount from you alone. 
02 A written roommate agreement is separate from the lease and is enforceable in small claims court. It cannot override lease terms but helps prevent disputes before they start.

Joint vs several liability: what every student tenant should know
When you sign a lease with roommates, the default legal structure in most US states is joint and several liability. This means all tenants on the lease are treated as a single group for rent payment, but each individual tenant is also personally responsible for the full amount. If your roommate cannot pay their share of the rent, the landlord can demand the difference from you. If neither of you pays, the landlord can evict everyone named on the lease — regardless of who actually owes what. An eviction filing appears on the credit and rental history of every tenant named in the lawsuit, even tenants who were paying their share consistently.
The liability structure is set by the lease, not by verbal agreements or informal splits. If the lease says "Tenant A and Tenant B jointly agree to pay $2,000/month," you are both individually on the hook for the full $2,000. A verbal agreement that "I pay $1,000 and you pay $1,000" is not binding on the landlord — it is an agreement between roommates only. Some leases, particularly for student housing complexes near universities, offer individual leases per bedroom. Under an individual lease, each tenant is responsible only for their own rent and the landlord collects separately. Individual leases are less common in off-campus rentals but are worth seeking if you are concerned about roommate liability. If you have a choice between a joint lease and individual leases, individual leases eliminate the financial risk of a non-paying roommate entirely.

This guide is for F-1 and other international students renting off-campus housing in the United States with roommates. It is also for domestic US students who are new to renting and want to understand roommate liability before signing a lease. What the law says about security deposits
State law governs every part of the security-deposit relationship between you and your landlord. There is no single federal rule that sets a maximum amount, a return deadline, or the deductions a landlord may take. Those details vary by state — check your state's landlord-tenant statute before you act. Some states cap the deposit at one month's rent; others allow a larger amount. Return deadlines range from two weeks to more than forty-five days. Interest rules also differ. Knowing your state's exact rule is the first step in deciding whether your landlord has broken the law. Some states also require landlords to hold deposits in a separate account or pay interest. Reviewing these rules now will tell you whether your landlord has already violated the law.
The absence of a federal rule means tenants cannot rely on a single source for deposit protections. A landlord who keeps a deposit for 45 days may be in full compliance with state law in some states but in violation in others. A tenant in New York has 14 days to receive the deposit or an itemised list; a tenant in Texas has 30 days; a tenant in California has 21 days. These differences matter when calculating whether the landlord has missed the deadline. Check the statute for the specific state where you rent, not a neighboring state or a general national guideline. Your state attorney general website or local housing court self-help center can direct you to the correct statute.

Cheap rent far from campus can cost you missed classes. Late arrival is a school problem, not a landlord problem.
Map three zones. Walkable, one-transfer transit, and car-only. Write the door-to-door minutes for each.
Price the hour. If a cheaper unit adds 90 minutes a day, you lose study time. Recalculate weekly, not just monthly rent.
Test the route. Ride the bus at 8 a.m. once. Apps hide transfers and weather delays.

02 Core rule: International students have the same tenant rights as US citizens; state landlord-tenant law governs deposits, repairs, eviction, and privacy — check your state's specific protections for each area. 
03 Documents: Lease, security deposit receipt, move-in inspection checklist, landlord correspondence, and a copy of the relevant state landlord-tenant statute sections. 
04 Timing: Verify all deadlines under your state law before taking action — deposit return periods, notice requirements, and eviction response windows all vary by jurisdiction. 
05 Main risk: Assuming all US states have the same tenant protections; each state's landlord-tenant statute sets different deposit limits, notice periods, and eviction procedures. 
06 Review status: Basic review for tenant rights available now; attorney-review tiers coming soon. 
In 60 seconds
Landlord-tenant law in the US is state-specific, not federal.
Every state has rules on deposits, leases, repairs, and evictions.
International students have the same tenant rights as US citizens.
Your school's housing office and legal aid can point you to state resources.
Always verify the current rule against your state statute before acting.
Why landlord-tenant law is state-by-state
The United States does not have a single national landlord-tenant statute. Each state writes its own laws, and some cities add local rules on top. This means the deposit limit, notice period, repair deadline, and eviction process that apply in one state may be completely different in the next.
For international students, this patchwork creates confusion. A lease clause that is illegal in California might be enforceable in Texas. A 30-day notice requirement in one state could be 60 days in another. The only safe approach is to check the specific statute for the state where you rent.
Your state attorney general website, local housing court, and school housing office are the best starting points for the current rule.
Key tenant rights every state protects
Despite the differences, every state protects a core set of tenant rights. These include the right to a habitable home, the right to privacy with reasonable notice before landlord entry, the right to a return of your security deposit with an itemized deduction list, and protection against retaliatory eviction.
The details vary. Some states cap security deposits at one month's rent; others allow two or three months. Some states require 24 hours' notice for landlord entry; others use a "reasonable" standard. Some states let tenants repair and deduct; others do not.
The consistent principle is that tenants have rights, and landlords cannot override them in the lease. Any clause that tries to waive habitability, allow unlimited landlord entry, or force you to give u

§ Key takeaways
01 Four required elements of CPT authorization on the I-20: employer name and address, start and end dates, full-time or part-time designation, and DSO signature and date. 
02 CPT cannot be back-dated; the start date on the I-20 controls when work may legally begin. 
03 Twelve months or more of full-time CPT at the same education level disqualifies the student from OPT at that level permanently. 
04 Part-time CPT does not count against the 12-month OPT cap, but full-time CPT is over 20 hours per week. 
05 Common DSO mistakes include authorizing CPT before a written job offer exists, authorizing for an elective rather than integral course, and failing to update SEVIS within 21 days of the start date. 
06 An attorney reviews the offer letter, the I-20 CPT page, and the course syllabus together to confirm the integral-curriculum requirement is documented. 
Last updated 2026-05-09 · Reviewed by Denise Platter Cabrera 
In 60 seconds
Primary authority: 8 CFR § 214.2(f)(10)(i) ; SEVP CPT policy guidance.
Core rule: CPT must be an integral part of an established curriculum and authorised by the DSO on the I-20 before any work begins.
Documents: signed I-20 with CPT page, employer offer letter, course syllabus tying the work to the curriculum.
Timing: CPT cannot start before the date on the I-20 and must end on or before the date on the I-20.
Main risk: 12 months or more of full-time CPT at the same education level disqualifies you from OPT entirely at that level.
Reviewed by Denise Platter Cabrera, Esq. (CA Bar #298948, Certified Specialist — Immigration & Nationality Law).
The rule in plain English
Curricular Practical Training is employment authorised by the DSO as an integral part of a degree program. The controlling source is 8 CFR § 214.2(f)(10)(i) . Unlike OPT, CPT does not require USCIS adjudication — the DSO authorises it directly on the Form I-20. That speed is the appeal; the cost is that almost all errors are made at school level and only become visible later.
The integral-curriculum requirement is the most important and most misunderstood element of CPT. For CPT to be valid, the practical training must be an integral part of an established curriculum — not merely beneficial or related to the field of study. This means the CPT must be tied to a specific course for which the student receives academic credit, or be a required component of the degree program (such as a mandatory internship for a hospitality management programme). Courses described as "elective," "optional," or "available" rather than "required" or "integral" create a weak CPT basis. A DSO who authorises CPT for a course that is only tangentially related to the program puts both the student and the school at regulatory risk under SEVP oversight.

The integral-curriculum test
CPT is authorized only when the practical training is an integral part of an established curriculum. The practical training must satisfy one of two conditions:
The student receives academic credit for the work.
The practical training is a required component of the program (an established practicum, internship requirement, or co-op that every student in the program must complete).
"It would be a good experience" is not a qualifying basis. The integral-curriculum tie must be documentable.

The DSO cannot authorize CPT without an offer letter that contains all of the following elements:
Job title — the specific role, not a generic description.

§ Key takeaways
01 Cap-gap extends both F-1 status and OPT employment authorization from the OPT end date to October 1, when the selected H-1B takes effect. 
02 Cap-gap applies only if the H-1B was cap-selected, a timely change-of-status petition was filed before OPT expired, and the petition is still pending or approved.

Cap-gap extends both F-1 status and OPT employment authorisation from the OPT end date to October 1, when the selected H-1B takes effect.
Applies only if: H-1B was cap-selected, a timely change-of-status petition was filed before OPT expired, and the petition is still pending or approved.

This includes students currently on their initial 12-month OPT period and students on the 24-month STEM OPT extension, as long as the H-1B petition with change of status was timely filed. The cap-gap extension bridges the gap between the end of OPT work authorization and the October 1 start date, ensuring continuous employment eligibility and F-1 status during this critical transition period.
If your H-1B petition was filed for consular processing instead of change of status, the cap-gap extension does not apply to you. Consular processing requires you to leave the US, obtain the H-1B visa at a US consulate abroad, and re-enter after October 1. This page covers the change-of-status scenario only. If you are unsure whether your petition was filed as change of status or consular processing, check the I-129 petition form or ask your employer's immigration attorney before making any travel or employment plans.

§ Key takeaways
01 Eight core documents in officer-review order: passport, DS-160 confirmation page, appointment confirmation, photo, Form I-20 (signed §11), I-901 SEVIS fee receipt, financial proof, and academic credentials. 
02 Financial proof must include a sponsor letter dated within the last 30 days and bank statements in the sponsor's name showing average balance — a sudden large deposit days before the application is a recognized refusal pattern. 
03 If funding is shared across multiple sources, document each one separately; officers refuse on 'funds insufficient' when one component is undocumented, even if the total is adequate. 
04 In the first 60 seconds the officer cross-checks DS-160 against I-20, confirms SEVIS fee paid, and reads the financial proof to verify the funded amount equals or exceeds the I-20 cost-of-attendance. 
05 Both §11 (student signature) and §3 (DSO signature) must be present on the I-20; an unsigned I-20 is a common mistake.

Last updated 2026-06-09 · Reviewed by Denise Platter Cabrera 
F-1 document checklist at a glance
Eight core documents, in the order a consular officer reviews them: passport, DS-160, appointment confirmation, photo, Form I-20 (signed §11), I-901 SEVIS fee receipt, financial proof, academic credentials.
Financial proof is the most frequently weak item: sponsor letter dated within 30 days + bank statements in the sponsor's name showing average balance, not a single peak deposit.
DS-160 and I-20 must agree on every fact: school name, program, dates, funding number. A single typo can trigger a 221(g) administrative return.
If you were previously refused, the same document set is not sufficient — you must add new material evidence that addresses the refusal ground.
This page is part of the F-1 visa rights: the international student's complete guide cluster. It exists to answer the document-assembly decision only; for interview strategy, read the F-1 visa interview prep checklist .
Why document order matters
Consular officers at most posts process 80 to 120 interviews per day. The officer has approximately two to three minutes per applicant in a non-immigrant visa interview. Within the first 60 seconds, the officer has already formed a preliminary impression based on three rapid cross-checks: the DS-160 against the I-20, the SEVIS fee status, and the financial summary. If all three align, the remaining two minutes are routine. If any one fails, the entire interview pivots to the failed item.
Presenting your documents in the order an officer expects them reduces cognitive friction. The officer should not have to ask twice for the same document. § Key takeaways
01 The SEVIS release date is the date the current school releases the record to the receiving school; after that date, only the new school can edit the record. 
02 Do not set the SEVIS release date until final admission is received, funding is confirmed, and the start date is confirmed with a transfer-pending I-20 ready to issue. 
03 After release, the student must enrol full-time at the next available term; failure to enrol terminates the SEVIS record.

§ Key takeaways
01 Five common violation patterns: dropping below full course load without DSO authorization; unauthorized employment; failing to extend the I-20 before program end; failing to transfer SEVIS within 15 days; and criminal conviction triggering visa revocation. 
02 Reinstatement on Form I-539 is generally available only within five months of the violation and requires showing the violation was beyond the student's control or due to a school error. 
03 Travel-and-re-entry on a new I-20 restarts the clock on OPT and CPT eligibility, but departure before filing reinstatement removes the I-539 option. 
04 For F-1 students admitted for 'duration of status' (D/S), unlawful presence usually starts only after USCIS or an immigration judge formally finds a violation. 
05 Reinstatement decisions currently average four to eight months, and premium processing is not available for I-539. 
06 The visa stamp is not automatically cancelled by SEVIS termination, but it cannot be used for re-entry while the termination is in place. 
Last updated 2026-05-09 · Reviewed by Denise Platter Cabrera 
In 60 seconds
Primary authority: 8 CFR § 214.1(g) and (h) ; 8 CFR § 214.2(f) ; SEVP reinstatement policy guidance.
Core rule: F-1 status is maintained by full-course-load enrolment, work only as authorised, and timely transfers/extensions. Any of these can be broken.
Documents: Form I-20, I-94, SEVIS record, transcripts, prior I-797s, any termination notice, employer letters.
Timing: reinstatement under Form I-539 is generally available only within five months of the violation. Beyond that, departure and re-entry on a new I-20 may be the only route.
Main risk: continuing to work or attend on a terminated SEVIS record. Each day is a separate violation and accrues unlawful presence.
Reviewed by Denise Platter Cabrera, Esq. (CA Bar #298948, Certified Specialist — Immigration & Nationality Law).
The rule in plain English
F-1 status is conditional. To maintain it you must enrol in a full course of study, work only as authorised by your DSO or USCIS, transfer to a new school under the proper procedure, and apply for any extension before your program end date. The controlling sources are 8 CFR § 214.1(g) and (h) and 8 CFR § 214.2(f) .
A violation does not automatically lead to deportation. It does end work authorisation immediately, may end SEVIS enrolment, and starts the clock on potential unlawful presence. Unlawful presence for F-1 students admitted for Duration of Status (D/S) typically starts only after USCIS or an immigration judge formally finds a violation — it does not begin automatically when a status violation occurs. However, once SEVIS is terminated and the violation is recorded, USCIS may back-date the unlawful presence finding. Accruing more than 180 days of unlawful presence triggers a 3-year bar on re-entering the US under INA 212(a)(9)(B)(i)(I); more than 365 days triggers a 10-year bar. Do not depart the US without understanding your unlawful presence exposure

This FAQ is for F-1 students preparing for OPT or STEM OPT, navigating CPT limits, managing SEVIS compliance, or dealing with a status violation. The questions reflect the most common situations we see from international students in USCIS forums and from our document review clients. Each answer has been reviewed by Denise Platter Cabrera, a licensed California attorney (CA Bar #298948), and is grounded in the Immigration and Nationality Act, 8 CFR regulations, SEVP policy guidance, and current USCIS adjudication practices as of mid-2026.
F-1 regulations around STEM OPT employer monitoring, CPT accumulation, and unemployment caps remain areas of frequent confusion and compliance failure. The 2026 policy landscape includes continued USCIS scrutiny of staffing-agency STEM OPT placements, evolving E-Verify requirements, and strict enforcement of the 90-day and 150-day unemployment limits — areas where adjudication standards have tightened measurably since 2024. The answers below reflect the current published rules and guidance.
The question list below covers the most urgent student-visa compliance topics. For deeper guidance on each subject, the linked articles at the bottom of this page give full step-by-step instructions, form references, and the specific regulatory citations that govern each area.
OPT and STEM OPT compliance requirements have received increased enforcement attention from USCIS in the 2024-2026 period, particularly around worksite verification, employer-employee relationship requirements for staffing agency placements, and electronic I-983 signature validity. The 90-day unemployment cap for post-completion OPT and the 150-day aggregate cap for STEM OPT remain areas where students unintentionally fall out of status by underestimating gaps between jobs or failing to report qualifying employment promptly through their DSO or the SEVP Portal.
CPT accumulation continues to be a frequent source of post-completion OPT ineligibility. The 12-month full-time CPT threshold under 8 CFR § 214.2(f)(10)(i) eliminates OPT eligibility permanently, not just for the current degree level. Students who have used part-time CPT do not accumulate time toward the 12-month limit, but any week in which more than 20 hours of CPT are authorized counts as a full-time week. DSOs are not required to proactively warn students that they are approaching the 12-month limit, making self-tracking the only reliable safeguard.

Optional Practical Training is a benefit, not an entitlement. To receive an Employment Authorization Document, an F-1 student must have a Designated School Official recommend OPT in SEVIS, receive an I-20 endorsed with that recommendation, and file Form I-765 with USCIS within a window tied to the program end date. Missing any link in that chain is the most common reason applications fail.

What Form I-589 Does and Who Qualifies for Asylum
Form I-589, officially the Application for Asylum and for Withholding of Removal , is how you ask the U.S. government for protection.
An asylum officer or immigration judge decides each asylum application on its own facts. No filing step guarantees a grant.
Asylum eligibility rests on two questions.
First, were you persecuted in the past, or do you fear persecution in the future, on account of race, religion, nationality, political opinion, or membership in a particular social group?

The law calls the standard a "well-founded fear." In practice, you must show the harm is more than harassment. Persecution means serious harm, such as threats to your life or freedom, torture, or sustained violence that your government cannot or will not control.

01 Primary authority: State landlord-tenant statutes on subletting and assignment, local housing court guidance, HUD fair housing resources, and university housing office sublet policies 
02 Core rule: Subletting does not release you from the original lease — you remain liable for rent and damages even if the subtenant defaults on payments or causes damage. 
03 Documents: Original lease, written sublet agreement, landlord consent correspondence, subtenant screening documents, and move-in condition photos. 
04 Timing: Request landlord consent in writing before the sublet begins; some states require landlords to respond within a reasonable timeframe (typically 7 to 14 days).

In 60 seconds
Most leases require landlord consent before subletting.
Subletting without permission can breach your lease.
You remain liable for rent and damage even after subletting.
A written sublet agreement protects you from common disputes.
State rules on subletting vary — check your state statute.
When your lease allows subletting
Most residential leases in the US address subletting in one of three ways: they prohibit it entirely, they allow it with the landlord's written consent, or they say nothing at all. The rule that applies depends on your lease and your state law.
If your lease prohibits subletting, doing it anyway is a lease violation that can lead to eviction. Even if the landlord has allowed informal sublets in the past, the written lease controls your legal obligations. If your lease allows it with consent, you must request permission in writing and wait for the landlord's response. Some states require landlords to be reasonable when withholding consent — California, New York, and Massachusetts are among the states that impose a reasonableness standard, meaning a landlord cannot arbitrarily block a qualified subtenant.
If your lease is silent on subletting, state law controls. Some states give tenants a right to sublet unless the lease explicitly prohibits it. Others default to requiring landlord consent. Check your state landlord-tenant statute before proceeding, and request any required consent in writing so you have a record of the landlord's decision. If you live in a rent-controlled or rent-stabilized unit in cities like New York, San Francisco, or Los Angeles, local rent ordinances may provide additional subletting protections that override your lease language — including a statutory right to sublet as long as the tenant continues to occupy the unit as their primary residence.

TN visa: the rule in plain English
TN classification permits qualified Canadian and Mexican citizens to work temporarily in the United States in listed USMCA professional occupations. The classification falls under the nonimmigrant category — it requires the applicant to demonstrate nonimmigrant intent (a temporary stay with a foreign residence) unless an exemption applies. The list of eligible professions includes accountants, engineers, computer systems analysts, scientists, and approximately 55 other occupational categories, each with specific educational and credential requirements.
The TN process differs significantly by nationality. Canadian citizens can apply for TN status at a U.S. port of entry (land border or pre-flight inspection) without filing a petition with USCIS first. They need only the employer support letter, proof of citizenship, and evidence of qualifications at the time of admission. Mexican citizens, by contrast, must obtain a TN visa from a U.S. consulate before traveling to the United States. The consular process requires a Form DS-160, an interview at the consulate, and a visa stamp in the passport before the applicant can seek admission at a port of entry. Canadians cannot obtain a TN visa at a consulate — they must apply at the border or pre-flight.

How TPS renewals work in 2026
Temporary Protected Status under INA 244 allows nationals of designated countries to remain in the US when conditions in their home country make safe return impossible. Designations are based on armed conflict, environmental disasters, or extraordinary conditions. TPS is not a path to permanent residence.
Approximately 16 countries maintain active TPS designations in 2026. Each requires filing Form I-821 and Form I-765 during specific re-registration periods announced in Federal Register notices. Check the USCIS country-specific page before filing.
Understanding TPS re-registration requirements
Temporary Protected Status re-registration requires submitting Form I-821, Application for Temporary Protected Status, during the designated re-registration period for the applicant's country. The re-registration period is announced in a Federal Register notice published by the Department of Homeland Security. The notice specifies the exact start and end dates of the re-registration period, the fee amounts required, the edition of Form I-821 to use, and the filing address based on the applicant's location. Re-registration periods are typically open for 60 to 180 days, and filing outside this window without good cause results in loss of TPS.

Most F-1 and M-1 applicants ages 14 to 79 must appear in person at a US embassy or consulate for the interview.

Rehearse short, factual answers about your program, funding, and ties to your home country to address Section 214(b).
Verify the current rules on travel.state.gov and studyinthestates.dhs.gov before you file, because requirements change.
Rehearsing answers for the 214(b) tie test
Consular officers deny most F-1 cases under Section 214(b) of the Immigration and Nationality Act, which requires you to prove you intend to return home after your studies.
Your document folder alone will not carry the interview; your spoken answers must reinforce the same story.
Practice aloud until your responses sound natural, not memorised.
Start with the three questions almost every officer asks: why this school, why this programme, and what you plan to do after graduation.
Tie each answer to concrete evidence. If you studied computer science as an undergraduate, explain how the US master's curriculum fills a specific gap.
When asked about post-graduation plans, name a role, an employer type, or an industry that exists in your home country, not a vague "maybe a job."
Prepare two or three examples of family, property, or employment ties.
A letter from a parent's employer, a property deed, or a return job offer carries weight when you mention it naturally.
Do not volunteer documents the officer did not request; keep them organised in labelled tabs so you can produce them in seconds.
Finish each answer in under one minute. Officers interview dozens of applicants daily, and rambling responses read as evasive.
If you do not understand a question, ask the officer to repeat it. A calm pause beats a rushed guess.
F-2 dependents: documents and interview notes
Spouses and unmarried children under 21 accompany F-1 students on F-2 visas, and their interviews follow a separate track.
The primary student must already hold a valid F-1 visa or be applying simultaneously.
Each F-2 applicant needs their own DS-160 confirmation, passport, and visa fee receipt, plus a marriage certificate for a spouse or a birth certificate for a child.
Financial evidence matters more for F-2 cases because the officer must see funds covering the dependent's living costs, not just tuition.
Bring bank statements showing available balance for at least one academic year, and if the student has an assistantship or scholarship, include the award letter.
The I-20 for an F-2 dependent is issued by the same school and lists the student's SEVIS ID; verify the name and date of birth match the passport exactly.

US work visas guide
US work visas fall into three broad groups: temporary employment visas (H-1B, L-1, TN, O-1A, E-2), employment-based green cards (EB-1A, EB-2 NIW), and the cap-gap bridge for students transitioning from OPT to H-1B. The right visa depends on your qualifications, employer type, nationality, and whether you seek temporary status or permanent residence. This guide orients you to the cluster, explains the key thresholds and risks — including the H-1B lottery, portability rules, and the Dhanasar framework — and routes you to the article that matches your situation. Every guide in this cluster is attorney-reviewed.
Quick answers live on the work visas FAQ . F-1 students bridging to H-1B should use the cap-gap guide and the F-1 / OPT hub . Confirm lottery, wage, and form rules on uscis.gov before your employer files.
Last updated 2026-05-19 · Reviewed by Denise Platter Cabrera 
The 5 most important things to know
H-1B lottery selection is not approval. Selection only permits the employer to file Form I-129. The petition must still prove specialty occupation, wage, and maintenance of status. See USCIS H-1B guidance.
H-1B portability under INA § 214(n) may allow starting work for a new employer upon USCIS receipt of a non-frivolous petition, but travel and paystub gaps create significant risk. Many attorneys advise waiting for the receipt notice before starting.
The EB-1A extraordinary ability classification is self-petitioning — no job offer or PERM required — but the standard is high. You must show sustained national or international acclaim and membership in the small percentage at the very top of your field.
The EB-2 National Interest Waiver requires proving substantial merit, national importance, and that you are well positioned to advance the proposed endeavor under the Dhanasar framework. Personal career benefit alone is insufficient.
Canadians and Mexicans apply for TN visas differently. Canadians often use port-of-entry or preflight inspection without a prior visa; Mexicans generally need a consular visa first. The TN is not a dual-intent visa, and pursuing a green card while in TN status can create complications.
Choose your path
Pick the guide that matches your current situation. If you are a professional with a US job offer, start with the H-1B or L-1 guide. If you have extraordinary ability or a nationally important endeavor, the EB-1A or EB-2 NIW guides explain the self-petition process. If you are Canadian or Mexican, the TN guide covers the USMCA professional route. F-1 students on OPT should review the STEM OPT and NIW paths to understand the bridge from student status to permanent residence.

Is H-1B lottery selection the same as visa approval?
No. Lottery selection means your employer is permitted to file a Form I-129 petition on your behalf. It does not mean USCIS will approve the petition or that you will receive an H-1B visa. After selection, the employer must prove three things: that the job qualifies as a specialty occupation, that you meet the educational or experiential requirements for that occupation, and that the employer will pay the required wage. USCIS may issue a Request for Evidence (RFE) or deny the petition if any of these elements is not adequately documented. Selection is only the first step in a multi-stage process that includes petition review, possible RFE response, and, if abroad, consular visa issuance.

What the fee increase means in 2026
A visa fee increase is a government charge change, not a university discount and not a processing-speed upgrade. Study Australia reports that the Student visa application charge (VAC) moved from AUD $2,000 to AUD $2,500 from 1 July 2026 for most applicants. Temporary Graduate (subclass 485) charges also rose in the same cycle — keep that product separate when you budget a student lodgement.
Headlines from the 2025 fee cycle can be stale. Always re-read the live Home Affairs listing on the morning you submit. Paying sooner does not buy a faster decision. Fee line: Primary applicant plus any dependants listed on the form.

Buffer line: Health exam, biometrics, and currency conversion.

Banking in Canada for International Students: Accounts, Credit & SIN (2026) | YouSafe 
Skip to main content Step 1: Get your Social Insurance Number first
A Social Insurance Number (SIN) is a 9-digit number issued by Service Canada. You need it before a bank can open an interest-bearing account or before any employer can pay you. Apply in person at a Service Canada Centre — bring your study permit, passport, and proof of enrolment. The SIN is issued on the spot and is free. You can also apply online or by mail, but in-person is fastest. Once you have the SIN, provide it to your bank when opening your account so that interest earned is properly reported to the CRA. Without a SIN on file, your bank may withhold tax on interest at the highest marginal rate.
Your SIN is confidential. Do not carry the card (Service Canada no longer issues plastic cards — you receive a paper confirmation). Store the number securely and provide it only to employers, financial institutions, and government agencies that have a lawful reason to request it. Do not provide your SIN to landlords, phone companies, or as general identification — they do not need it.
Step 2: Choose a student bank account
All five major Canadian banks — RBC, TD, Scotiabank, BMO, and CIBC — offer student accounts with no monthly fees. Most also offer a sign-up bonus (typically $50–$100) for new student accounts. You will need your passport, study permit, and proof of enrolment to open the account. The bank will ask for your Canadian address and phone number — a temporary address is fine, but update it when you move.
Student accounts typically include unlimited debit transactions and Interac e-Transfers, which is how most Canadians pay rent and split bills.
International student accounts at Scotiabank and RBC are specifically marketed to newcomers — Scotiabank's StartRight programme and RBC's Newcomer Advantage offer additional perks such as no-fee international money transfers for the first year and a dedicated newcomer advisor.
Online-only banks such as Tangerine and Simplii also offer no-fee accounts but may require a Canadian credit history to open — they are better as a second account after you have established a relationship with a major bank.
Step 3: Start building Canadian credit history
Canadian credit history does not transfer from your home country. You start from zero, and building credit takes time. The fastest way to start is a secured credit card: you deposit $500–$1,000 with the bank as collateral, and the bank issues a credit card with a limit equal to your deposit. After 6–12 months of on-time payments, you can apply for an unsecured card and the deposit is returned. Use the card for one small recurring purchase each month (a phone bill or a streaming subscription), pay the balance in full by the due date, and never use more than 30% of the credit limit. This pattern builds a positive payment history that Equifax and TransUnion report to lenders.
Avoid applying for multiple credit cards in your first year — each application triggers a hard credit inquiry, and multiple inquiries in a short period signal risk to lenders. If your first application is declined, wait 6 mo

F-1 Port of Entry: What Actually Happens at US Airport Immigration (2026) | YouSafe 
Skip to main content The document packet: what to hand the officer
Carry these in your carry-on bag, not checked luggage. You will need them at primary inspection:
Valid passport with F-1 visa foil — must be valid for at least six months beyond your intended stay
Form I-20 signed by you and your DSO — check that the program start date has not passed
SEVIS fee receipt (Form I-901) — print a copy even though the payment is electronic
Financial documents — the same bank statements or sponsorship letters you used for the visa interview
Admission letter from your US school — not required by regulation but often requested
Do not hand over your phone or unlock it unless the officer directs you to. You are not required to provide social media passwords. The officer may ask to see your return ticket or onward travel — having a printout of your itinerary is helpful but not required.
Primary inspection: what the officer asks
The officer will scan your passport, review your I-20, and ask a small set of standard questions. Answer directly — do not volunteer extra information:
"What is the purpose of your visit?" — "I am here to study. I will be attending [school name] for [degree program]."
"Where will you be staying?" — Provide the address. If temporary housing, say so: "I will stay at [address] for the first week and then move to campus housing."
"How are you funding your studies?" — Name the funding source. If family, say "My parents are funding my studies." Do not describe part-time work plans — F-1 students cannot work off-campus in the first academic year.
"Do you intend to return to your home country after your studies?" — Answer honestly. "I plan to complete my degree and then evaluate my options." The officer is testing nonimmigrant intent, not extracting a promise.
The 30-day rule: you may enter the US up to 30 days before the program start date on your I-20. If your flight arrives earlier, CBP may deny entry or admit you as a visitor (B-2), which is incompatible with F-1 study.
Secondary inspection: what it is and what it is not
If the primary officer refers you to secondary inspection, it does not mean your entry will be denied. Secondary is a more detailed review conducted in a separate area. The officer may verify your SEVIS record, call your DSO, review your financial documents in detail, or ask additional questions about your study plans. The process can take 30 minutes to several hours depending on the port and the volume of referrals. You may not use your phone in secondary unless the officer permits it.
Common triggers for secondary: your SEVIS record shows a status other than "Active," the program start date on your I-20 is within a few days (raising concern about timely arrival), your name matches a watchlist entry (often a false positive), or the primary officer noticed a discrepancy between your stated plans and your documents.

The common bridge is employer-sponsored employment-based preference (often EB-2 or EB-3) after H-1B or another nonimmigrant status, or family-based sponsorship when a qualifying relative is a U.S. citizen or permanent resident. Immigrant Spouse Programs: CR-1, IR-1, K-1 | YouSafe 
Skip to main content Back to Blog There is no single "immigrant spouse program" in U.S. immigration; couples usually need to choose between a spouse immigrant visa, a K-1 fiancé(e) route, adjustment of status, or consular processing. The safe choice depends on marriage status, petitioner status, where the foreign partner is located, financial sponsorship, and any immigration-history risks. 
The short answer
"Immigrant spouse programs" is a practical search phrase, not one single official program. Married couples usually look at CR-1/IR-1 , adjustment of status, or consular processing. Engaged couples may look at K-1 if the petitioner is a U.S. citizen. Route choice depends on location, status, petitioner category, financial support, and immigration history. The Travel.State.Gov Family Immigration page explains that U.S. citizens can petition for a spouse, while lawful permanent residents can also petition for a spouse but face different visa availability rules. 
The main spouse and fiancé(e) routes
U.S. family-based immigration has two broad categories. Immediate relative visas are for close family relationships with a U.S. citizen: spouse, unmarried child under 21, or parent. The number of immediate relative visas is not limited each fiscal year. Family preference visas are for more distant relationships and for spouses of lawful permanent residents. These categories have annual numerical limits, which means waiting periods may apply. 
A U.S. citizen can file an immigrant visa petition for a spouse through Form I-130 , Petition for Alien Relative. A lawful permanent resident can also file Form I-130 for a spouse, but the spouse falls into the family preference category, not the immediate relative category. This distinction affects visa availability and potential waiting time. 
The K-1 fiancé(e) visa is available only to a foreign-citizen fiancé(e) of a U.S. citizen. A lawful permanent resident cannot file a K-1 petition. The K-1 route requires the couple to marry within 90 days of the foreign partner's arrival in the United States, after which the foreign spouse must file for adjustment of status. 
Adjustment of status is the process of applying for lawful permanent residence from inside the United States, typically using Form I-485 . Consular processing is the route through the State Department and the National Visa Center, with the final interview at a U.S. embassy or consulate abroad. The choice between these routes depends on lawful entry, current status, petitioner type, and other factors. 
Because adjustment eligibility is fact-specific, couples should verify USCIS instructions before assuming that in-country filing is available. 
CR-1 and IR-1 spouse immigrant visas
The CR-1 and IR-1 are spouse immigrant visas for legally married spouses of U.S. citizens. The process generally starts with Form I-130 , Petition for Alien Relative, filed by the U.S. citizen petitioner. After USCIS approves the petition, the case moves to the National Visa Center for document collection and fee processing, and then to the U.S. embassy or consulate where the beneficiary lives for the visa intervie

BridgeUSA Summer Work Travel is a U.S. Department of State exchange program that lets eligible full-time post-secondary students work in seasonal or temporary U.S. jobs for up to four months during their summer break. A safe file needs a designated sponsor , DS-2019 , DS-160 , passport, photo, interview plan, vetted job, and clear housing and transportation details. Who the J-1 Summer Work Travel program is for
The program is for students who meet 22 CFR 62.32 : full-time enrollment in an accredited, classroom-based, post-secondary institution outside the United States, active pursuit of a degree or full-time course of study, and at least one completed semester or equivalent before applying. Final-year students can qualify if they meet those requirements at application. 
Sponsors must also verify conversational English and reading comprehension through recognized language tests or documented interviews, and select students who intend to participate in the cultural part of the program, not only the work component. 
The program runs during your summer vacation or long academic break, lasts up to four months, and cannot be extended. You must return home before classes resume, though participants can be admitted more than once if otherwise eligible. 
If you are from a Visa Waiver Program country, you may participate without a pre-placed job, but you still need sufficient financial resources and pre-departure job-search guidance from your sponsor. Students from non-Visa Waiver countries must have pre-arranged, fully-vetted employment before the sponsor issues the DS-2019.

7 OPT Application Mistakes International Students Make (2026) | YouSafe 
Skip to main content 1. Filing too early or too late
USCIS must receive your I-765 no earlier than 90 days before your program end date, and no later than 60 days after your DSO enters the OPT recommendation into SEVIS. The 90-day window is measured from the program end date on your I-20 (not your graduation ceremony date). Filing even one day before the 90-day window results in denial. Filing after the 60-day post-recommendation window also results in denial. Set a calendar reminder and track the exact date your DSO made the SEVIS entry — the 60-day clock starts from that date, not the date you signed the I-20. If you are approaching the deadline and something is missing, file with what you have rather than missing the window entirely. USCIS may issue an RFE for the missing item, which gives you time to respond, whereas a late filing is a hard denial with no RFE option.
2. I-20 not updated with OPT recommendation
Your I-20 must show the OPT recommendation on page 2, with your DSO's signature and the date the recommendation was entered in SEVIS. Submitting the I-20 you used for your last visa renewal — without the OPT recommendation — results in denial. Request a new I-20 from your DSO specifically for the OPT application. Verify page 2 shows "OPT Requested" or "OPT Pending" and the recommendation date. If the I-20 is signed more than 30 days before USCIS receives your application, it is considered stale — get a fresh signature from your DSO.
3. Photo that does not meet USCIS specifications
USCIS photo requirements are specific and enforced by automated scanning. The photo must be 2x2 inches, taken within 30 days of filing, on a plain white or off-white background, with a full frontal view of your face, no glasses, no head covering (unless religious), and no shadows. A photo taken at a drugstore passport booth is usually compliant, but a cropped selfie or a scan of your passport photo from two years ago will be rejected. The rejection is typically a "rejection notice" rather than a denial, meaning you can refile — but the clock resets and your EAD processing starts over. The USCIS photo tool on their website can check compliance before you print.
4. Wrong edition of Form I-765
USCIS periodically updates Form I-765. Using an expired edition results in rejection. Before you print, check the USCIS website for the current form edition date in the bottom-left corner of the form. Download a fresh copy on the day you prepare your packet — do not rely on a PDF you saved months ago. This is the single most common USCIS lockbox rejection and is entirely preventable.
5. Address errors and missed mail
Your I-765 asks for both a physical address and a mailing address. If your mailing address is your current apartment but your lease ends before your EAD is likely to be approved, the card will be returned to USCIS as undeliverable. Use a stable mailing address — a trusted friend's address, your DSO's office (with permission), or a private mailbox — that will be valid for at least 6 months after filing. OPT to H-1B Transition 2026: Cap-Gap Timing for F-1 Students | YouSafe 
Skip to main content Back to Blog The OPT to H-1B transition 2026 is not secured by selection alone; for F-1 students on OPT, the real risk is the gap between employment authorization expiry, the employer's petition filing date, and the October 1 H-1B start date. The cap-gap extension can bridge that interval, but only if the petition is filed at the right time, in the right status, and with the right change-of-status request. 
The FY 2027 cap calendar
The timeline for the fiscal year 2027 H-1B cap is now fixed. The initial registration period opened at noon Eastern on March 4, 2026, and closed at 5:00 p.m. Eastern on March 19, 2026. USCIS completed the selection process on March 31, 2026, and notified registrants through their online accounts. Petition filing began on April 1, 2026, and runs through June 30, 2026, a 90-day window. All FY 2027 cap-subject petitions must use the February 27, 2026 edition of Form I-129. 
Do not treat selection as the finish line. A selected registration only gives the employer permission to file an H-1B cap-subject petition during the filing window; the student still needs the petition filed as a change of status at the right time for cap-gap protection to do useful work. 
The cap-gap rule
The cap-gap extension is an automatic regulatory bridge under 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(vi) . If an employer files a timely, non-frivolous cap-subject H-1B petition requesting a change of status while the student is still in valid F-1 status including during post-completion OPT, STEM OPT, or the 60-day grace period the student's F-1 status is automatically extended. If the student has unexpired OPT or STEM OPT employment authorization at the time USCIS receives the petition, both status and work authorization are extended until April 1 of the fiscal year for which H-1B status is requested, or until the validity start date of the approved petition, whichever is earlier. This extension replaced the former September 30 endpoint under a DHS final rule effective January 17, 2025 . The extension terminates automatically if the H-1B petition is rejected, denied, revoked, withdrawn, or if the change of status request itself is denied. 
Four edge cases that break the bridge
Pending STEM OPT extension at H-1B selection
A student whose initial 12-month OPT is expiring but who has a timely-filed STEM OPT extension application pending with USCIS may continue working for up to 180 days while the application is pending. If the student is selected in the H-1B lottery during this 180-day window, the employer must file the cap-subject petition before the original OPT EAD expires to secure a clean cap-gap extension of work authorization. If the employer files after the original EAD expires but while the STEM OPT application is still pending, the cap-gap may still apply for F-1 status but the work authorization piece becomes precarious. The student should coordinate closely with their designated school official to ensure the SEVIS record reflects both the pending STEM extension and the pending H-1B petition. Skip to main content Back to Blog Section 21 has been abolished, but Ground 4A means some student landlords still have a route to recover possession at the end of an academic cycle. The key question is not whether the landlord says "student tenancy"; it is whether the property, notice, timing, and statutory ground actually fit. 
The short answer
From 1 May 2026, Section 21 no-fault eviction has been abolished for new notices in England. Most private student house-share tenants now have assured periodic tenancies with no fixed end date. Ground 4A creates a possession route for certain student HMO landlords, but only where the property, student status, advance-notice, timing, and notice conditions fit. The landlord still needs the correct notice and county court process ; a text message saying "you need to leave in June" is not enough. 
What changed on 1 May 2026
The Renters' Rights Act 2025 changed private renting in England. Three changes matter most for students in private house shares. 
Section 21 is gone. Landlords can no longer issue no-fault eviction notices. Every eviction now requires a valid possession ground and a Section 8 notice. 
Fixed-term tenancies are banned for most private renting. Existing assured shorthold tenancies converted to assured periodic tenancies on 1 May 2026. New tenancies must be periodic from the outset, with no fixed end date, and continue until the tenant ends them, the landlord regains possession, or both parties agree to end. 
Private student tenants renting from private landlords are likely to have assured periodic tenancies. This applies to most student house shares and HMOs let by private landlords. Purpose-built student accommodation (PBSA) and university halls operate under different rules, so Ground 4A may not apply. 
Do not assume that all student tenancies became APTs. Tenancy type depends on ownership, management, and the statutory student-accommodation rules. 
Ground 4A in plain English
Ground 4A is a mandatory possession ground introduced by the Renters' Rights Act 2025 and explained in the GOV.UK grounds for possession guidance . It allows landlords of certain student HMOs to seek possession so they can re-let the property to a new cohort of students at the start of the academic year. The Renters' Rights Act 2025 enacted text is the primary legislation source, but tenants should use GOV.UK guidance and advice to check how the ground is being applied in practice. Because it is a mandatory ground, the county court is required to order possession if the conditions are satisfied and the proper procedure has been followed. 
The ground applies only to houses in multiple occupation. An HMO is a property occupied by at least three tenants forming more than one household who share toilet, bathroom, or kitchen facilities. A typical four-bedroom student house share is usually an HMO; a self-contained studio is not.
